To the faithful Christians, greetings and apostolic blessing. Just as the Jews should not be granted the license to presume in their synagogues beyond what is permitted by law, so too should they not suffer any prejudice in matters granted to them. Therefore, although they prefer to persist in their obstinacy rather than recognize the words of the prophets and the mysteries of the Holy Scriptures and come to the knowledge of Christian faith and salvation, since they seek our protection and the help and compassion of Christian mercy, we, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Calixtus, Eugenius, Alexander, Clement, Celestine, Innocent, and Honorius, Roman Pontiffs, admit their petition and grant them the shield of our protection. We also decree that no Christian shall compel them to come to baptism unwillingly or forcibly, but if any of them voluntarily takes refuge among Christians for the sake of faith, once their intention has been revealed, they shall become Christian without any dispute; for it is not believed that anyone holds true faith in Christianity if they are known to have come to the baptism of Christians unwillingly. Furthermore, no Christian shall presume to wound or kill their persons without the judgment of the land's authority, or take their money or alter the good customs they have hitherto had in the region they inhabit. Moreover, in the celebration of their festivals, no one shall disturb them with clubs or stones, nor shall anyone demand from them forced services, except those they have been accustomed to performing in past times. Additionally, countering the depravity and avarice of wicked men, we decree that no one shall dare to mutilate or diminish the Jewish cemetery, or exhume buried bodies under the pretense of obtaining money. If anyone, having known the tenor of this decree, rashly attempts to contravene it, which we hope will not happen, they shall suffer the peril of losing their honor and office or be punished with excommunication, unless they correct their presumption with worthy satisfaction. However, we wish only those who have presumed nothing against the subversion of Christian faith to be fortified by the protection of this defense. Given at Perugia, by the hand of Brother Joseph, of the Florense Order, notary of Lord Pope Gregory IX, on the 3rd day before the Nones of May, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord's Incarnation 1235, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the same Lord Pope Gregory IX.

To the archbishop, cantor of the Corinthians, and the archdeacon of Thebes.

The petition presented to us by our beloved sons, the prior and convent of the monastery of Daphne, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Athens, has shown that, although a case between them, on one side, and Albert Bokaron, knight, in the diocese of Negroponte, the guardian of the daughters of the late Bocfaron, his brother, on their behalf, on the other side, regarding their farmstead of Lichonia and its appurtenances, which the said knight unjustly held, had been entrusted by legates of the Apostolic See to diverse judges, and could not be concluded by them for quite some time, we gave letters of mandate to our venerable brother, then-elect archbishop of Corinth, and his colleagues, to have the letters obtained on either side and the processes held through them exhibited to them, and to approve those they deemed worthy of approval, rejecting the rest, and to conclude the case with a canonical decision.

And although the opposing party had been summoned to the judgment by the authority of the said letters, yet because of the frequent outbreaks of war and the devastation of the city of Thebes, often ravaged by the Greeks, the processes held were accidentally lost, and the seal fell from the said letters, no process was made by the same letters.

And when we later directed our letters to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Thebes, and his co-judges, that they should lawfully restore to the right and property of the said monastery whatever had been unlawfully alienated or sold from the same monastery’s goods, suppressing all opposition, and the said Albert, when summoned about the aforementioned farmstead, argued that such letters were invalid, as they did not mention the prior ones, the said judges, after a long discussion, declaring that they should not proceed based on the same letters, suspended the business; and thus they have so far obtained no benefit from so many labors and expenses. Concerning the fruits received from the said farmstead, determine what is just, setting aside any appeal. Witnesses, moreover. Moreover, the said citizens and certain others, who were placed under the ban of Blessed Remigius, without his assent, fortifying the said city against the aforesaid archbishop, and raising walls above its ditches around it, took for the material of their fortifications the pavements of the public roads, the tombs of cemeteries, and stones designated for the construction of the Major Church; and, having destroyed certain houses of the archbishop, which are called halls in the local language, they inflicted so many damages and such grievous injuries on him and his church that it would not only be long but also tedious to recount them all individually. And if even then they do not care to return with ready mind to the mandate of the archbishop, you shall have their revenues and debts and other goods, wherever they may be found, detained, as long as they persist in excommunication, notwithstanding any oath or pledge of faith, if perchance debtors are bound for paying their debts, and, if necessary, summon the aid of the secular arm to repress their stubbornness; contradictors. To the masters and brothers of the military orders of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem. Perhaps it seemed little to you that almost throughout the entire Christian world many accuse you, who often suspect evil even of good deeds, unless in these days you bring into action what may justifiably cause scandal against you. Behold, we have heard and received with sadness the grievous news that you, the appointed guardians of the Holy Land, which is the cord of the Lord's inheritance, seem to be striving to destroy it. For, on a slight pretext of certain mills, over which a controversy arose between you and was said to have been settled by our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Ravenna, a legate of the Apostolic See, you have turned your weapons against each other, inflamed by the spirit of anger and the fervor of indignation. You, who have taken up the cross after Christ, have vowed to lay down your lives for your brothers and the defense of the said land; this appears to be nothing other than exposing the remaining relics of the said land to the pagans and greatly scandalizing the entire Christian people, whose deficiency in the protection of the aforementioned land was hoped to be supplemented by your diligence. When we recollect how this holy institution was fitting and worthy, pleasing to God, in your predecessors for the Eastern Church, we are compelled to be more deeply amazed and gravely disturbed, forced to believe by many that your principal aim is that your territories be expanded in the lands of the faithful, whose intent should be to rescue from the hands of the infidels the land consecrated by Christ's blood. Indeed, this is not the alteration of the right hand of the Most High, but rather a turning of the right hand to the left, because when you decided to serve God by leaving the secular world, you again entangle yourselves in worldly affairs. Perhaps you have taken the occasion from the fact that, at your supplication, the Apostolic See sometimes allowed you to defend your camps against Christians too, if necessity demanded, with moderation for blameless protection, not considering that privilege deserves to be lost by those who abuse the power granted to them. Those who, forsaking the rules of their order, wish to divert to common rights of others, should be judged by common rights; for it is fitting that those who adopt a similar life to others should undergo the same discipline in laws with them. Therefore, by the authority of this present mandate, we strictly command you, under the threat of excommunication, to present yourselves by competent procurators, sufficiently instructed on this matter, to our presence by the next month of March, to humbly receive the apostolic mandate. Meanwhile, completely desist from mutual hostilities, raising no war among yourselves or waging war against each other; otherwise, we command by letters to our beloved sons, the abbots of the Temple of the Lord and of Saint Samuel in Acre, to not delay in promulgating the sentences of excommunication against you and of interdict against your lands. Given at Perugia, the tenth day before the kalends of September, in the ninth year.

Since a case that is ongoing between the noblewoman M., Countess of Brittany, and the nobleman [name missing], Viscount of Thouars, in the diocese of Poitiers, concerning certain revenues, possessions, and other matters related to the dowry of the said countess, as she claims, after various commissions and different approaches to various judges obtained from the Apostolic See on either side, we had assigned to our beloved sons, the priors of Ponte Uncti, Ebredun, and Herbetis Jucal, in the said diocese, at the instance of the same countess: finally, the same countess proposed that although more than four years had passed disputing both before the initial judges and the current ones, the case had not yet proceeded to litigation, due to the malice of the other party, by which she had not yet been able to obtain her justice; we, desiring to bring the litigation to an end, commanded the said prior of Ponte Uncti and his co-judges that, if this were the case, within four months after receiving our letters, proceeding in the case according to the form given to them, they should conclude it with due outcome if it proceeded with the consent of the parties; otherwise, they should remit it to us, sufficiently instructed, setting a competent term for the parties to present themselves before us to receive just judgment, with God's help; and, if an appeal were made by any party and apostolic letters were not obtained concerning the appeal, they should take care to assign both parties a certain term to appear before us in person or through suitable representatives to receive justice. And since the parties had litigated before the said judges with the authority of the earlier letters directed to them, the same viscount, feeling unjustly aggrieved, as he said, because two of those judges, after litigation concerning his appeal had been contested before them and their colleague and discussed, had associated a certain William the priest, who claimed to be a subdelegate from the third judge, although no faith had been made to him concerning this subdelegation, clearly suspect to the same, to them against his protest, appealed to the Apostolic See. Moreover, the same judges, to whom the countess subsequently presented the letters obtained from us, the tenor of which is expressed above, wishing to proceed by them, the same viscount proposed before them that, since the said countess had falsely suggested the case had been disputed for more than four years and not yet proceeded to litigation due to the malice of the other party, for which the case had been prolonged, they could not and should not proceed; and because the said judges, without knowing this, as he said, attempted to proceed to the decision of the case against the form of the apostolic mandate, against his objection, and were unwilling to desist from this grievance, humbly requested, he again took appeal to our hearing. Yet those judges, according to the tenor of our mandate, set a certain term for the parties to present themselves before us. But the said viscount, anticipating the term, without making any mention of it, obtained certain letters from us concerning his appeal to the treasurer, subdean, and Master R., granary officer of Saint Martin of Tours. Therefore, the countess's proctor appearing before us within the term set for him, we granted him our venerable brother R(ainald), Bishop of Ostia, as an auditor; before whom the same proctor petitioned that such letters, as obtained with the truth concealed, and their process be revoked as void, and the said viscount be condemned to legitimate expenses, since he had not sent a suitable respondent within the term set for him, but only a proctor to obtain and contradict appeared for him; and moreover, since the said countess could not obtain her justice due to the delays and malice of the opposing party, she requested the whole case be recalled to the Apostolic See; the proctor of the said viscount opposed, claiming the aforementioned should not be done. The same auditor, after hearing the proposals on both sides and diligently inspecting the apostolic letters and the dates thereof, fully understanding the reasons and allegations of both parties, faithfully recounted them to us. Therefore, wishing to counter such malice and delays, to provide healthily for both parties, and to put an end to the litigation, we decided to recall the entire case, and all letters and processes had by them, saving the right of expenses for the said countess, to the apostolic examination. Therefore, we command your discretion by apostolic writings to ensure that you assign to the parties a peremptory term on the first Sunday of Lent, on which day they should present themselves before us in person or through suitable proctors, sufficiently instructed, with the same letters and processes, all their proofs and reasons, to receive justice on the aforementioned matters

**Translation to English:**

To the abbot of Saint Celsus of Milan. Since a long time ago, our predecessor, of blessed memory, Pope H., decided to entrust the case that was being argued between the abbot of Saint Silanus of Romagnano, on one side, and the commune of Vercelli, on the other, regarding damages inflicted by the same commune on his monastery, to our venerable brother, the bishop of Pavia and his colleagues. They then issued a definitive sentence, condemning the said commune to two thousand and three hundred imperial pounds. Following an appeal to the Apostolic See, the case was committed to our dear son, the archdeacon of Milan and his co-judges. They upheld the sentence regarding one thousand three hundred pounds, but ruled that an error was made concerning the remaining one thousand pounds. The same abbot, regarding this point, appealed, while the commune requested to confirm the sentence. When the procurators of both parties appeared before our predecessor, each insisted on confirming the sentence issued by the archdeacon and his co-judges as it favored their side, and annulling it where it opposed them. Since our predecessor could not ascertain the merits of the sentence through them, he directed his writings to the bishop of Cumania and the provost of Rondenario, of the diocese of Cumania, and the archpriest of the Decumans of Milan, by the assent of the same procurators, to confirm or annul the sentence, removing the obstacle of appeal, as justice required. The same provost and archpriest, and Lanterius Scaccabarocius, the ordinary of Milan, were delegated by the Apostolic See to investigate the merits of the sentence, replacing the bishop of Cumania, who had died. They upheld the sentence given by the archdeacon and his co-judges for one thousand one hundred and fifty pounds but annulled it for the remaining one thousand one hundred and fifty pounds. Consequently, the commune appealed to our audience. Furthermore, since the monastery had not received any benefit from the sentences issued by the bishop of Pavia and his co-judges for the said abbot, as they were not executed, we later directed our writings to the abbot of Saint Julian and his colleagues to execute the sentence, as justice required, suppressing objections, and condemning the other party to pay twenty-five imperial pounds for expenses. Since the commune and its syndic and potestà of Vercelli refused to obey, they rightfully declared sentences of excommunication and interdict against them and the entire city. However, even then, the aforementioned abbot, weary from many labors and expenses, could not obtain any benefit due to the obstinacy of the other party, and thus requested the Apostolic See's providence to assist him. When the abbot and Ivorinus, the procurator of the potestà and commune, appeared before us, we appointed our dear son, Sinibald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, as the auditor. The abbot requested that the sentence, upheld by the provost of Rondenario and his co-judges for one thousand one hundred and fifty pounds, and the sentence by the abbot of Saint Julian and his colleagues for twenty-five imperial pounds for expenses, be executed, and that the excommunication and interdict sentences be observed inviolably until proper satisfaction was made. The procurator objected, arguing that unless apostolic letters sealed with a bull were shown, it was not proven that the archdeacon of Milan and others were judges, and similarly for those delegated by them through the showing of letters of subdelegation or excuse, and he also claimed that the procurators or syndics referred to in the sentences were not actually such. The cardinal, having listened to both sides and fully understood the merits of the case, ordered the execution of the sentences for one thousand one hundred and fifty imperial pounds, as well as the twenty-five pounds, saving the right of expenses. Therefore, what was faithfully done by him in our presence, we approve, and by apostolic writing, we command your discretion to carry out these sentences; those who resist, etc. Given at Perugia, the fifth day before the calends of September, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius Papa IX abbati Sancti Celsi Mediolanensis mandat ut sententias a cardinali S. Laurentii in Lucina promulgatas, quoad mille centum et quinquaginta, nec non et viginti quinque libras imperialium, executioni mandet, contradictores compescendo. Dat. Perusii, V kalendas septembris, anno nono.

To the Archbishop of Sens, the Bishop of Troyes, and Robert of the Order of the Friars Preachers. Ildebrandiscus, a citizen and merchant of Florence, presented himself before us and stated that some time ago in France, he had frequently conversed with certain heretics whom he believed to be Catholics, and gave ten Tournois shillings to one of their servants, bowing his head in reverence to them on multiple occasions. Later realizing they were heretics and fearing danger to his soul, he confessed this in the forum of penance to the prior of the Friars Preachers and Brother Matthew, of the Order of Friars Minor, residing in Troyes, who imposed a salutary penance on him. Nonetheless, he approached the Apostolic See and humbly requested that we provide for him in this matter. Therefore, we instructed our venerable brother, the Bishop of Florence, by our letters to inquire thoroughly into the sincerity of his faith, life, morals, and person, and after receiving from him a sufficient and suitable surety and oath that he would comply with our mandate in all things, to send it sealed to the Apostolic See. The same bishop, having diligently executed this, forwarded the inquiry conducted against him, with the aforementioned sureties, along with his letters containing the details of the matter, to our presence. Upon opening by our venerable brother, the Bishop of Palestrina, nothing was found against him that would harm his reputation or pose any other danger; rather, the witnesses examined testified commendably to his purity of faith. However, as a precaution, we have imposed another salutary penance through our beloved son, Brother Raymond, our penitentiary. We command that, if you find anything else against him, you report it faithfully to us and do not allow him to be unjustly troubled by anyone in person or possessions due to this matter; and that you restrain such troublemakers by ecclesiastical censure, etc. If not all, etc. Notwithstanding the indulgence by which, for cases delegated by apostolic letters, you, Brother Robert, are not obliged to investigate unwillingly. Given at Viterbo, on the 11th of March, in the ninth year (of our pontificate).

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa [nomen non specificatum], archiepiscopo Senonensi, episcopo Trecensi et Roberto de ordine fratrum Praedicatorum mandat ut, postquam inquisitione facta contra Ildebrandiscum Florentinum mercatorem nihil contra fidem repertum est, eum a molestationibus indebite liberum permittant, et si qua alia contra ipsum reperirent, fideliter referant; molestatores per censuram ecclesiasticam coerceant. Datum Viterbii, V idus Martii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Nevers, the provincial prior of the Order of Preachers in France, and Master J. de Monte Mirabili, archdeacon of Paris. Peter Vogrini, a layman from Silviniac, in the diocese of Clermont, approached the Apostolic See and explained to us that when, at an earlier time, we had directed our letters to the archbishop of Bourges, of blessed memory, and to the bishop of Auxerre to inquire into the crime of heretical depravity in the town of Caritate, the said bishop, the archdeacon of Auxerre, and the prior of Belli Latrici, to whom the same archbishop had entrusted his responsibilities, summoned him. Although they had no jurisdiction over him, as he was not from that town, he voluntarily submitted to their jurisdiction, inquiry, and orders, and because nothing sinister could be found against him after a diligent inquiry, he cleared his innocence, as required by them, through ten priests and clerics and as many knights and citizens. And when, later on, some of his rivals sought in many ways to defame his reputation, we, at his instance, instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Clermont, his diocesan, with our letters to inquire more diligently into these matters and to decide what should be deemed expedient for his welfare. The said bishop of Clermont, conducting another inquiry into the same matter and announcing in places where he had lived that if anyone wished to bring something against him, they should appear before him at a specified place and time, because no one appeared against him at the said place and time, and because nothing could be found against him, and moreover, because it was clearly established to him from the aforementioned purgation and also because our venerable brother, the archbishop of Sens, and many other prelates of the kingdom of France bore laudable testimony regarding his life, behavior, and reputation through their letters, he declared him innocent of the aforementioned crime. And when later we had sent our letters to brother Robert of the Order of Preachers to inquire into the aforementioned crime in the kingdom of France, and the same brother summoned him before himself, the aforementioned Peter, coming into the presence of the said brother and the bishop of Clermont, voluntarily submitted himself to their jurisdiction and orders concerning these matters, having sworn an oath, while retaining his legitimate defenders. And they firmly promised him that neither of them would cite or proceed against him without the other, but that they would observe the order of law regarding him. However, because it was certainly reported to Peter that the said brother, contrary to his promise, ordered him to be cited alone and before himself alone to a place that was not safe and publicly threatened to seize him and came to the said place with armed force, before the term of such citation, he appealed to the Apostolic See in the presence of certain abbots. Nevertheless, at the said term, he sent a certain clerical nephew of his to the said brother to propose what should be proposed on his behalf and to renew the appeal made by him. And when the same cleric appeared before the said brother on the appointed day, the said brother, for the sole reason that he came on behalf of the said Peter, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the cleric and perpetually suspended him from office and benefice; who, because he was absolved by the same brother under this condition, that he could not otherwise obtain absolution, renounced the matters proposed for the said Peter at his command and promised that he would not appear any more on his behalf. Therefore, the same Peter, fearing, not unjustly, that danger was imminent to him because of this, set out on a journey to the Apostolic See; upon whom, while on such a journey, the said brother Robert and a certain brother from the Order of Friars Minor, whom the said bishop of Clermont had sent only to excuse himself, although he had been cited by the same bishop of Clermont, pronounced a sentence of excommunication. Wherefore, the same Peter humbly supplicated us to mercifully provide for him regarding this. Therefore, not wishing that the depravity of so great a crime should remain unpunished or that the purity of innocence should succumb confusedly, we command your discretion by apostolic letter that, if you find that the said sentence of excommunication was pronounced after such an appeal, declaring it to be completely null and revoking whatever may have been rashly attempted after it to its proper state, you should inquire into the truth of the foregoing matters, and what you find about this, you should faithfully report to us so that we may proceed in this matter as we see fit according to God. Given at Viterbo, on the sixth day before the ides of November, in the ninth year [of our pontificate].

**Translation to English:**

To the priors of Saint Roman of Castro Airaud, of Belle Fontaine, and of Buisser, of the diocese of Poitiers. The noble woman Isabella, formerly Queen of England, sent us a petition showing that, some time ago, she had brought a case against the noble man Simon de Pissiaco, of the diocese of Paris, concerning certain properties and other matters pertaining to her dowry, in the presence of the prior of Le Fauga and his co-judges, appointed by us. These judges, due to his manifest contumacy, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him, in accordance with justice, which he stubbornly endured for more than three years. Later, the said Simon, claiming that the judges pronounced the sentence against him without reasonable cause and without prior warning, contrary to the general statutes of the council, obtained certain letters from them and others from the late abbot of the Major Monastery of Tours and his co-judges, in the usual form from us. Meanwhile, the said abbot having passed away, his co-judges, exceeding the limits of our mandate, unjustly relaxed this sentence without receiving any security from Simon. Therefore, the said noble woman humbly supplicated us to assist her with paternal providence, since in this case, prolonged for almost a decade, a formal contestation of the lawsuit could not be obtained due to the evasions of the other party. Therefore, wishing to counteract malice, as we desire peace for all, we mandate that, having the letters obtained on both sides and the proceedings through them exhibited to you, you should hear the case and, if it proceeds with the consent of the parties, decide it with fair judgment or agreement, with the appeal removed, at least within a year after the receipt of these presents; otherwise, sufficiently instructed, you should refer it to our examination, assigning a peremptory and suitable term for the parties to present themselves in our presence in person or by a competent procurator to receive a just sentence, God willing. The witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding the constitution issued in the general council regarding two diets, yet in such a way that beyond a third or fourth day outside their diocese, the other party should not be drawn. Provided it is not into the land of the said noblewoman, etc. What if not all, etc. Given at Viterbo, on the 13th of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa [Gregorius IX] prioribus Sancti Romani de Castro Airaudi, de Bello Fonte et de Buisseria, Pictavensis diocesis, mandat ut causam inter nobilem mulierem Isabellam, quondam reginam Angliae, et Symonem de Pissiaco, super possessionibus et rebus ad dotem spectantibus, audiant atque infra annum terminent, appellatione remota; sin minus, instructam remittant ad examen apostolicum. Dat. Viterbii, III idus martii, anno nono.

Translation to English:

To the dean, cantor, and Elias Gerald, canon of Angoulême. We have learned from our beloved sons W., the prior, J., the sub-prior, P., the sacristan, B., the provost, and certain other monks of Saint Michael of the Hermitage in the diocese of Poitiers, that although the said monastery previously flourished spiritually and temporally, it has now declined in both aspects due to the negligence, or rather the malice, of Aimeric, who acts as its abbot. This decline is so severe that without the swift intervention of the Apostolic See, it is unlikely to recover. Aimeric, ensnared by perjury and other various crimes, has unlawfully procured his position as abbot of the monastery. Moreover, he is so negligent and lax in the reformation of monastic discipline that due to his insolence, the regular observance is nearly extinct. Furthermore, he has become a source of death rather than life to his subordinates, associating himself with those of ill repute while ignoring their transgressions and disregarding those who have lived commendably in the monastery from their youth. When reproached for these and other outrages by the monks, he threatens them with excommunication and deprives them of their duties. Not content with these threats, he sends them to remote places to prevent them from witnessing his dishonorable conduct and dissuading him from his excesses and sins. They also added that the aforementioned abbot, inconsistent in his words and deeds, is squandering and wasting the goods of the monastery, living secularly and so indiscreet in the administration of temporal affairs that the goods of the abbey seem to vanish and perish under his management; committing many other outrageous acts to the peril of his soul, the dishonor of monastic integrity, and the scandal of many, all of which call for apostolic correction. Therefore, since, according to the Apostle, our daily concern is the continuous care of all churches, we command you to personally visit the monastery, keeping only God before your eyes, and exercise the duty of visitation on our behalf, correcting and reforming it. Given at Viterbo, on the 11th day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

Regesto in Latin:

Papa (Gregorius IX) decano, cantori, et Heliae Geraldi, canonico Engolismensibus mandat ut, auditis querelis de Aimerico, abbate Sancti Michaelis de Heremo Pictavensis diocesis, qui monasterium in spiritualibus et temporalibus per negligentiam et malitiam deciderit, visitationem personalem faciant et reformationem monasticae disciplinae corrigant. Datum Viterbii, XI Kalendas Januarii, anno nono pontificatus nostri.

**Translation to English:**

To the abbot of Latiniacum, of the diocese of Paris, and the prior of Saint Martin of Paris, of the Cluniac order. The beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the Major Monastery of Tours, have humbly petitioned us that, since the seal of the monastery was furtively taken by some sons of iniquity when the monastery was without the solace of an abbot, and many letters and blank documents were sealed and delivered to certain merchants and other persons without the connivance of the greater and sounder part of the convent of said monastery, under an oath not to reveal this, to the great detriment of the monastery itself, we should deign to provide for its indemnity with fatherly solicitude. Wherefore, we command that, releasing the aforementioned oath by apostolic authority, you make a general admonition in the places where you deem it expedient, that those who have these documents and letters should seek to return them, or reveal those who possess them if they know, pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against those who presume otherwise, and ensuring that it is observed inviolably until due satisfaction, with no appeal allowed. For we decree that the aforementioned letters and documents have no force, so that the same monastery should not be troubled by them in any way. Given at Viterbo, on the 7th day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year. 

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX abbati Latiniaci Parisiensis dioecesis et priori Sancti Martini Parisiensis Cluniacensis ordinis mandat ut, sigillo Majoris Monasterii Turonensis furtive sublato et litteris sigillatis furtive traditis, juramentum huiusmodi relaxent ac generalem monitionem faciant ad restitutionem litterarum vel earum revelationem, excommunicationem in transgressores proferentes et eam usque ad satisfactionem condignam inviolabilem observantes. Litteras et cedulas vires non habere decernit. Datum Viterbii, VII idus martii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the Abbot of Saint Severus and the Archdeacons of Levitania and Basel in the dioceses of Adur and Tarvisio. Falling into grave dissolution, as we have been informed by the clamorous insinuation of the Archdeacon of Vallis Veteris, B. of Audans, and certain other canons of Lascur, the canons of the aforementioned church, publicly keeping the daughters of concubines, unite them in a manner like that of seculars, endowing and enriching them with the goods of the said church, and applying its income to their family's use, thus squandering the church's goods, and do not hesitate to engage in shameful pursuits. Moreover, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Lascur, is known to be the cause of these things, who, like a thief not entering through the door, had himself consecrated as bishop in place of another whom he knew to be canonically elected, although he was ineligible. He, irregularly conducting himself in the regular church, promotes those who offer him more money to orders and benefices, as if they were more worthy; and, stained with sacrilege, perjury, and various other crimes, he does not dare to correct the errors of others, since he internally responds to himself that he has committed the same acts he seeks to correct. However, since it is culpable to relax punishment for those faults by which the state of the Church is subverted, and with the shepherd treading on precipitous paths, a fall is prepared for the flock, we command you, personally going to the place and having God alone before your eyes, if you find the aforementioned bishop defamed over these matters, to inquire more fully into the truth of these matters, and faithfully inform us by your letters of what you find concerning this bishop, so that we may proceed in these matters as we see fit according to God. In other matters, without appeal, correct and reform there what you know requires correction and reformation; contradictors, etc. If not all of you, etc. Given at Viterbo, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX abbati Sancti Severi et archidiaconis de Levitania et Basiliaquensi, ex insinuatione archidiaconi Vallis Veteris et aliorum canonicorum, mandat ut, cum episcopus Lascurrensis ob irregularia et criminosa acta infamatus sit, veritatem plenius inquirant et nobis per litteras intimant, ut procedamus secundum Deum; et in aliis, sine appellatione, corrigant et reforment quae correctione indigent. Datum Viterbii, XV Kalendas Januarii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Pisa. We are compelled to marvel greatly and be disturbed because, as our beloved son, the prior of Nocera, our subdeacon and legate of the Apostolic See in Sardinia and Corsica, has shown us through his complaint, you received his envoys, sent to you on his behalf, with less than due respect, asserting that you alone are the legate of Sardinia, and presumptuously forbade him from entering the city of Pisa, threatening that if he did otherwise, he would suffer harm and loss from the Pisans. And although he did go to Pisa and found no one there, except your kinsmen and supporters, who inflicted dishonor and injury upon him, yet they, armed, approached his lodging by night and threw stones at it, and dared to seize his servants and clerics on the public street. Furthermore, though repeatedly asked to provide him passage to Sardinia, you responded that you were not obliged to do so unless you received a special mandate from the Apostolic See; and although you are bound by oath to treat the legates of the Apostolic See honorably and assist them in their needs, you, unmindful of your own salvation and divine fear, dared to act otherwise and, placing a stain on your honor, refused him the necessary provisions without hesitation. You did not consider that it should have sufficed as an offense to the Apostolic See that you presumed to exercise the office of legate in Sardinia without having received or requested our license. However, since we cannot, nor should we, overlook this under any pretense, we strictly order you by the authority of these presents to personally present yourself before us by the beginning of the forthcoming Lent, which we assign to you as a peremptory term, regarding the fact that, without our special mandate and contrary to ancient and approved custom, you usurped the office of legate in Sardinia and inflicted the aforementioned injuries upon the said legate. Otherwise, you shall know that from that time you will be suspended from your pontifical office. Moreover, we wish and mandate that you pay the expenses which the said legate is known to have incurred in Pisa and will incur on his passage and otherwise to Sardinia. Should you presume to contravene our mandates in this matter, we instruct our beloved son, the primicerius of Lucca, by our letters, to compel you to do so. Given at Viterbo, on the ides of December, in the ninth year.

**Regesto:**

Papa Honorius III archiepiscopo Pisano mandat ut, ob usurpationem legationis in Sardinia et Corsica sine mandato speciali, et ob injurias illatas legato Apostolicae Sedis, se personaliter coram ipso repraesentet usque ad initium Quadragesimae proximo venturae, alioquin a pontificali officio suspensum se noverit. Insuper mandat ut expensas legati Pisis factas et in itinere in Sardiniam solvat. Dat. Viterbii, idibus decembris, anno pontificatus nono.

**Translation to English:**

To Adam, archdeacon of Rennes, Geoffrey, archdeacon of Saint-Malo, and Roger, archdeacon of Coutances. Our venerable brother, the bishop of Avranches, has conveyed to us through his petition that, having previously directed letters to him, instructing him to proceed with the correction of his subjects by both our authority and his own, he visited the monastery of Mont-Saint-Michel, which is subject to his diocesan rule. Exercising the office of visitation with both authorities, and having carefully considered the state of its head and members, he issued salutary and fitting statutes regarding the reinstatement of monks to priories, newly imposed pensions, and those increased contrary to the statutes of the general council. Also concerning the consumption of meat, the rendering of accounts from the obedientiaries four times a year, and other matters. The abbot and convent did not oppose, but rather accepted the regulations for over a month. Later, understanding that they were failing in these matters, especially those previously mentioned, the bishop admonished them to observe these regulations. When his admonitions proved ineffective, he summoned them to appear before him on a fixed date. They did not attend sufficiently and showed contempt for the statutes. The dean of Avranches, acting with the bishop’s authority, suspended the abbot from entering the church and the convent from celebrating the divine office. When the bishop suspended the priests of Mont-Saint-Michel for their faults and excommunicated them due to their obstinacy, the abbot and convent falsely claimed before the late archbishop of Rouen that they had full jurisdiction over these priests. They asserted that the sentences were prejudicially issued. They appealed to the archbishop, ensuring the bishop was summoned to answer both the appeal and other matters. Although these sentences were not prejudicially issued, the abbot and convent sought their revocation, claiming them to be contemptuous of the church of Rouen. They obtained a mandate from Richard, priest of Saint-Cécile in the diocese of Coutances, to pronounce the sentences void if not revoked by the bishop. Without proper legal procedure, these sentences were declared null and void. The archbishop, when the bishop appeared before him, failed to adjudicate fairly, leading to the appointment of Brother Henry, prior of the Dominican Order in Paris, as an arbiter. Although the arbitration was accepted by one party, the abbot and convent did not adhere to it, leading to further discord. The bishop suspended them from divine offices and seized their tithes due to continued offenses. The abbot and convent appealed to the archbishop of Rouen, causing prolonged litigation. They infringed upon the bishop’s jurisdiction and were accused of numerous grievances, including withholding income from churches, preventing sufficient ecclesiastical services, and impeding the bishop’s jurisdiction. They were asked to observe the statutes and release funds improperly held. They faced condemnation for breaching the arbitration agreement. The bishop sought enforcement of penalties against them. Due to the failure to progress in inquiries, the bishop restored prior sentences and actions due to the adversarial party's evasion. Given these circumstances, it was requested that the matter be remedied by Apostolic authority. The bishop also sought to have the abbot and convent pay the penalties and observe sentences unless a suitable inquiry was conducted. The matter was ordered to be concluded by agreement or judgment, and if unresolved, returned to the Apostolic See for final decision. 

**Regesto in Latin:**

**Papa Honorius III** archidiaconos Redonensem, Macloviensis, et Constantiensem monet et mandat ut, considerata querela episcopi Abrincensis de visitatione monasterii Montis Sancti Michaelis et neglectis statutis synodalibus, ad correctionem subditorum procedant. Cum abbas et conventus Montis in rebus statutis deliquerint, episcopus eos ad sui praesentiam evocavit. Contemptis monitionibus et sententiis suspensionis atque excommunicationis, abbas et conventus ad sedem Rothomagensem appellaverunt. Papa mandat causam coram arbitris finiri, et si non, ad Sedem Apostolicam remitti. Acta Viterbii, X Kalendas Februarii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Sens and his suffragans. After many afflictions and long wanderings in the desert, Israel was led into the Promised Land; after many battles, the toil of war was gently wiped away by the hand of peace, and with the battles quieted, the land of distribution was possessed by the measuring line. But, lest the people of the Lord, in the pride of their hearts, should rise up from the abundance of riches and peace, and believe that their own hand has achieved these things, and thus grow lukewarm in the observance of divine law, they could not completely destroy their enemies. The Lord left certain nations to test them after Joshua's death so that, being trained among them, they might learn the custom of fighting with enemies, and, oppressed among them, they might bear the fear of the Lord within themselves, for affliction gives understanding to the ear. Therefore, even though the Mother Church of the Catholic faith, after many persecutions and the glorious passions of the blessed martyrs, has extended its borders more widely throughout the world, and the vineyard of the Lord, planted in the blood of Christ, is now fruitful with many branches, and the scepters of rulers have been exalted, still, there are some who try by various means to inflict the Church with the wound of headship and to deprive it of the treasure of liberty and faith. For, as we have heard with sorrow and wonder, our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of France, and the barons of the realm, have acted against the Church, which regenerated them into sons from the womb of sanctification, etc., up to they should respond in ecclesiastical judgment. However, if the said king and barons would carefully consider how the illustrious memory of Charlemagne, etc., as above, up to, should not be curtailed in the time of the said king. Therefore, we request, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord Jesus Christ, by apostolic writings, commanding you that you, setting up a fortified city and an iron pillar, following the example of the Prophet, should not be afraid in the defense of ecclesiastical liberty; but with such constant strength of an armed heart, which no arrow of persecution can penetrate, you should bravely oppose yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord, using confidently the liberty which you still possess and have used until now, and proceeding against the rebellious as is fitting, declaring null attempts against ecclesiastical liberty, and not allowing yourselves or your subjects to be despoiled of its benefit. Knowing firmly that since we love the Gallican Church with special charity among the other churches of the world, we shall extend to you, with the Lord's help, all manner of counsel and assistance in preserving your rights and liberties. Moreover, since Pope Honorius of happy memory, our predecessor, etc., as above, up to he promulgated, we have decided to send you its tenor, so that you may cause it to be solemnly published and kept in your dioceses, notwithstanding any indulgences or privileges whatsoever from the Apostolic See, with the appeal set aside. The tenor is as follows: Know, etc., as above, to the end. Furthermore, since in such matters negligence of great fault is apparent, if any of you perhaps have been negligent in these things, they will not escape the censure of ecclesiastical discipline. Given at Viterbo, on the 13th day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX archiepiscopo Senonensi et suffraganeis ejus mandat ut in defensione ecclesiasticae libertatis intrepide agant et statuta contra libertatem ecclesiasticam irrita nuntient, promittens consilium et auxilium in juriis conservandis; insuper mandat ut decretum a praedecessore Honorio promulgatum publice servetur, negligentes censura non evasuros. Dat. Viterbii, XIII kalendas martii, pontificatus anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the archbishop, the dean of Saint Symphorian, and Master G. of Laon, canon of Reims. Michael de Cerisiaco, a priest, has shown us in a tearful petition that when he attended the synod of Noyon, our venerable brother, the bishop of Noyon, allegedly driven by a grudge against him—provoked by insulting words exchanged with the bishop's nephews—had him seized by his servants and imprisoned. Accusing him falsely of having associated with heretics and certain ill-believing individuals and of engaging in their customs, he detained him, although Michael publicly denied the charges, professing his firm belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and was willing to undergo examination before the bishop and you, brother archbishop, and to provide security for his possessions. Despite this, the bishop ordered him detained in iron chains and later, after nefariously defaming him among reputable people, kept him captive for a long time, forbidding any of his friends to speak with him, and eventually locked him within the walls of his tower. When Michael, persistently pleading for a proper examination and to be brought to your investigation, was nonetheless not released until his friends were extorted to provide a surety under penalty that he would not be further harassed for the accusations. Furthermore, when the priest detained by the bishop, by the bishop's will, swore by himself, William the priest, and certain other clerics that he was innocent of the charges, the bishop still forced him to swear to abide by his orders. After this, the bishop, giving no measure to his grievances, suspended him from office and benefice, retained a horse of his, and subjected him to various injuries; Michael suffered heavy damages beyond the expenses incurred for prison guards and others, as all considerations of equity towards him were disregarded. Therefore, overwhelmed with tears, he humbly beseeched us to mercifully provide for him in this matter, as he, exhausted of his ecclesiastical and worldly goods, preferred to appeal to the Apostolic See for the repair of his reputation, dearer to him than any temporal wealth. Therefore, we command that if this is true, unless a legitimate accuser appears against the priest within three months of receiving this letter, and after receiving his canonical purgation, if he is found free from the charges, to compel the bishop—after monition and by our authority—to remit the oath he imposed, restore the surety taken from his friends, and provide due satisfaction for damages and injuries, lifting the suspension, removing any obstacles of evasion, as justice demands. If not all of you can act, particularly you, brother archbishop, etc. Given at Viterbo, December 5, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa (Gregorius IX) archiepiscopo, decano Sancti Simphoriani et magistro G. de Lauduno, canonico Remensi, scribit de querela Michaelem de Cerisiaco, presbyterum, contra episcopum Noviomensem, qui eum per servientes suos capi fecit et carceri mancipari sub falsis criminibus associationis cum haereticis. Papa mandat inquirendum et, si presbyter innocens reperiatur, episcopum compellendum ad relaxationem suspensionis et satisfactionem pro damnis irrogatis; nisi legitimus accusator intra tres menses compareat. Datum Viterbii, nonis decembris, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the master and brothers of the House of the Hospital of Saint Thomas the Martyr in Acre. Your devotion has clearly informed us how the late Richard, King of England, while engaged in the service of the Holy Land, constructed a certain house in the city of Acre, in honor of God and Saint Thomas the Martyr, and for the benefit of the canons regular, for the remission of his sins, so that hospitality and the statutes of their order might be maintained there. However, after the king was prevented by death, who had intended to open the royal munificence for this purpose, the canons of that house had no means of comfortable sustenance. The house, depressed by poverty and close to peril, has long struggled. In the course of time, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Winchester, who traveled to those parts on pilgrimage, observed the house in its location and resources unsuitable for the regular order, and due to the dissolution and neglect of the canons, miserably fallen. With the counsel of our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, and the magnates of that kingdom, and with the cathedral and metropolitan churches then being vacant, he transferred it to a more fitting location, the said canons being removed, and you, living according to the rule of the Teutonic Order, were substituted for the aid of the Holy Land. Although the same bishop could not rightfully do this, yet we, considering his pious purpose and laudable intention, and inclined by your supplications, supplementing this defect from the fullness of our power, confirm by apostolic authority what was usefully and providently done in this matter and fortify it with the protection of this present writing, such that the place itself by this is not exempted in any way from the jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. Therefore, let no one infringe on our confirmation, etc. Given at Viterbo, on the nones of February, in the year of our pontificate.

**Regesto:**

Papa [nomen papae] magistro et fratribus domus Hospitalis Sancti Thomae martyris Acconensis mandat, ut domus a Rege Ricardo Angliae in Accone fundata, propter neglectum canonicorum et consilio episcopi Wintoniensis ad locum aptiorem translata, confirmetur pro subsidio Terrae Sanctae, auctoritate apostolica, non obstante defectu juris. Datum Viterbii, nonis februarii, pontificatus nostri anno [anno pontificatus].

### Translation to English:

To the Archbishop of Vienne, Legate of the Apostolic See. 

Elated by the winds of pride and elevated in a chariot not of Elijah, but of Pharaoh, Elias de Ventadorn, accompanied by a multitude of Egyptians, afflicts and oppresses the monastery of Tulle with so many injuries and losses that its convent is compelled to expire shortly, unless, with the Lord's deliverance, Elias and the army of the aforementioned Pharaoh are submerged in the midst of the waves. For, as we have perceived from the tearful insinuations of our beloved sons, G. de Rupe, chamberlain, Guido de Veteribus Campis, cantor, Gaubert, almoner, G. de Aquira, infirmarian, Estorgius, refectorian, P., prior of Florance, Robert, prior of Blanac, Guido, provost of Ralarent, P., prior of Saint Clement, G., prior of Sparac, and some other monks of the monastery, after the passing of Bernard de Ventadorn, their former abbot, who throughout his life endeavored to appoint some relative of his as his successor, the said Elias, his nephew, who, although not yet a cleric nor professed in any regular order, presumes to act as a monk. Supported by secular power, driven by audacity rather than authority, he has occupied and plundered the castles, fortresses, towns, and possessions of the said monastery, causing the shedding of much blood and the death of many, and has exposed these to robbers, and he still dares to forcibly detain them. However, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Limoges, diocesan of the place, having fully understood this, ordered him with letters under penalty of excommunication to return the occupied properties to the convent of Tulle and instructed the convent to proceed with the election of an abbot, removing foreign monks and secular persons from the election process, with God alone before their eyes. However, on the day set for discussing the election, seeing the multitude of armed and secular persons brought in by the same Elias, the monks appealed repeatedly to the Apostolic See, compromising the election outcome to four monks of the place, swearing to provide as pastor and father the one deemed more suitable from the monastery's community. And because two of them, supporters of the same Elias, stated they would not proceed unless they had the liberty to decide as they pleased, and since Elias refused to return the aforementioned castles and fortresses to the convent or place them in the hands of a trustee, nor allow secular persons and armed men to leave the monastery's cloister, those monks, threatened with death by the armed men unless they accepted Elias as abbot, appealed again to our court. Furthermore, Elias, with some of his accomplices, disregarding canonical form and neglecting the larger and wiser part of the chapter, sought to be inauspiciously elected abbot and transported by foreign monks and armed men to the abbot's seat, without having received or requested confirmation, relying on his powerful lineage, and involved himself in the administration of the monastery, receiving, through violence, fidelities and oaths from its people. Consequently, many monks, intimidated by threats and arms, were forced to grant him their services. Moreover, assembling a multitude of armed men, Elias approached the town of Roche-Amador and its castle, properties of the monastery, not as a monk but as an enemy, entered the castle after much bloodshed, and stripped the townspeople of all goods, blasphemed the image of the Blessed Virgin, revered by the world and celebrated for miracles and gifts, by stoning it and desecrating it with repeated trampling. But because if a wolf assumes the place of a shepherd, it is inevitable that he will devour the flock by lacerating it with his jaws, we command you to personally visit the place, having God alone before your eyes, and if you find the situation as described, to completely exclude Elias from the administration of the monastery, compelling him to return the aforementioned castles, fortifications, and goods to the monastery, and compelling his supporters to compensate the convent for the damages and injuries, using ecclesiastical censure without allowance for appeal, and, if necessary, invoking the aid of secular authorities to curb their malice. Further, ensure that a suitable person is provided to the monastery through a canonical election, and that necessary expenses for pursuing this matter are supplied to the monks from the monastery's goods, as they have no personal property. Given at Viterbo, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

To the abbots of Trois-Fontaines and Orval, of the dioceses of Châlons and Trier. When our beloved sons, the priors of Grandpré, Courmicy, Issy, Saint-Lambert, and Bernay-en-Champagne, along with Nicholas, a canon of the monastery of Saint-Denis in Reims, of the Order of Saint Augustine, came into our presence on behalf of themselves and their companions, we absolved them from all sentences of excommunication that are said to have been pronounced against them after an appeal had been made by them to us, or after they had begun their journey to come into our presence. These sentences were reportedly pronounced by both their abbot and Godfrey and Stephen de Provins, canons of Reims, to whom we had decided to entrust to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Reims, the correction and reformation of the monastery, or other judges obtained by the aforementioned abbot after the same appeal, through our beloved son Stinibald, the presbyter cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. Given at Viterbo, on the 8th of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius Papa IX, abbatibus Trium Fontium et Auree Vallis in diocesibus Cathalaunensi et Treverensi mandat ut absolvant priores de Grandi Prato, de Curmissiaco, de Issia, de Sancto Lamberto, et de Berniaca Curte, cum Nicolao canonico monasterii Sancti Dionisii Remensis ordinis sancti Augustini, a sententiis excommunicationis latas post appellationem ad Sedem Apostolicam, priusquam iter ad praesentiam Sancti Pontificis suscepissent, a suo abbate et canonicis Remensibus; recepta tamen ab eis fidejussoria cautione; iisdem eorum sociis simile beneficium impendere jubet. To the same. The church of Bourges being deprived of the consolation of a shepherd, the beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Bourges, deliberating on the substitution of a future bishop, elected the beloved son Master Alberic Cornuti, dean of Saint Martin of Tours, as their archbishop, humbly beseeching us to deign to confirm this election with apostolic authority. For we, diligently examining the said election as it befits, because we found it to have been done less canonically, have annulled it, not due to the person to whom laudable testimony is given but due to the flaw in the election, as justice demands, reserving the faculty of electing to the aforementioned dean and chapter out of grace. However, when the same dean and chapter had again convened to deliberate on the election, and, their votes being divided, the greater and wiser part of them elected the same master, and he, when asked persistently by them, refused to consent in any way to the election made of him: We, having held diligent deliberation with our brothers on these matters, considering that by mutual consent of the electors and the elected, since he did not consent, no spiritual marriage was contracted, noting that from the time of this last election, so much time has elapsed that the provision of the said church has devolved to us, and wishing to provide for it, which among all metropolitans rejoices in the special privilege of dignity, a person who is suitable for such a burden and honor, we have granted you, whom the testimonies of many trustworthy and credible people have commended, to be archbishop and shepherd of the aforementioned church, and granting you license to proceed to the same church, we have decided to commit to you its full administration, both spiritual and temporal, with the hope proposed to us that, by the guidance of Him who, giving virtues, bestows rewards and adds grace upon grace, the aforementioned church will receive pleasing increases in both through your diligent study. Since it is fitting for you to respond reverently to the divine calling, we earnestly request, admonish, and exhort your fraternity, through apostolic writings, that embracing humbly and devoutly what has been done by us, indeed by the Lord, you proceed to the same church, to conduct its care so faithfully and prudently that you may be able to render a worthy account of it to God. Given at Viterbo, on the 6th day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

To Alexander, Bishop of Coventry, and his canonically appointed successors, in perpetuity. In the eminent Apostolic See... Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously accede to your just requests and take under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the church of Coventry, over which you are known to preside by God's authority, and we fortify it with the privilege of this present document; decreeing that whatever possessions and goods the same church justly and canonically possesses at present or may acquire in the future, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. He also attempted to oppress certain women in the same monastery, where a refuge is established and where one ought to serve the Lord with a pure heart and body, and was often shamefully found with married women, so that he labored under public infamy for the crime of adultery; for which reason certain men left their wives, and he, often redeeming his guilt with money, has hitherto escaped canonical punishment. Removing good and discreet men from the monastery, he retained fools, boys, and other useless people, so that he might more freely indulge in pleasures. Furthermore, when he obtained letters from us to a certain canon of Châlons for certain matters, he presumed to use a similar seal of the aforementioned judge, in his name, for summoning, excommunicating, and absolving; by which occasion the judge himself was captured at Châlons the same week the abbot's procurator was captured at Paris for false privileges, and it was publicly spread throughout France and Burgundy that the abbot himself had committed the crime of this forgery. We, indeed, having thoroughly inspected the privileges sent to our presence, found that the one fabricated under the name of our predecessor, Pope Eugene of blessed memory, was entirely false, and that another obtained from Pope Alexander of happy memory was falsified. Therefore, we command you to diligently and carefully investigate the above matters, reporting faithfully to us what you find, and assigning him a suitable term to present himself in our presence, to receive punishment according to his merits. While this question was pending before him, the bishop nonetheless summoned him to ordinations under the title of the chapel. He humbly requested both from the bishop and from Hameric Odart and Laurentio, canons of Le Mans, to whom the bishop had delegated his powers to hear his arguments, that, since the bishop was compelling him to ordinations because of the chapel, he should completely suspend the aforementioned question, or, at the very least, cease from this coercion until it was proven that the chapel had such a cure, which he denied, especially since these two things seemed contradictory—that he was claimed to be deprived by the chapel yet was ordained under its title. He did not refuse to be ordained to it if he could retain it with another benefice, as was granted to him by the Apostolic See. But because the aforementioned auditors and the bishop refused to hear him on these matters unjustly, he decided to appeal to our hearing; however, the bishop, ignoring the appeal and adding grievance upon grievance, deprived him of the chapel, bypassing the due order of law, while he was personally pursuing the appeal. But even if the chapel has such a cure, which he entirely denies, he could with good reason be ignorant of it, especially since the blessings of the nuptial rites are performed in the parish church, the bodies of the deceased are carried there, and the priest thereof provides them with ecclesiastical sacraments, through which and other means he asserts the cure of souls pertains to the said church. To the Archbishop and Treasurer of Corinth and the Dean of Patras. To the bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See. We have received from our venerable brother, the bishop of Brescia, information that the monastery of St. Euphemia in Brescia, under his jurisdiction, had become spiritually and temporally weakened due to the malice of its inhabitants. The monks of the monastery unanimously granted him the power to provide an abbot. After careful deliberation, he appointed as abbot our beloved son A., a monk of St. Paul of the Cluniac order, a prudent and honorable man, through whose diligence the monastery was believed to be restored to its proper state. All the monks, except a certain young man named F., who prematurely aspired to the position, willingly accepted him, offering obedience and reverence. However, F., with the help of some powerful friends and by corrupting certain monks, presumed to stubbornly rebel against the abbot. Both the abbot and the monks obtained various letters from us addressed to different judges, but the case could not proceed due to jurisdictional disputes among the judges. Meanwhile, the goods of the monastery were being squandered by F. and his followers and their friends. The bishop of Brescia humbly petitioned us to call this matter to the examination of the Apostolic See. Wishing to safeguard the monastery, we assigned the matter to our beloved son, the abbot of Cerreto of the Cistercian order, and his co-judges, instructing them firmly to retrieve the letters obtained by both parties and the processes that occurred through them, to hear the case, and, with the consent of the parties, to conclude it; otherwise, they were to send it back to us sufficiently instructed. They summoned the monks legally, but neither they nor a suitable representative appeared. They set a peremptory term for presenting their legal defenses, yet they ignored it. The judges, having received the arguments of the abbot and the processes presented by the delegated judges, set another peremptory term for the parties to present themselves before us to receive a just sentence. But when the time came, neither the monks nor any representative appeared. At the insistence of Ar., the abbot’s procurator, we appointed our venerable brother, the bishop of Ostia, as auditor in this matter. Upon opening the acts of judgment transmitted by the judges, he found, as confirmed by public instruments, that the abbot held possession of spiritual and temporal matters. Yet, the Patriarch of Antioch, then legate of the Apostolic See, assigned the temporal care of the monastery to Henry Golte without consulting the abbot due to scandals, causing the abbot to lose both spiritual and temporal possession. The monks, though bound by numerous excommunications, could not be persuaded to turn from their evil ways, prompting a request for us to provide a suitable remedy. Desiring to counteract their malice and provide for the monastery to prevent significant loss due to the absence of a pastor, we instructed our venerable brother, the bishop, and our beloved sons Rodulf and Lanfranc, canons of Bergamo, to remove any occupants, restore the abbot to his spiritual and temporal possessions, defend him, and suppress the opposition by ecclesiastical censure, invoking secular arm assistance. They sought support from the noble power of Brescia, who refused. They went to the monastery with some God-fearing soldiers, but F.'s brothers, Vitestus and Izulinus, with followers, attacked them with swords and stones, injuring the noble R. of Rodengo and ejecting the judges contemptuously. Consequently, the judges excommunicated Vitestus, Izulinus, and their followers. Furthermore, the power of Brescia compounded the contempt by compelling the soldiers to provide surety due to their lawful access with the judges. Therefore, we command you to ensure that, if true, Vitestus, Izulinus, and their followers are publicly declared excommunicated until due satisfaction, avoiding them as just, and send F., suspended, to our presence. Compel the power to release the surety through ecclesiastical censure if he does not comply. Ensure no disturbance in the community of Brescia, etc. Given at Interamna, on the Kalends of July, in the tenth year of our pontificate.
