The archdeaconry of Salins, with all its revenues from its jurisdictions, was allegedly granted by the request of the canons of the Church of Saint John to the Church of Saint Stephen, and it is presumed that all was done rightly and in order. For, if the instrument of a notary is to be trusted, if it declares that something was done in his presence, then much more should the instrument of an ordinary judge, which is undoubtedly an authentic instrument; and thus both the handing over and the consent of the chapter are legitimately proven. Nor was the subscription of the canons necessary in this case: both because it should not be properly called alienation when it is not given to a person strange to it, but to its own church; and because it does not seem contrary to reason that a bishop can transfer one of his churches to another or subject it to another, and remit episcopal rights in some part of his diocese even to a stranger, reserving something for himself in the name of a pension, especially if this is strengthened by the confirmation of the Roman Pontiff; and also because subscription is not of the essence of the contract. Nor is it a mere handing over, as alleged on your part, since it was done for a reason, namely to avoid scandal or discord that had already arisen between the said churches of Saint John and Saint Stephen, as is asserted to be contained in the letters of Anseric, in which he offered to prove that the seal of the chapter of Saint John was appended. But even if it had been a mere handing over, it is not true that ownership would not be transferred by it, since ownership is transferred by handing over and usucaption, and nothing is so naturally equitable as the will of the owner who wishes to transfer his thing to another being ratified. As for what you alleged, that spiritual things cannot be understood by the name of revenues, the same archdeacon responded contrariwise that such an interpretation was too forced, since it is not expressly found that spiritual things cannot be comprehended under the term revenues. For from the fact that the same Anseric in the handing over excepted only one thing, namely the services of the archbishop passing through, it is understood that he granted all others universally. Furthermore, what you alleged about the confirmation of the Roman Pontiffs, the said archdeacon declared to be frivolous, since it was not a simple confirmation as is usually done in common form, but it was done with the certain knowledge of those confirming. For that which is otherwise invalid in itself is strengthened by the protection of confirmation, if it is done with certain knowledge. As for what you alleged, that the said archdeacon could not use concession and prescription, the same archdeacon said this does not obstruct, since, as he asserts, it pertains to the plaintiff who cannot say he is the owner from various causes, but it is otherwise in the defendant who is not prohibited from using diverse defenses. Which concession, even if it seemed less sufficient, should suffice for a title, since a less sufficient title gives a cause for prescribing. Nor is what you proposed on your part about interruption true, as he asserts, because, although he confessed certain acts, those acts do not induce any interruption. When the same cardinal prudently and faithfully reported these and other things that were proposed before him to us and our brothers, we, having held a diligent discussion on these matters, with their counsel, for caution, having relaxed the sentences of interdict and excommunication placed on the premises and not annulling in any way the process of the aforementioned people of Chalon, we condemn the said archdeacon concerning all the above matters by sentence, imposing perpetual silence on him, and prohibiting him that he should not, either by himself or by others, presume to molest you or your successors concerning these and other matters pertaining to episcopal jurisdiction, since, even if it were established that the consent of the chapter was present in the aforesaid concession, and nothing reasonable were alleged against it, it should not, however, be extended except to the temporal things that come from the revenues of the jurisdictions; in all of which revenues from the archiepiscopal jurisdictions and jurisdiction, no prejudice from this sentence should be generated against the said archdeacon and the archdeaconry of Salins, to whom all his rights in these are reserved intact. Let no one therefore infringe our definition etc. But if anyone etc. Given at the Lateran, on the 4th of June, in the thirteenth year.

To the same. We are deeply moved by the heavy and grievous burdens and labors that our beloved son, Raymond Bernard, prior of Manso, is known to have endured for the sake of ecclesiastical liberty. We sympathetically share his sufferings and pains with paternal affection, and we grieve from the depths of our hearts. For when the nobleman, the Count of Toulouse, unjustly deprived him and his church of Manso, including secular jurisdiction and possession or quasi-possession belonging to the same church, extorting an oath of fealty from the men of the said town, that same prior was eventually restored to all things, along with the fruits received from them and those that could have been received, through the authority of our sentence, after the merits of the case were known, by the deans of Saint Andrew and Saint Severin of Bordeaux. The said count was condemned to make appropriate satisfaction for expenses, damages, and injuries caused by him to the same prior and church.

And because the aforementioned count not only stubbornly refused to obey the sentence but also, through himself and William Arnold, his seneschal and other accomplices, treated the prior more harshly than before, rashly violating his oath concerning this matter, those judges first pronounced sentences of excommunication against them, and finally, as the count's contumacy became manifest, pronounced sentences of interdict against his land and any place he might come to, as justice demanded. Although we, considering those sentences valid, ordered them to be inviolably observed until due satisfaction was made, and although those sentences were aggravated as required by the obstinacy of the aforementioned count, the Bishop of Sorano, then the legate of the Apostolic See in those parts, following the impulse of his will and not the judgment of reason, without consulting the prior, unwarrantedly relaxed those sentences without satisfaction having been made and without observing any form of justice, to the grave prejudice and almost irreparable harm of the prior and church.

Wherefore, the same prior humbly supplicated us that, since, worn out by labors and exhausted by expenses, and also broken by a long illness he suffered at the Apostolic See, he is not sufficient to prosecute the matter, and because the process of the bishop ought to be considered null by law since it was presumptuously undertaken contrary to the form of law, we might command it to be declared null. Although the bosom of the Church ought to be opened to those who humbly return to its command, yet because in the absolution of such people the right of another ought not to be entirely absorbed, we command you to earnestly admonish and induce the above-mentioned count and seneschal to fully and completely make satisfaction for the premises within two months from your admonition, without causing them any further trouble concerning this matter; otherwise, since such absolution is not valid by law, we decided that henceforth they and their land should be returned to the original sentences of excommunication and interdict, which, after the lapse of this period, you shall see to be inviolably observed until due satisfaction, all appeals, contradictions, and excuses ceasing. Notwithstanding the constitution concerning two days [etc., as noted above in the letters numbered 5076, to the end]. Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of March, in the third year.

**Translation to English:**

To Rusudan, queen, and David, her son, illustrious king of the Georgians. 

We rejoice exceedingly for you, dear children, as the miraculous light of the Word of God has become known to your loving hearts, and that, as you have written, the faith in your lands has remained firm and unblemished since the time of the nascent Church. We also rejoice further that the Son of God, lowering the heavens of His mercy, has led you to the knowledge of His name. However, our conceived joy is diminished by your letters informing us that the Tartars, enemies of the Catholic faith, have invaded your kingdom and inflicted severe damage upon you, thus wounding the joy we had gained. Nevertheless, we take renewed delight in the fact that, although you initially turned your backs to these enemies, you ultimately managed to secure a decisive victory over the victors and inflicted heavy losses upon those who dared to take up arms to your detriment. 

It is fitting that you should also sympathize with us, as we suffer many persecutions from the enemies of the faith at this time. Beyond the Saracens who attack the Catholic faith in the parts of Spain and Syria, there are others who have apostatized from the faith of Christ and, attacking the Church of God with whatever strength they can muster, seek to introduce a new sect of perdition and to exterminate the faith of salvation and human redemption from the earth. Nevertheless, we hope that our Redeemer, after this storm, will bring calm and will not fail to crush the adversaries of the Apostolic See beneath His feet.

Therefore, dear children, cease to marvel if the army of the Roman Church has not come to your aid against the said Tartars, because this has been hindered by the malice of the Saracens, whom we have commanded to be attacked in the said Syria, and by the distances between lands, which barely allowed them to come to us, preventing us from sufficiently sending aid to you, we who are laboring unceasingly with all our might for the defense of the Christian faith in Italy and the said regions of Syria and Spain. 

Hence, as we have been unable to assist you in any other way, we have decided to send our letters to your sincerity so that, though you could not have known our love for you by the expected aid, you might at least recognize the sign of the charity we bear towards you through this writing. 

Regarding your request and petition to unite your house with ours, we exalt your greatness with higher praise in the Lord, for this will more fully accomplish the perfection of your salvation, and our joy for you will be fulfilled in a measure pressed down and shaken together, if perhaps anything had been omitted for your salvation until now. For there is one Catholic Church. Wherefore, dearest children, it is fitting that you and all others subject to your jurisdiction humbly recognize the Roman Pontiff, the successor of blessed Peter, as the vicar of Christ, the father and head of your faith, lamenting that you did not do this in past times, and that you unite yourselves with him and the Roman Church, and be diligent in obeying in those matters which pertain to the salvation of your souls, for we ask nothing else from you. Thus we earnestly admonish, beseech, and exhort your highness, imploring you by the sprinkling of the Blood of Jesus Christ, to recognize the Roman Church as your mother, to obey its pontiff, and to diligently lead your subjects to the obedience of the Apostolic See, so that by this your crown may be doubled in heaven, as by your effort the East and West shall unite in the bond of ecclesiastical unity. Moreover, we urge you to kindly receive our beloved sons, brothers Hugucione, Jacob, Benevenutus, Rubinus, Peter, Bernard, Lambert, and Guizard, of the Order of Preachers, who are powerful in Word and in whom life invigorates doctrine, and doctrine informs life, as what is read in their conduct they expound in their words, and to heed their salutary counsel. 

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January, in the thirteenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX Rusudani reginae et Davidi regi Georgianorum significat se gaudere de fide eorum firma et de victoria contra Tartaros, hortans eos ut Romanam Ecclesiam matrem recognoscant et obedientiam praestent. Dat. Laterani, idibus januarii, anno tertiodecimo.

But the same provost of Saint-Omer and Master William of Cornillon, a canon of Morinensis, to whom the said bishop wholly delegated his powers, after the legitimate excuse of the said provost of Wastines, erroneously announced that the appeal of the same woman was legitimate and the aforementioned sentence of excommunication did not stand. From which the said knight, appealing to the Apostolic See, obtained from us letters directed to our venerable brother, the bishop of Cambrai, containing the instruction that he should, if proceeding with the consent of the parties, conclude such a case with a canonical end; otherwise, he should remit the same case to us sufficiently instructed, setting a peremptory term for the parties, by which they should present themselves before us in person or through competent procurators to receive a sentence. When the process of the same case was finally remitted to the examination of the Apostolic See, and the aforementioned knight personally appeared before us for this reason, we granted our beloved son, Robert, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace, as auditor. But, as the same woman neither came nor sent a representative at the term set for her, nor afterwards, even after being long awaited, the cardinal himself, having diligently examined the merits of the case, revoked the process of the aforementioned provost and William, declaring, as justice demanded, the definitive sentence of the same Reims officials to have been justly pronounced and the preceding sentence of excommunication to be observed inviolably. Therefore, we command that the same sentence of excommunication be inviolably observed by our authority, until proper satisfaction is made, with the appeal being set aside. If both cannot act, etc. Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the calends of June, in the fourteenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Honorius III episcopo et decano Atrabatensibus mandat ut sententiam excommunicationis in Margaretam, relictam quondam Walteri de Senebecha, pro causa matrimoniali cum Johanne de Fossa, inviolabiliter observari faciant, appellatione remota, usque ad satisfactionem condignam. Dat. Laterani, V kalendas junii, anno quartodecimo.

To the bishops of Paris and Soissons, and to Master G. Goin, canon of Reims. We have long learned from the insinuation of the beloved sons of the chapter of Bayeux that Odo of Ville-Terrici, the former dean of Bayeux, on the day he was elected dean, solemnly swore in the chapter of Bayeux that he would have himself ordained as a priest as soon as possible, as the administration of the deanery and the custom of the church required. However, he ignored his oath and delayed this for seven years, ultimately discarding his clerical habit and tonsure, becoming a secular knight to the detriment of his soul and the scandal of many. He then, in the presence of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Sens, and many others, swore and contracted marriage in fact with the daughter of Geoffrey de Belliacot, a knight of the diocese of Auxerre, alleging that he was not in holy orders.

Furthermore, understanding that this marriage, or rather cohabitation, could be challenged because he was in the order of subdeacon, he wished to return to the deanery, which he had renounced, and to prevent the election of a new dean at the said church, he made a frivolous appeal to us through his procurator. Since the aforementioned matters were said to be so notorious in those parts that they could not be concealed by any subterfuge, we instructed Masters Hugh of Pisa, then cantor and now archdeacon of Rouen, Simon of Sens, and Peter known as Caligarius, canon of Morigny, by our letters, that if they found faith in these matters or any of them, they should enjoin the chapter to provide for a dean by canonical election within three months; otherwise, they should command the bishop of Bayeux, of blessed memory, to provide for a suitable person as dean by apostolic authority, suppressing opposers, etc.

Later, when the procurator of the said Odo appealed from Peter and the sub-delegates of the aforementioned judges to our hearing, we committed this cause to you, brother bishop of Soissons, and you, son G., with a certain form. However, although it is said that you proceeded for some time in this matter, as we have heard, you did not finally conclude it. Desiring to bring this matter to an end, we command your discretion, in which we have full confidence in the Lord, by apostolic letters, to diligently inquire into the truth of the aforementioned excesses of the said Odo. If you find that they are substantiated or any of them, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See or any other proceedings through them, provided that no contestation of the suit has proceeded through them, proceed in the same cause according to the form given to the aforementioned judges, and decree the said Odo deprived of all ecclesiastical benefice.

And because we do not wish him to incur peril to his soul, since it does not befit him, constituted in holy orders, to live secularly, we instruct that, having enjoined him penance for these excesses, he be received anew as a canon and brother in the church of Bayeux, if it can be done without scandal, otherwise in the church of Lisieux or Coutances, and be provided with a prebend as soon as the opportunity offers, notwithstanding a certain number of canons, any oath or any firm agreement, or if others have been provided by our mandate, or the constitution of the two diets decreed in the general council, provided no part exceeds a fifth or sixth, etc. Opposers, etc. If not all, etc. Given at the Lateran, on the calends of December, in the thirteenth year.

Against him, among other things, your procurator proposed that the instrument by which Ubertino tried to prove the excommunication was false, as was clearly evident from its content, and that the sentence of excommunication had been pronounced after a legitimate appeal had been made to us, and that Ubertino had been summoned to the election, and no letters of prohibition to prevent the election from being held had been presented to you on behalf of the legate. We have further heard that the said C. and B., her accomplice who acted as the prioress of that monastery, heard the confessions of all the sisters and the religious residing in the monastery before taking up the same order, enjoining them that if they ever wished to confess to another, they should have this form only of confession about all their sins, namely: "My fault, because neither do I love my abbess nor my prioress, and not showing them due reverence, I have not kept diligence in the canonical hours." Moreover, what is more heinous and horrible to hear, she would sometimes reproach those confessing their sins to her with all the sisters listening and sometimes publicly disgrace them; and just as she then afflicted them with beatings, so now she does not hesitate to afflict them, one of them dying from the beatings of the aforementioned prioress before they adopted the rule of the said order; she often tormented them with severe hunger, having alms given to the same monastery sold for common benefit out of piety, and forbade two sick sisters from having light or care, who, with no one seeing, passed away from this world. What more? Not content that she herself and her aforementioned sister frequently struck several of the aforementioned sisters with clubs, and that the said C., inflamed with a spirit of fury, wounded one of them with a sword, she forbade those adhering to her from confessing to anyone about the violent laying on of hands on the same sisters except to herself, violently extorting an oath from two of the same sisters to stand by her commands. But, lest such pestilent ones, known to be members of Satan, rejoice to persecute and crush the spouses of Christ thus, we command that, if the truth supports the aforementioned, you compel the oft-mentioned C. and her accomplice who are said to have been cloistered elsewhere before they entered the same monastery, to undergo perpetual penance in some reclusory, invoking if need be the aid of the secular arm. Moreover, those who adhered to the said pestilent ones, that they take up the aforementioned Cistercian order according to their promise, you carefully induce with the prudence given to you by God; and if they perhaps will not comply with your admonitions, you endeavor to place them in other monasteries of the order of St. Benedict. Opponents, etc. Given at the Lateran, the ides of December, in the fourteenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX abbati Sancti Galgani, Vulterane diocesis, mandat ut, si veritas suffragatur, C. monialem et B. sociam eius, quae pestilentes et sathane membra dicuntur, ad perpetuam poenitentiam in reclusorio compellat; et illas quae adhaeserunt, inducat ad susceptionem ordinis Cisterciensis, alioquin disponat collocandas in aliis monasteriis ordinis sancti Benedicti; contradictores puniat. Datum Laterani, idibus Decembris, anno quarto decimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Vienna, and the bishops of Béziers and Carcassonne.

The petition presented to us by our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Auch, as well as the bishops, and our beloved sons, the prelates, chapters, and convents of the province of Auch, stated that, although we had previously given you instructions in our letters to impose the payment of eight thousand livres Tournois, less one hundred, on the churches of the provinces of Vienne, Arles, Narbonne, Auch, and Bordeaux, and the dioceses of Albi, Cahors, Mende, and Rodez, considering their resources, in proportional amounts. This sum was owed to our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Bordeaux and the bishop of Agen, to Raimundo de Caturco, a layman, and to the executors of the testament of the late John Biston, as well as to Peter de Borneol, by the noble man, the Count of Montfort, who had long labored in the regions of the Albigensians for the cause of peace and faith. You were to compel them to pay this sum to the said creditors through ecclesiastical censure, after prior admonition and putting aside any appeal. However, without considering the meager revenues of the churches of the province of Auch, and without consulting them, you improperly imposed one thousand five hundred livres Tournois upon this province to be paid to the aforementioned creditors in the name of the said count; an appeal was made to us from this on behalf of these parties.

Therefore, we, understanding that burdens are more easily borne when fitted to the shoulders of those who carry them, have deemed it necessary to moderate your imposition on the said province. We ordain that our venerable brother, the Bishop of Lectoure, who, having been long stationed at the Apostolic See for his and his church's business, has borne heavy expenses, along with his diocese, be absolved from such a contribution, and that one hundred and fifty livres be paid by our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Narbonne, and one hundred and fifty by the Bishop of Toulouse, one hundred by the Bishop of Agen, and one hundred by the Bishop of Poitiers, with the prior imposition on them preserved, to the aforementioned creditors in the name of the said count, without any difficulty.

Therefore, we mandate through apostolic writings that you nullify any actions presumed after such an appeal and compel the said Archbishop of Auch and his province to pay one thousand livres within the established terms, ensuring the remainder of the said money is paid to the aforementioned creditors according to your regulation without any difficulty. Opponents, etc. But if not all, etc.

Given at Grottaferrata, on the calends of August, in the fourteenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX archiepiscopo Viennensi, Biterrensi et Carcasonensi episcopis mandat ut, appellatione interposita, mille libras archiepiscopus Auxitanus cum provincia solvat, taxationem moderando, et residuum pecuniae creditoribus in nomine comitis Montis Fortis secundum ordinationem suam persolvatur. Datum apud Criptam Ferratam, kalendis augusti, anno quartodecimo.

Translation to English:

To the Archbishop of Sens. The authority of the Apostle's dignity, the ship of Peter, decreed to not unworthily call upon the hands of the strong, namely kings, prelates, princes, and other faithful ones, so that, by multiplying cries, it may awaken the sleeping Lord and, assisted by the counsel of many, make the pressing burdens lighter, happily seeking the desired haven of the expedition. However, as we have learned for certain, that singular son of the Church, once elevated and defended by the aid of the Apostolic Mother and Province, was then transferred to the summit of the Empire by maternal support when he was devoid of any assistance. Not content with that injury, he, repaying with unjust reward, breaks into his father's throne, indevoutly attempts to lay bare the mother’s modesty and sell the sanctuary, still arming insidious plots against it, forbidding prelates summoned by us from approaching through his terrors, so that, lacking any calumny, he may not allow her, whom he besets with grave troubles, to breathe even in the solace of her sons. Therefore, since such a holy purpose of general utility, assumed under the trust of divine favor, ought not to be delayed by human cunning, we earnestly beseech and admonish your fraternity, strictly commanding by apostolic writings in the virtue of obedience, that, preferring God to man and placing the merit of obedience before difficulties, you do not omit to personally come to the Apostolic See until the next forthcoming feast of the Lord's Resurrection, so that the mother, strengthened by the presence of her sons, may, with divine providence removing the obstacle of the adversary and opponent, conclude the beginnings of her pious intention in happy completion. For we, with the Lord's favor, will take care to provide for all that are necessary for executing such a great matter, as the bearer of these presents will more fully communicate to you. Moreover, we desire and command that you instruct your suffragans and their chapters, abbots, etc., as noted above in the letter numbered 5420, to not postpone. Given at the Lateran, the Ides of October, in the fourteenth year.

Regesto in Latin:

Papa (Gregorius IX) archiepiscopo Senonensi mandat ut ad Sedem Apostolicam accedat usque ad proximum festum Resurrectionis Dominicae, ut, roborata filiorum praesentia, adversarii impedimenta sublata, pietatis consilia feliciter impleantur. Dat. Laterani, idibus Octobris, anno quartodecimo.

**Translation to English:**

The letters of the legate regarding the obligation of the possessions of the churches of Genoa. To the most holy father in Christ and lord, lord Gregory, by the grace of God, the supreme pontiff of the Holy Roman Church, Gregory of Romania, your devoted servant, prostrates himself at your feet. Upon arriving in Genoa, Brother Nicholas proposed that you entirely desired for me to procure galleys, ships, and other vessels for transporting and returning prelates and others coming to the council, with sufficient surety received from the community of Genoa for the promises made. With much labor and distress, which cannot be adequately explained in brief words, I accomplished this with the counsel of all those whom you mentioned in your letters, as many sought to obstruct the affair, and without counsel, I could accomplish nothing in these matters unless I first paid a thousand marks to the community of Genoa for the preparation of the galleys and transports, which they count in the convention and payment. Of these thousand marks, I received three thousand five hundred and fifty pounds of Genoese currency, which I paid them; and I gave two hundred pounds of Genoese currency to merchants who lent the said marks for payment. For these marks, the Genoese prelates pledged their possessions to the merchants. And I wrote to the lord bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, to pay five thousand and fifty-seven marks of silver, which fifty-seven I promised to the merchants for their salary, including these thousand marks I received; and the merchants are bound to give two thousand marks to your envoys in Genoa, within a month after reception in France, and another two thousand marks in the following month. And if this money is not entirely necessary for this business, the remainder will be used as you please. I send to Your Holiness the agreements made concerning the aforementioned business enclosed with these presents. To this end, for the entire service which I have rendered to you and the Roman Church, I earnestly request and humbly beseech that you grant me permission to return, as I no longer wish to remain in Genoa. Please have Master Peter of Guarcino recommended regarding the church of St. Sixtus of Genoa, for whom I previously appealed to you. Given at Genoa, the 20th of December.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX, Gregorio de Romania, mandato quod procuravit galeas et alia vasa pro prelatis et aliis ad concilium venientibus conducendis, et postulatione ut redeundi licentiam tribuatur. Datum Janue, XX die Decembris, anno quarto.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Albi, the prior of Saint Caprasius of Agen, and the archpriest of Saint Gervase of the diocese of Albi. Our venerable brother, the bishop of Toulouse, has informed us that we had previously learned that he had received a considerable sum of money from the redemption of crusaders' vows. By our letters, we instructed him to pay from this amount the debt owed by the Roman Church to Bulgarinus, a citizen of Genoa, for principal and expenses. Having paid 420 pounds of Tours currency, which he received from the redemption of said vows, he sought to pay the remainder, which reached a sum of 600 pounds, from his own resources to the said citizen to avoid being seen as disobedient to our mandate.

Although we later ordered through our venerable brother, the bishop of Agen, and his colleagues that satisfaction be given to the same bishop concerning the money which our venerable brother, the bishop of Carcassonne, and his colleagues were said to have received from the redemption of vows of crusaders of the dioceses of Toulouse and Carcassonne, it was found through an investigation made by the same bishop of Agen and his colleagues that the bishop of Carcassonne and his aforementioned colleagues had received nothing from these redemptions, and satisfaction has not yet been made to him in this regard. Therefore, he has humbly recurred to us, devoutly beseeching us to order satisfaction to be made to him from the redemption of vows of crusaders of the dioceses of Cahors, Toulouse, and Albi for the aforementioned 600 pounds which, in addition to the 420 pounds, he asserts to have paid to the said citizen.

Therefore, not wishing for the obedience of the aforementioned bishop to be detrimental to him, we command you to ensure that satisfaction is made to him from the redemption of vows of crusaders of the aforementioned dioceses of Cahors, Toulouse, and Albi, excepting those who, being accused of the crime of heresy, have taken up the sign of the cross for the aid of the Holy Land, after the truth has been fully inquired into concerning these matters, through those whom you ascertain to have received these redemptions. Opponents, etc. If all are not, etc. Given at the Lateran, on the 3rd nones of March, in the fourth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa [Nomen Papae] episcopo Albiensi, priori Sancti Caprasii Agennensis, et archipresbytero Sancti Gervasii Albiensis mandat ut de redemptionibus votorum crucesignatorum diocesium Caturcensis, Tolosanae, et Albiensis, exceptis infamatis de crimine haeresis, episcopo Tolosano satisfaciant pro sexcentis libris quas de proprio Bulgarino civi Januensi persolvit. Dat. Laterani, III nonas martii, anno quarto.

**Translation to English:**

Memorial of Brother Nicholas, of the Cistercian Order. First, you shall present all letters to Gregory of Romagna, and you yourself, along with Peter of Guarcino, shall secretly deal with the authority of Genoa, having received an oath from this authority to keep secret what is proposed to them by you, regarding the imminent business expressed in our letters, taking the actions you deem expedient, according to the form expressed in the apostolic letters; and, if you deem it appropriate, you may reveal our plan to William of Nigro, under the same caution, and with their counsel, you may communicate the aforementioned business to other devotees of the Church, under the same caution; so that, aided by their advice and help, you may firmly strengthen the Church's purpose. Concerning the freight of ships, galleys, and smaller vessels for conveying and returning prelates and others who are coming to the council, you shall prudently and cautiously induce the Genoese to receive a moderate amount of money, and endeavor that the money for freight payment be received in the Kingdom of France, or take out a loan under the caution and obligation of the prelates, as expressed in our letters, to be paid at a certain term and annually. We, however, strictly command you, in virtue of obedience, to put such effective effort into this business that our plan may in all ways be happily accomplished, and the Roman Church is not in any way defrauded of its intention; especially as we command the prelates that they will have safe passage going and returning by the ships, galleys, and smaller vessels of the Genoese, concerning whom we should not be accused of falsehood. You shall also propose to the aforementioned that this which is done, by the Lord as the doer, shall pertain to the honor of God, the exaltation of the Church, their perpetual liberty, and the increase of their city. You shall also tell them that, although it is hoped by many counts, barons, and other noble and trustworthy men that a safe passage by land for the prelates can be obtained, yet because we trust more in the constancy, faith, and devotion of the Genoese, we wish them to gain more honor from this. Furthermore, know that we have commanded that the amount you, son Gregory, deem to be expressed in your letters be paid to the aforementioned Genoese by the legate of France and others where the Church's money is kept. And although the Genoese are accustomed to giving a well-armed galley for two hundred pounds of Genoese money for one month, as we have already learned by experience, you should strive to obtain it for less if possible. We consider ships necessary for carrying a multitude of clerics and others. You shall also make provision with the Genoese regarding suitable places where the prelates and others coming to the council may be received.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius Papa IX Fratri Nicolao ordinis Cisterciensis mandat ut litteras ad potestatem Januensem deferat et cum Petro de Guarcino secreto agat super negotio imminenti in litteris expressis, sub cautionibus congruis. Spiritum cooperantiae cum Guglielmo de Nigro et aliis Ecclesiae devotis hortatur ad firmandum Ecclesiae propositum. Mandat ut pecunia pro naulo navium in regno Francorum solvatur et ut de loco receptionis praelatorum cum Januensibus provideatur. Datum Laterani, anno pontificatus nostri tertio.

**Translation to English:**

To the dean and chancellor of Paris, and Master Vernacius, a canon of Treviso, residing in Paris. On behalf of our beloved sons, the provost and chapter of the church of Casletensis, it was presented to us that the abbot and convent of Chokes, of the Morinensis diocese, brought them to court before the abbot of Mariolo and his colleague, by apostolic authority, over certain tithes which they claimed belonged to them. Eventually, the case was brought to us by appeal, and we decided to assign it to J., the said Major, a canon of Atrebatensis, and his colleagues. Two of them, in the absence of the third who neither delegated his duties to another nor excused himself legitimately, improperly proceeded both in the appeal and the principal matter. The intention of neither party was well-founded, nor was there a proper contestation of the suit, nor a renouncement of evidence, nor was the case concluded. However, they pronounced an unjust definitive sentence against them. The said provost and chapter appealed this sentence to our hearing, obtaining the assignment of their appeal to the dean of Noyon and his co-judges, under the condition that, if matters were as stated, they should restore everything to its proper state that had been rashly attempted after the legitimate appeal was interposed to us; they should hear the matters proposed from both sides and, if it proceeded with the consent of the parties, terminate the case justly and have their decisions firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. Otherwise, sufficiently instructing the case, they should remit it to the apostolic examination and assign a suitable peremptory term for the parties to present themselves before us through a suitable procurator to receive a just sentence from the Lord. Since the parties consented that the judges should terminate the case without appeal and without remitting it to us, the said judges, having entirely revoked the process of the said canon and his co-judges, knowing the case from the beginning, pronounced a definitive sentence against them regarding both the said tithes and the restitution of certain received fruits, decreeing that they should desist from further collection of the said tithes and allow the said abbot and convent to peacefully collect the same tithes in the future, although the latter party had not entirely founded their intention. The dean of Lille was granted as executor to enforce the said sentence, and letters of confirmation of the sentence were obtained from the Apostolic See in common form. Therefore, it was humbly petitioned on behalf of the said provost and chapter that, since the Casletensis church is harmed by the enormous loss due to the aforesaid sentence, from which they could not appeal due to an express renunciation, and the said executor has pronounced sentences of interdict and excommunication against them, we should assist them with the benefit of restitution in full. Therefore, we command that if it is thus, relaxing such sentences according to the form of the Church, after first receiving sufficient and suitable security from them that, if it appears that they were reasonably pronounced, they will comply with the mandate of the Church regarding those matters for which they were issued, you should, after hearing both sides, admit the aforementioned provost and chapter to appeal by the benefit of restitution in full, notwithstanding the prior renunciation. Once this is interposed, proceeding legitimately in the matter of the appeal, if it proceeds by the will of the parties, you should ensure to confirm or overturn the said definitive sentence, removing the appeal, as ought to be done according to the law. Otherwise, sufficiently instructing the matter, remit it to the apostolic examination and assign a suitable peremptory term for the parties to appear before us through a suitable procurator to receive a just sentence from the Lord. Witnesses, etc. If not all, etc. Given at the Lateran, 15th kalends of February, in the fourth year [of our pontificate].

**Latin Regesto:**

Papa [Author] decano et cancellario Parisiensibus et magistro Vernacio, canonico Tervisino, mandat quatenus, pro causa inter praepositum et capitulum ecclesiae Casletensis et abbatem ac conventum de Chokes super decimis agitata, sententias interdicti et excommunicationis relaxent, si rationabiliter promulgatae non fuerint, et restitutionem in integrum concedant. Si autem res taliter se habet, negotium ad examen apostolicum remittant. Dat. Laterani, XV kalendas februarii, anno quarto [Date].

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See. Since the Roman Church has received a large sum of money under burdensome conditions for the defense of the faith and ecclesiastical liberty, and has not yet satisfied the creditors, even though some due dates for payments have passed, as a result, these creditors, pressing us with urgent complaints, claim that they have incurred significant losses: because the payment of such debts cannot be further delayed due to growing inconveniences without serious detriment to the Church, we have decided to earnestly request and admonish the beloved sons, abbots and convents of certain monasteries of the orders of Saint Benedict, Cluny, and Premonstratensian, whose names are sent to you in a list under our seal, as well as the preceptors and brothers of the Templar and Hospitaller orders in France, by giving them letters with our mandates, that each of the abbots with their convents and the preceptors with their brothers promptly provide a specified sum of money for the payment to these creditors, to our beloved son, Brother Richard of the Templar's house, in the name of the Church, as a loan, for the reverence of us and the Apostolic See, to be fully repaid within at least six months after receiving these letters, from the aid of the English Church. Wherefore, we earnestly ask and exhort your fraternity, commanding you through apostolic letters that if it happens that the creditors cannot be satisfied from the English aid within the appointed terms, so that the Apostolic See does not incur serious harm and the Romans do not become disturbed, from which a danger could easily arise for the main business, since we wish the Gallican aid to remain untouched for the greater necessity of the Church, you diligently involve yourself with the abbots and others mentioned above, that they assist the Church with a loan in this present necessity according to our mandate. For we, binding the same Church by apostolic letters, upon the advice of our brothers, direct our letters to our beloved son Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legate of the Apostolic See, and to the collectors of the aforementioned English aid, that they do not delay assigning the money collected and to be collected for the support of the Church in the English regions, to be delivered to the aforementioned brother in Paris to satisfy the abbots and others noted above. Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of November, in the year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX episcopo Penestrino, Apostolicae Sedis legato, mandat ut diligenter interponat partes suas apud abbates et alios supradictos, ut pecuniam mutuo concedant pro solutione creditorum Ecclesiae Romanae, quam fratri Riccardo de domo militiae Templi tradant, restituendam de subsidio ecclesiae Anglicanae. Dat. Laterani, nonis novembris, anno pontificatus nostri.

Transcript of the instruments concerning the preparation of the ship. In the name of Christ. Amen. Since Lord Gregory of Rome, Legate of the Apostolic See, on behalf of the Lord Pope, by special mandate of the Lord Pope, requested from the community of Genoa to grant galleys and armed ships for the expenses of the Lord Pope or other envoys of the Lord Pope, for the transportation and return of prelates of the churches and other persons to the general council to be held by the Supreme Pontiff, the said Lord Legate, in the name and on behalf of the Supreme Pontiff, on one side, and Henry, son of the late William Judge, syndic of the Genoese community, specially appointed for this by the power and councilors of Genoa, called and gathered to this council by horn and bell, in the usual manner, and also the councilors themselves, on the other side, agreed among themselves regarding the aforementioned galleys and ships and their armaments to be granted to the Lord Pope or his envoys or envoy as follows: that is, the said syndic promised, on behalf of the community, to grant and provide to the Lord Pope or his envoys ten armed galleys for transporting and returning the prelates and others to the council, in such a way that in each galley there will be one hundred and eight sailors and officers, and twenty-six subordinates, and forty supernumeraries, including four chief sailors, one boatswain, one purser, and ten crossbowmen, each of whom shall have two crossbows, one of horn and the other of wood, and in each galley, there shall be one turret crossbow and thirty pieces of iron munitions; and the commune of Genoa will grant and provide this for a compensation or price of 275 pounds for each galley and per each month, at all expenses of the Genoese commune, the Lord Pope or his envoys, or the Lord Legate on behalf of the Lord Pope, making payment of the said reward or price to the Genoese commune for two months, and this before the galleys are armed; **Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Palestrina, Legate of the Apostolic See. Previously, upon hearing that the monastery of Grandmont was gravely disordered both spiritually and temporally, we, in order that it might rise to a state of prosperity and that matters of welfare and tranquility might arise therein, recall having provided, with the counsel of our brothers, that without any difficulty all sentences of interdict and excommunication which had been promulgated against the prior or some of the brothers of the same monastery due to such disorder should be lifted, and that two visitors from the Cistercian and two from the Carthusian orders should be appointed to the Grandmont order, who would, once a year for the following three years at their general chapter, without appeal, establish and reform whatever they recognized needed to be established or reformed in the order, ensuring that these things, without the hindrance of an appeal, would be firmly observed; we also provided that definers, inspectors, or visitors, chosen from the aforementioned order, would examine, correct, determine, and define each matter, saving the rule and constitutions of the same order approved by the Apostolic See, with the remedy of appeal withheld; and, if any doubt should arise, they would send messengers who were not from their order to the Apostolic See, awaiting an apostolic response on this matter. However, so that our provision might have full effect, we commanded our beloved sons, the Abbot of Savigny and the Abbot of Maceyra, of the Cistercian, and the Prior of Louvemont and the Prior of Glanfeuil, of the Carthusian orders, by our letters, to personally go to the place, first releasing the aforementioned sentences and granting a dispensation to the aforementioned brothers if they had celebrated divine services bound by the aforementioned sentences in the meantime, and to correct and reform there whatever they knew needed the office of correction and reformation, both in head and members, appointing, within the said three years, visitors, inspectors, and definers who were indeed discreet men fearing God, from the same order, who would also establish there whatever they might see needed to be established in their order, saving the rule and institutions aforementioned, without appeal, proceeding in all the above simply and without the noise of judgment. Truly, as the procurators of Elias, formerly prior of the aforementioned monastery, having only the mandate to petition and contradict, proposed in the presence of our beloved son Stephen, priest cardinal of the title of Santa Maria in Trastevere, whom we gave as auditor to the parties, the venerable brother our bishop of Poitiers and his colleagues wishing to proceed in the investigation which we had committed to them before the aforementioned provision at the instance of some brothers of the same monastery against the said Elias, it was proposed on behalf of the same prior before them that, both because of the appeal legitimately made for him, since they admitted as witnesses the said brothers bound by excommunication, and exhibited the names of the witnesses produced against him alphabetically, contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, and because the commission made to the aforementioned abbots and priors by which their jurisdiction was revoked, they could not and should not proceed in the investigation itself; and, if they presumed to proceed otherwise, an appeal to the Apostolic See was made for the said prior by his procurator. As some prelates approached the See, and many returned due to fear of the sea, he, upon hearing of the imminent arrival of the remaining ones, laid ambushes and had them detained, along with our venerable brother, the bishop of Palestrina, and our beloved son Ottone, the cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legates of the Apostolic See. As if it were not enough that he had wronged the Church in manifold ways, he inflicted upon it an immeasurable offense. 

Although such actions disturb the minds of the faithful, their hearts should not be swayed, nor should their sincere spirits be bent. Rather, they should support the Church against this persecutor with even greater favor, as they perceive the grave injury he has caused it. Therefore, we urgently admonish, ask, and exhort your community, commanding that you remain steadfast in devotion to the Church. Trust in the Lord and His mighty power; resist His enemies as the most valiant warriors of Christ. Do not let the shock of sudden wicked acts dismay your hearts; rather, let the zeal for God inflame them towards the defense of the Church.

For we intend, with God’s guidance, to provide for these matters, hoping that His right hand will assist us, leading to the defeat of the wicked, the glory of the Most High, the strengthening of the Catholic faith, and the enhancement of ecclesiastical freedom. To the Emperor, without title and attribution. Upon receiving your letters with customary kindness, regarding the matters that our venerable brother, Archbishop Reginus, and our dear son, the master of the house of St. Mary of the Teutons, have reported to you on our behalf, we noticed your surprise to the extent that you expressed disbelief, as if suggesting we do not hold the person of the Bishop of Ostia accountable and have allowed certain actions that he would never have contemplated. In this matter, with a witness in heaven, we find it necessary to respond that the person of the Bishop of Ostia would not have been burdened by the actions of others within the Church, in matters where it is known you have gravely offended us by cruelly exposing some clergy and laity of the Kingdom to disgraceful death during peace negotiations, not without serious injury to the Apostolic See and great insult to the Creator, indeed not without significant offense to our person and detriment to your honor. If you consider rightly, you were the source and origin of these actions and thus bear sole responsibility, rightly subject to blame, with your conscience testifying against you if it requires. But since the Knower of all desires peace, we long for the saving grace of your soul, we pass over the foregoing in silence, sending you the form of peace arranged by the common agreement of our brothers through your princes. Through the same Reginus and our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Salzburg, the Bishop of Regensburg, and our dear son, the noble Duke of Austria, and the aforementioned master, whose words you can trust and who can convey to you the purity of our intention towards you in these matters, we earnestly request and admonish you to reject the book of scandals and adhere to the cultivation of peace, proceeding confidently in its execution, believing that if Mother Church finds you devoted and faithful, she will elevate you with powerful virtue as her son and with virtuous power will exalt you above the sons of men.

Our venerable brother, the bishop of Coria, presented in our presence the matter that the master and brothers of Alcántara, of the military order of Calatrava, who profess the Cistercian order, presume to conduct divine offices through their chaplains and brothers in the churches of de Mascoras, Alcántara, and Portezolo, as well as other churches subject to diocesan law in his diocese that are placed under ecclesiastical interdict by him with ordinary authority, as required by justice. Furthermore, they abuse the privileges and indulgences granted to them by the Apostolic See, refusing to pay the tithes owed from possessions acquired after the general council. They violently seize the bishop's third of the aforementioned and of Moralegia churches, and of all places where they hold temporal dominion in the diocese of Coria, and deprive the bishop of cathedral rights, procurations, and other episcopal rights against justice, denying him the due obedience and reverence. Without consulting the bishop of Coria, they built a monastery in the village of Alcántara in the said diocese, whose prior, installed there by them, later refuses to show him the obedience and reverence due. Moreover, the said master and brothers forcibly expelled his predecessor of good memory, Gerard, and his men from the castle of Ceclavín, which he had built and caused to be inhabited. Not content with these actions, they illegally withhold tithes pertaining to the churches of the said diocese, redeemed from the hands of laymen without his request, and unjustly impede him from instituting and removing clerics in Ceclavín, Alcántara, and the district of St. John de Mascoras, as pertains to him. They injure him regarding the episcopal rights of the town of Valencia and other matters, even though an agreement had been made between them on this issue. Since various letters from the Apostolic See have been obtained by both sides concerning the aforementioned and other diverse articles, through which almost no process has been held, and fearing that due to the malice of the other party, these cases, which have been prolonged due to the cavillations of that party, might become eternally unresolved, he has requested us to providentially safeguard him and the indemnity of his church.

To the noble man, the Duke of Carinthia. We received your letters with the usual kindness and carefully understood them, commending your sincerity with worthy praises in the Lord. You show yourself as a zealous supporter of both the Roman Church, your mother, and the Empire, displaying the due affection of faith and devotion, ready to labor personally at the Apostolic See for negotiating peace, not sparing efforts or expenses. However, since that man, not content with his diligent wickedness having disrupted the affair of the Holy Land, continues stubbornly in his malice, still occupying the land of the patrimony of blessed Peter and aiming to occupy another, there is no hope for his conversion who, in rebellious aversion, has chosen to elevate himself in pride, which indeed customarily brings the elevated down, with God casting down the proud from their seats and exalting the humble. Hence, although we would gladly see your person in presence, lest after many labors and expenses, if you could not call him back to the command of the Church, being frustrated by the fruit of your diligent intention, you would consider yourself deceived, we have not enjoined your coming to us, lest we seem to impose an occasion of confusion upon you; yet we leave it to your judgment, lest anyone suspect us of spurning the counsels of peace. ### Translation to English:

To the bishop of Sabina and Thomas, Cardinal Priest of the title of St. Sabina, legates of the Apostolic See. We have received your letters with usual kindness, and having understood their contents, we and our brothers could not help but be moved because, when a calm serenity was hoped for after the dark storms, a darker storm has come, taking away the pre-conceived hope and instilling fear for the future. Many are murmuring and saying: How can it be believed that what is so severely violated at the conclusion of this negotiation will last? Or how can a scar be healed if it is cut with more severe wounds? However, so that the innocence of the Church may shine and justice be revealed, and the intent of our wishes may be clear to all, we mandate you, by apostolic writings and with the advice of our brothers, that if appropriate satisfaction is offered regarding those matters attempted anew after the journey you undertook, as you wrote, proceed in the name of the Lord according to the form entrusted to you. Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of [month], in the very beginning of peace, that it has proceeded to such things, and that those who stood for the Church in temptation are more frightened than usual, and not without reason, we, from what has been reported to us, hope that Frederick, the so-called emperor, can be easily persuaded to provide an oath of security to those who adhered to the Church. We command that in all possible ways, you should insist that he furnishes the said oath, because he initially strongly resisted making the oath that Your Holiness knows, to fully pardon those who did something against him. But, after various reasons were shown to him, we have induced him in such a way that, as we believe, the business of peace will not be broken because of this.

But because the abbot of Dryburgh and his colleagues declared by interlocution that they should proceed in the principal matter, notwithstanding this objection, Nicholas and Cecilia, feeling unduly aggrieved by this, appealed to the Apostolic See. To the Bishop of London. According to the commission given to you, you have informed us that some clerics of your diocese, due to their violent laying of hands on clerics and religious men, have fallen under the canon of the promulgated sentence, and some of these clerics, without obtaining the benefit of absolution, have received sacred orders and ecclesiastical benefices, and have ministered in the orders thus received. Others, without a certain title and with the agreement that their presenters would not be challenged over their provision, have sought to be promoted to orders and have celebrated after being promoted in such a manner. Therefore, trusting in your discretion and prudence, by the authority of these presents, we commit to you that, having imposed suitable penance, you may, on this occasion, grant the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church to those who have violently laid hands, provided their excesses are not so grave or enormous that they ought rightly to be sent to our presence. And you may dispense with clerics and religious who, having been excommunicated and suspended, celebrated divine offices and were promoted to orders, and ministered in them, as you know to be expedient for their salvation, removing those from benefices who obtained them while excommunicated, and ensuring they are conferred by those to whom they pertain. However, we do not wish those who recently incited sedition against the Apostolic See to be included in the grace of this dispensation and absolution. When he finally returned to the monastery by order of the aforementioned dean, although the abbot and convent received him as they had promised, they began to act more wickedly against him, afflicting him cruelly with various tortures, insults, and beatings while he was held under custodial restraint, until, compelled by force and fear, he resigned from the monastic life and order he had professed, though he could not lawfully do so. Through what you intimated to us by your letters, it was understood that his election was canonical in form, and the same provost was said to be a noble man by birth, prudent and circumspect in spiritual and temporal matters, who labored faithfully and steadfastly for the cause of peace and faith, not fearing loss of goods or dangers to his person. For the confirmation of this election, both you and the said bishop earnestly petitioned us, with many letters not only from prelates but also from other religious persons presented to us, who bore laudable testimony to him. Because we wanted to have fuller certainty of the merits of the elected, we gave you and our venerable brother, the Bishop of Carpentras, a mandate in our letters to admonish the elected on our behalf to present himself personally before us by the recent feast of All Saints. But, afflicted by Him who strikes and heals, he could not come to us, hindered by the weakness said to be incurred from illness. Since our beloved son in Christ, Bernard, succentor of Narbonne, procurator of the same chapter, humbly petitioned us to, with paternal compassion toward the pressures and difficulties of his church, and considering the state of the land, from whose disturbance there is fear, be pleased to confirm this election from the benignity of the Apostolic See, representing to us letters from our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Aragon, and several prelates who commend the same provost in many ways and earnestly petition for him: Therefore, having held diligent counsel and discussion with our brothers on this matter, unwilling that the provision of this church be further delayed, lest it incur grievous harm in spiritual and temporal matters due to prolonged vacancy, and placing full confidence in the Lord in your circumspection, we command that if you find the same provost, after diligent consideration of his life, knowledge, circumspection, prudence, the utility to the same church, and the state of the land, not unworthy and useful to the state of the aforementioned land, you should take care to confirm his election by our authority and ensure that obedience and reverence are shown to him by the subjects of the Church of Maguelonne and the gift of consecration is conferred. To the Archbishop of Sens and his suffragans. 

Having previously understood that in certain provinces, the seamless robe of Christ, which the hands of the crucifiers spared, was being torn by those who crucify Him again in His members, and that the reptiles which once lay hidden in the dust, insidiously lurking at the heel to topple the rider with the horse, now rise up openly and plot evident treachery against the Catholic faith, and also that small creatures which secretly used to damage the Lord’s vineyard were now openly burning the Lord’s harvest with torches tied to their tails: we have directed apostolic writings to the brothers of the Order of Preachers, who have zeal for God and are mighty in deed and word, so that they might rise up powerfully to crush the head of such reptiles, to capture the little foxes, and to restrain with bit and bridle the jaws of those who tore the Church of Christ, and to bring back the wandering sheep to the fold on their shoulders, and also to scrape away with the file of their preaching the rust of ancient corruption from infected souls, so that they might enter clean into the sanctuary of the Lord and reach the heavenly homeland. Moreover, it was neither the intention of the mandator nor the will of the writer that these writings should be issued concerning other provinces than those infamed with heresy; but if perhaps a contrary outcome has followed, we believe that it was due to ignorant occupation or deceitful surreption, and therefore we wish them to lack effect, as the intention of the mandator was not effective cause. Thus, you may not be rebuked like the servant who did not hand over the talent entrusted to him to the bankers for interest, but instead buried it in a napkin. Rather, like the one whom the Lord found faithful over a few things and set over many, may you be worthy to be raised to eternal joys. Furthermore, because these brothers are more suitable for confuting heretics inasmuch as their life enlivens their doctrine and their doctrine informs their life, as what is expounded in words is read in their conduct, we believe it useful for the business of the faith that you call upon them to extirpate the errors of perverse doctrines, as you see fit.
