**Gregorius IX** archiepiscopis Bisuntino, Lugdunensi, Viennensi, Tarantasiensi, Ebredunensi, Aquensi, Arelatensi et Narbonensi, eorumque suffraganeis, episcopis Lemovicensi, Caturcensi, Rutenensi, Albiensi, Mimatensi, Aniciensi, Agennensi, Lectorensi, Petragoricensi, Vasatensi et Convenarum, abbatibus, prioribus, decanis, archidiaconis, prepositis, archipresbiteris et aliis ecclesiarum prelatis mandat ut legatum, episcopum Soranum, recipiant cum honore et eum adiuvant in reformatione Provincie, hereticis pravitatibus abolendis; alioquin sententiam a legato latam ratam habebit. Dat. Anagnie, X kalendas septembris, anno tertio.

**Translation to English:**

In the name of Our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. We, John, abbot of the monastery of Brondulo of the Cistercian order, and Brother Albric, prior of the Dominican friars of Venice, by the commission of Lord Pope Gregory, personally approached the church of Saint Andrew by the shore. With God alone before our eyes, we had their statutes presented to us. Having diligently considered the difficulties contained therein, we found certain things to be of such great burden that the brothers of the aforementioned church could not endure them without severe bodily harm and damage to the said place, as they testified to us very clearly. Therefore, when they devoutly and humbly beseeched us to act mercifully towards them, by the apostolic authority with which we are invested in this matter, having taken careful counsel, and considering the aforementioned burdens of the brothers and the benefit of those present and those who will serve the Lord in this place in the future, since we hope that this order should, by the grace of the Lord, spread both in numbers and in houses, as we see clearly from day to day, since so many flock to them that the places they now have cannot accommodate them: we deemed it necessary to dispense with them so that they shall fast according to the institutions of the Cistercian order, that is, from the feast of the Holy Cross until Easter, they shall keep a continuous fast; however, the prior shall have the authority to dispense for those working outside the cloister and for those traveling, as he sees fit, except during general fasts established by the Church. From Easter until the feast of the Holy Cross, they shall eat twice a day, except on fasts established by the Church. In the entire Advent and Lent, and general fasts established by the Church, and every Friday, they shall partake of Lenten food, unless Christmas Day comes on that day, or they are in places where it is otherwise customary, or unless it is a principal feast. At other times, they can consume eggs, cheese, and milk; they shall have two cooked dishes each day, if possible, besides fruits, and what the prior or his deputy may add if they see fit and the resources allow. Also, regarding the habit, the brothers shall have two tunics, a cloak, one scapular with lamb or sheep skins, and a simple scapular to be used during labor and other house duties; a hat or hood, or woolen cap, a woolen shirt, linen trousers, and appropriate footwear, a belt, and a knife. They shall not wear woolen cloth unless serving at the altar. They shall not sleep on mattresses in their convents, but it will be permissible to lie on straw and woolen or felt covers. They shall have one linen or woolen sheet with a cloak or coverlet. They may have feather pillows, which shall be two feet in length and one and a half in width. They shall sleep in woolen shirts and girded. All of the above shall be used by both clerics and lay brothers. Also, women shall not be admitted to live closely together. No member of your college shall have any personal property. All shall abstain from the eating of meat and animal fat generally, except for the weak and sick, for whom the rector shall compassionately provide. In these and all other matters, it shall be lawful for the rector, with discretion, the mother of all virtues, to dispense according to each one's weakness, infirmity, and necessity, in clothing, in food, and in regulated permissions. Therefore, let no one... Given at the Lateran, the second day before the calends of June, in the twelfth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius Papa IX Iohanni abbati de Brondulo et fratri Albrico priori fratrum Predicatorum de Venetiis mandat ut visitent Sanctum Andream de Litore, et statuta eius reformando, concedant dispensationem de jejuniis et aliis observantiis secundum instituta Cisterciensis, pro utilitate fratrum et loci. Dat. Laterani, II kalendas junii, anno duodecimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the archpriest of Prato, in the diocese of Reggio Emilia. As has been reported to us, when our venerable brother, the bishop of Verona, by the mandate of our venerable brother, the bishop of Brescia, appointed executor by the Apostolic See, publicly declared excommunicated the murderers of the late Guido, bishop of Mantua, along with their supporters and anyone generally offering them aid or counsel, and placed the city of Verona under ecclesiastical interdict as long as these sacrilegious persons remained in the aforementioned city, Master Anselm, a canon of Verona, presumptuously appealed to our hearing in favor of these individuals and to the derogation of ecclesiastical liberty. And when, for this reason, he was suspended from office and benefice by our venerable brother, the bishop of Vicenza, and summoned to our presence, he appeared before us and secured our dear brother Rainerius, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, as his auditor. Before whom, denying that he had made such an appeal, and since no legitimate accuser appeared against him, he is said to have obtained certain apostolic letters addressed to the prior of St. George in Braida of Verona and his colleagues regarding his purgation under specific form. And, although two years have elapsed since the time of obtaining these letters, the said Anselm has still not used them. Therefore, we strictly command you, in the virtue of obedience, to investigate whether this is the case, and unless the said canon purges himself of this offense within a sufficient term to be assigned by you, with a legitimate number of compurgators above all exception, you are to ensure he is canonically punished as convicted, fulfilling our mandate in such a manner that we are not forced to attribute another's guilt to you. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa [Gregorius IX] archipresbytero de Prato, Reginfel diocesis, mandat ut, si invenerit verum esse quod Anselmus Veronensis canonicus, qui appellaverat contra excommunicationem homicidarum et interdictum civitatis Veronensis, nondum usus est litteris apostolicis de purgatione sua, ipsum, nisi infra terminum a se praefigendum cum compurgatoribus legitimis se purgaverit, tanquam convictum canonice puniat. Datum ut supra.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Tyre, the Bishops of Acre and Antaradus. We have received a serious complaint from our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, concerning the Prince of Antioch, who, before receiving the honor of the principality and being considered as prince, should receive investiture from the Patriarch of Antioch by the banner and swear fealty to him and the Church of Antioch. This practice has been established since the Church received such an oath from the ancestors of the noble Bohemond VI, Prince of Antioch, who themselves received investiture of the principality from the same Church. However, this noble individual, departing from the footsteps of his predecessors for his own will, refused to receive the aforementioned investiture as it is due and customary, and to swear the oath of fealty. Furthermore, he raised himself against his mother church of Antioch, unlawfully extending his hands to grievous harm and injuries upon its people and others under its jurisdiction, against justice and the form of the agreement made between the said patriarch and the late Bohemond VI, father of the said noble. When the castellan of the fortress of Cursarius, an official of the aforementioned Church, sentenced a murderer who diabolically slaughtered a priest of the said fortress to hanging, the noble man banished this castellan, although he had no jurisdiction over him, and forbade his officials and bailiffs from administering any justice to the patriarch’s men and the church or others under their jurisdiction, being exceedingly grievous and injurious to them otherwise. Therefore, unwilling to endure the undue burden on the patriarch and the church, and having full confidence in the prudence of your discretion in the Lord, we command your fraternity, with the assent of the patriarch and the procurator of the other party, to admonish the said noble to provide due satisfaction for the aforementioned grievances and injuries, and to refrain from presuming similar actions in the future, by ceasing entirely from such grievances against them and their men. You should diligently and effectively induce him to this, compelling him, if necessary, through ecclesiastical censure, the appeal being removed, with the truth having been ascertained. Notwithstanding the constitution regarding the two days issued in the general council. If not all, etc. Given at Anagni, on the second day before the Kalends of August, in the twelfth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX archiepiscopo Tyrensi, episcopis Acconensi et Anteradensi mandat ut, recepta querela a patriarcha Antiocheno de principe Antiocheno, qui investituram de principatu et juramentum fidelitatis ab eo recipere renuerit, ipsum nobilem moneant et cogant ut satisfactionem praestet et ab huiusmodi gravaminibus desistat, per censuram ecclesiasticam si opus fuerit, appellatione remota, veritate cognita. Dat. Anagnie, II kalendas augusti, anno pontificatus sui duodecimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Palestrina, our vicar. Having received with usual kindness the letters which your fraternity sent to us concerning the excesses of the canons of the church of St. Mark in your city, and having diligently understood what was contained in them, as was proper, we, with the counsel of our brothers, by the authority of these presents, command you to remove Saxo and Palmerius, the canons, and Peter, the mansionary of the same church, who, having cast aside clerical modesty, attacked with arms the priest of the church of St. Lawrence of Assisi and grievously wounded him, from the aforesaid church of St. Mark permanently, and to confine them in certain places until our pleasure is known, for the performance of penance, and if they are rebellious to you in this, degrade them and leave them to the secular court for punishment. Indeed, suspend Peter Berardi, who, although he did not strike, was nonetheless present armed with the armed men, permanently from office and benefice, receiving nothing at all from ecclesiastical revenues. Also, strive to remove Romanus the priest, who, many times before the crime was committed, said in the hearing of the canons of the same church of St. Mark: "Cursed are those who eat the bread of the Church and do not care for its honor!" permanently from the same church. Those who contradict, etc. Given at Anagni, on the Nones of October, in the twelfth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Honorius III episcopo Penestrino, vicario nostro: Mandat ut Saxonem et Palmerium, canonicos, ac Petrum, mansionarium ecclesiae Sancti Marci, propter gravem in sacerdotem ecclesiae Sancti Laurentii de Asisia excessum, perpetuo ab eadem ecclesia amoveat et in locis certis pro poenitentia detineat, insuper Petrum Berardi ab officio et beneficio suspendat; Romanum presbyterum similiter amoveat pro verbis scandalosis contra ecclesiam prolatis. Dat. Anagnie, nonis octobris, anno pontificatus duodecimo.

Translation to English:

To the Bishop of Tripoli. A petition presented to us by the noble man Odo of Montbéliard, constable of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, stated that when our venerable brother, the Bishop of Paphos, sought to claim the tithes of the capitation of the village of Tarsus, in his diocese, from him and had summoned him to his presence for this purpose, the aforesaid constable raised the objection that, when, in the past, during the acquisition of the aforementioned island, it was providently decided by the late elects of Nicosia and Paphos, then legates of the Apostolic See in those parts, with the consent of the illustrious memory of Amalric, King of Cyprus, and later confirmed by the Apostolic See, that such tithes on capitation should not be paid on that island, but only other tithes, which are rightfully owed to the churches in the Patriarchate of Jerusalem, he could not and should not be compelled to pay tithes on the aforementioned capitation against the form of the aforementioned statute, as they had never been paid on the said island. But, since the aforesaid bishop, ignoring this objection, instructed him that unless he fully satisfied the aforementioned tithes within a certain period, he would then pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him, the said nobleman, feeling aggrieved by this against justice, appealed to our hearing. Therefore, we command that if this is so, having revoked, etc., up to: what has been attempted, you should hear it; firmly observe. Otherwise, suspending the same cause, the appellant, etc. Notwithstanding the constitution, etc., provided that beyond a fourth or fifth part the other party, etc. Witnesses, etc. Given at Anagni, on the 7th day before the ides of October, in the twelfth year.

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX episcopo Tripolitano mandat quatenus, si constet quod episcopus Pafensis decimas capitationis casalis Tarsis contra statutum ab Almarico rege Cypri et Sedem Apostolicam confirmatum exigat, revocet attemptatum et causam audiat, alioquin causam suspendat. Dat. Anagnie, VII idus octobris, anno duodecimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the Chancellor of Paris. We cannot and should not let pass the great and serious offense which Theobald of Cicons, the brother of the cantor of Saint Stephen of Besançon, and his accomplices have audaciously attempted against our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Besançon, with wicked daring. For, as the same archbishop has informed us in his complaint, they have rashly laid violent hands on him, disregarding the fear of God, and have plundered him and his household of horses, donkeys, books, pontifical ornaments, and other belongings. They have wickedly captured one of his associates, a canon of Besançon, and held him in prison for a long time. They have also rashly invaded and pillaged the archbishop's villages, inflicting serious harm and injuries upon him and his people, and they continue to do so. Since these wrongdoers, who are said to be under the power of noble men, barons, bailiffs, and other nobles of Burgundy, contemptuously disregard the excommunication which they are known to have incurred because of this, and refuse to return to the command of the Church, it is fitting that those whom divine fear does not call back from evil should at least be restrained by temporal discipline. We command that you should more earnestly admonish and induce the said barons, bailiffs, and others to compel the wrongdoers, by virtue of the power given to them, to fully restore what was taken from the archbishop, to make due satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted upon him, and to cease entirely from similar deeds henceforth, using excommunication against their persons and interdiction against their lands, if necessary, without allowing any appeal. Moreover, to ensure that such an enormous crime is punished not only in those who commit it but also in their descendants, we hereby decree by this present decree that no male descendant of these offenders shall be admitted to ecclesiastical office or benefice unless by a special grace of the Apostolic See. Notwithstanding any constitution, etc., provided it does not extend beyond the fourth or fifth degree, etc. Given at Anagni, on the 12th of August, in the year...

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa nuntiat cancellario Parisiensi ut baronibus, balivis aliisque nobilibus Burgundiae mandet, ut malefactores, qui excommunicationem contempserunt, archiepiscopo Bisuntino ablata restituant et de dampnis satisfaciant, cessando ab iniuriis futuris, sub poena excommunicationis et interdicti. Praeterea, statuit ut nullus filius virilis sexus descendentium ad officium ecclesiasticum admittatur nisi per specialem gratiam Sedis Apostolicae. Datum Anagnie, II idus Augusti, anno pontificatus.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Novara. Our venerable brother, the Bishop of Vercelli, has shown us through a sent message that, although previously, when Oddone de Mandello was the podestà (chief magistrate) of the city of Vercelli, on behalf of the commonality of the same city, the consuls of the Societies of Saint Eusebius and Saint Stephen, as well as officials, councilors, and other citizens of the aforementioned city, took a precise oath to adhere to our and the said bishop's mandates regarding matters for which they were bound by the chain of excommunication, we had instructed you with our letters to demand from them both the holding of fortifications and the pledges and sureties for obeying such mandates. However, they, adding sins to sins and continuing in their wickedness to their own damnation, have contemptuously refused to do so, ignoring the sanctity of the oath and the sentence of excommunication, even though you have repeatedly requested it under the obligation of the oath given. We command that, under the threat of anathema, you explicitly strive to prohibit any city or nearby place from assuming power or a leader over those persisting in their obstinacy with the podestà, council, and citizens of Vercelli, putting the city or place that does so under ecclesiastical interdict as long as he remains there. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Honorius III episcopo Novariensi mandat ut, ob pertinaciam communitatis Vercellensis in contemnendo mandata et excommunicationem, interdicat ne civitas vel locus vicinus potestatem vel rectorem de Vercellensibus pertinacibus assumat, sub poena interdicti ecclesiastici. Datum Laterani, anno pontificatus eius undecimo, die VII.

**Translation to English:**

To: The Abbot of Saint Aubert of Cambrai, the Dean, and Master William, canon, formerly official of Arras.

From the complaint of our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Corbie, of the order of Saint Benedict, directly pertaining to the Roman Church, we have learned that the mayor and jurors of Corbie, in the diocese of Amiens, who are under the spiritual and temporal jurisdiction of the same monastery, have with a spirit of pride and impiety, presumed to capture and imprison some of their servants, subjecting them to grave injuries, and ultimately depriving them of their goods. Furthermore, they have assaulted the monastery, convening a part of the commune, and violently laid hands on the abbot himself. Not satisfied with expelling some monks of the same monastery, who were sent by the abbot to safeguard the goods of a certain local citizen, they presumed to lay hands on them and otherwise threatened them. Although the said abbot has, due to these and many other serious excesses, pronounced sentences of excommunication and interdict on the town of Corbie by his own authority, as justice required, they, under the pretext of a frivolous appeal to the Apostolic See, which they claim to have sent but did not pursue within the legal time, have refused to comply with the Church's mandate.

Moreover, to show themselves manifest contemners of Catholic purity, they have presumed to bury the excommunicated and interdicted in the cemeteries of the same monastery and in a certain atrium they newly constructed for such burials, against the prohibition of the said abbot and convent. Therefore, lest these matters pass unnoticed and these presumptuous individuals gain the freedom to so damnably offend God and his faithful, we command you to solemnly publish the aforementioned sentences every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lit, and mandate their publication throughout the province of Reims, ensuring that they are avoided by all until they make satisfactory amends. Furthermore, you shall utterly demolish the aforementioned atrium upon verifying the truth, with opposition, if any, quelled.

To the said abbot and convent, render such favor and assistance as you deem appropriate to counter the malice of the opposing party, invoking, if necessary, the aid of secular authority. Given at Anagni, on the Ides of August, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Gregorius IX, Abbati Sancti Auberti Cameracensis, Decano et Magistro Guillelmo, canonico, quondam officiali Atrebatensibus, mandat ut sententias excommunicationis et interdicti contra majorem et juratos Corbeienses, qui in abbatem et monachos monasterii Corbeiensis ausu nephario manus injecerunt, sollempniter publicet, et atrium pro excommunicatorum sepultura noviter constructum demoliri curet, adhibito si necesse fuerit auxilio brachii secularis. Datum Anagnie, idibus Augusti, anno duodecimo.

**Translation to English:**

To John, archdeacon of Silviniac, and .. chancellor of Tours, residing in Paris, and master Pletrol 2 de Papa, canon of Paris. The petition presented to us by the nobleman Archembaud, lord of Bourbon, contained that, when our venerable brother .. archbishop of Bourges, asserting that he ought to swear an oath to him, to attack his rebellious subjects in the diocese of Bourges, except for our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the French, until they return at his command, had summoned him to take such an oath before him by his own authority: on his part, it was proposed by way of exception before him that neither he was bound to the taking of the aforesaid oath, which had never been rendered by him or his predecessors, lords of Bourbon, nor could the same act as judge and plaintiff in his own cause, especially as he was prepared to offer him the fulfillment of justice before a competent judge. And because the said archbishop, having not admitted this legitimate exception of his, nevertheless demanded the aforesaid oath from him contrary to justice, feeling himself unjustly aggrieved, he appealed to our audience. But the archbishop, disregarding the appeal, pronounced, as it is said, sentences of excommunication against him and interdict on his land. Therefore, he asked us to declare the said sentences null or to order them to be lifted as a precaution. However, because certainty could not be achieved regarding the right or defense of the said nobleman, and hence it could not be determined whether the appeal was just or unjust, we command that, after having summoned those who ought to be called, you hear the case and, if it proceeds from the will of the parties, finish it by agreement or judgment; and so on. Otherwise, remit it sufficiently instructed to the apostolic examination, setting a suitable peremptory term for the parties, by which they may appear before us through suitable procurators, to receive a just sentence, with the Lord as our author. Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the calends of September, in the year... 

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX Johanni, archidiacono Silviniacensi, cancellario Turonensi, et magistro Pletrol 2 de Papa, canonico Parisiensi, mandat ut causam inter Archembaudum dominum Borbonensem et archiepiscopum Bituricensem de juramento praestando audiant et, si ex partium voluntate procedat, concordia vel judicio terminent; alioquin ad apostolicum examen remittant. Dat. Anagnie, V kalendas Septembris, pontificatus nostri anno...

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Mantua. Once, upon being informed by certain individuals that, with the discord having arisen in the city of Verona, some of the clerics of the city and diocese of Verona were forced to go into exile from their churches; and that by others, who remained in the same city and diocese, elections and institutions, or rather intrusions, of clerics were proceeding with the violence and fear imposed by laymen, both in the cathedral and other churches, against canonical sanctions: we, lest the excess of such presumption pass as an example to others, entrusted by our letters to our beloved sons, the archdeacon, the vicedominus, and a certain former master Albert, canon of Brescia, to revoke by our authority such elections and institutions to nullity, prohibiting the presumption of similar actions in the future; restraining the contradictors (etc., up to:) by coercion. The aforementioned archdeacon and colleagues, proceeding lawfully in the execution of the apostolic mandate, found that Episcopellus the cleric was instituted as a canon of Verona through the force and fear of laymen, rather, he was intruded; with the said master having departed from human affairs, and the same archdeacon committing his duties to the archpriest of Prati to pronounce the sentence, the same vicedominus and archpriest, upon wise counsel, revoked the institution or intrusion of the said Episcopellus by definitive sentence, enjoining the chapter of Verona to have due regard, pronouncing a sentence of excommunication on the contradictors and rebels. Moreover, because the said Episcopellus is said to hold such canonry and prebend as occupied, we command your fraternity to ensure that the same Episcopellus is summoned on our behalf to appear personally before us within a month after your citation, to fulfill the course of justice regarding this matter; compelling him to do so, if necessary, by ecclesiastical censure, postponing appeal. Given.

**Regesto:**

Papa Gregorius IX episcopo Mantuano mandat ut Episcopellum clericum Veronensem, qui per vim laicorum in canonicum intrusus est, citet ut coram eo compareat ad justitiam perferendam; si opus fuerit, per censuram ecclesiasticam compellendo. Dat. Laterani, anno pontificatus nostri tertio.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Antaradus. Previously, our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, presented to us that a dispute had arisen between our venerable brothers, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, the Archbishops of Tyre and Petra, the Bishop of Sidon, and of blessed memory, the Bishop of Beirut, and their chapters on one side, and himself on the other. The issue was regarding the claim that the aforementioned Archbishops of Tyre and Petra, and particularly the Bishops of Beirut and Sidon, along with their dioceses, should be subject to him and the Church of Antioch by patriarchal right. He desired this dispute to be settled by the Apostolic See. We, to remove the cause of scandal and to strengthen the bond of charity between the parties, instructed them with our letters, if we remember well, to appear in our presence by the first of June of the following year, which we assigned as a peremptory term, through procurators sufficiently instructed with their documents and other reasons, to do and receive what justice might advise concerning the matters. But they neither appeared within the term nor after the term, having been awaited for a year and more. Eventually, we found in the register of Pope Eugene of happy memory, our predecessor, a certain agreement mediated by him concerning the aforementioned matters between the parties, which we send to you enclosed under our seal. Therefore, although we could legally proceed against the Patriarch of Jerusalem and the others as contumacious, we still wish to accommodate them, saving the expenses incurred by the same Patriarch of Antioch due to their contumacy. We command you to cite the same Patriarch of Jerusalem and the others, and our venerable brother, the current Bishop of Beirut, on our behalf, to either observe the same agreement, if they wish, or to present themselves in our presence through sufficient and suitable procurators, within a suitable term assigned by you, which we wish to be designated as peremptory, to do and receive what reason shall dictate concerning these matters. Otherwise, do not delay to pronounce a sentence of suspension against them. You shall faithfully report back to us whatever has been done concerning this. Given at Anagni, on the 14th of the Kalends of September, in the twelfth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa destinat episcopo Anteradensi, ut patriarcham Jerosolimitanum, Tyrensem et Petracensem archiepiscopos, ac Sydonensem et Beritensem episcopos ex parte sua citet, ut compositionem cum patriarcha Antiocheno initam servent, aut se in termino competenti per procuratores idoneos conspectui apostolico representent, sub poena suspensionis. Datum Anagnie, XIIII kalendas septembris, anno duodecimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the illustrious King of Portugal, the spirit of wiser counsel. If you were to reflect properly on how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God, you would cautiously refrain from offending the Holy Church, His spouse, which He has redeemed with His own blood, and her servants. Know indeed that it has come to our attention that you, under the pretext of a certain pernicious constitution said to have been issued by your great-grandfather, namely, that a woman found with an ecclesiastic person should be seized, your officials and some of your other vassals often break into the houses of such persons in the diocese of Braga, and whether women are found with them or not, etc., as above, in the letter noted under number 2753, for the Church of Portugal, with a few changes, up to the amount of money. Furthermore, if it ever happens that our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Braga, and his vicars [etc., as above in the same letter, with adjustments, up to:] necessary, you compel them to undergo forced labor and other dishonorable burdens, and to observe both your and your barons' and officials' bans and statutes; among which you have enacted in hatred of God and the Church and her ministers, a statute, namely, that if anyone has donated any possessions to a church or monastery in life or bequeathed in their last will, it is not permissible for the church to receive them, nor for them or any ecclesiastic person to acquire any possessions, exempt from all burdens of tribute or service; from this the devotion of the faithful and the will of the deceased is wickedly impeded. Moreover, if any ecclesiastic person [etc., as above, in the same letter, up to:] oppressing them with grievances; on account of which the churches and monasteries have been reduced to such a miserable state of destitution that they cannot support their own ministers. Hence, the same archbishop has often diligently warned you to compensate the churches and monasteries and ecclesiastical persons for the damages and injuries inflicted upon them by you and yours, restraining your own person, officials, and subjects from the molestations of the churches concerning the aforementioned or similar issues. But, while you pass the warnings of the same archbishop with deaf ears, the same, after prolonged warnings and expectations, unable to endure further the burden on the churches equitably, has excommunicated, in your presence and that of your barons and other men, as well as bishops and many religious, both the barons and all others who, either by your command or by their own authority or rather by rashness, under any pretext, presume to aggravate the churches, monasteries, or ecclesiastical persons of the diocese of Braga against ecclesiastical liberty in the aforementioned or similar ways. Therefore, we, wishing both to provide for your salvation, and to protect, as we are bound, the indemnities of the churches and ecclesiastical persons, strictly forbid by the authority of these presents that you dare to defame ecclesiastical persons, or break into their houses or plunder their goods, in the aforesaid or any similar manner, through yourself, or your officials or vassals. If indeed the archbishop or his vicars proceed against ecclesiastical men, etc., as above, in the same letter, up to: ceasing entirely. Otherwise, since no one should incur the danger of their own soul, know that we have given strict orders by our letters to the same archbishop that if you do not care to fulfill the aforesaid within three months after the receipt of our letters, or their publication in the place where you shall be, and have competently satisfied the churches and monasteries for the damages and injuries inflicted on them by you and yours, firmly promising by your patent letters that you will observe, and cause to be observed, the articles expressed above, since they pertain to common law, providing full security to the same archbishop and his, restraining yourself and your barons, officials, bailiffs, and subjects from oppressing the churches, the same archbishop shall execute all the above chapters, removing the obstacle of any contradiction and appeal, repressing the contradictors; furthermore striking you with the sentence of excommunication, he shall place the locations to which you happen to come under ecclesiastical interdict, while you remain there, and shall cause the same sentences to be inviolably observed by our authority until due satisfaction is made. Notwithstanding the indulgence said to have been granted to you by the Apostolic See, that no one may dare to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict upon you or your kingdom. If indeed you persist in this obstinacy for a longer time, the Roman Church will otherwise provide for these matters, with the Lord as guide. To Rollandus, our subdeacon and chaplain, legate of the Apostolic See. Among other things that are to be executed through your diligent effort, we wish and strictly command you by the authority of these presents that you ensure the castle of Monte Acuto, which our beloved daughter in Christ, the noble lady... of the judiciary of Torres, through the hand of our beloved son, master Alexander, our chaplain, donated to the Roman Church, and was formerly entrusted to the custody of our venerable brother, the bishop of Empurias, be assigned to you as soon as you can, imposing a fitting penalty on the said bishop for the negligence he showed regarding the custody of the said castle. Do the same with the castle of Monte Cutiano, which the aforementioned noble lady is bound to assign freely to whomever we have commanded, when we wish; and let it be diligently guarded by our beloved son, the noble man Peter, judge of Arborea, for the peace of Sardinia and the security of the said lady. And since the said noble lady must marry one by whom the rights of the Roman Church will be preserved inviolate, and we wish to provide for her a husband of such a character who will befit her nobility and be able to defend and protect her land with a strong hand, ensure that the same lady is so honorably and so respectfully guarded by the above-mentioned nobleman, her cousin, until she is given in marriage, that no sinister suspicion may arise concerning her, and no injury may be inflicted on her by her adversaries. Furthermore, since the judiciary of Gallura, which [..] son of Ubaldo, a citizen of Pisa, is said to have unlawfully invaded, is of the jurisdiction and property of blessed Peter, we wish and command that, having gathered the Sardinians, and if the judge himself should wish to object, you receive the same judiciary of Gallura into your hands and ensure it is diligently guarded by the said nobleman until our will is made known. You shall ensure that the fortifications and all possessions of both the judiciary of Gallura and Torres are adequately supplied with all necessities for at least two years, and that faithful and suitable custodians are appointed in them. Subsequently, you shall do the same with the castle of Acquafredda, located in the province of Cagliari. Do not make any concession to the nobleman Rainerius, count, or anyone else of the land of the aforementioned judiciary of Cagliari, which the wife of the said count should only hold during her lifetime; nor grant or confirm any fief or possession to any Pisan or Genoese in all of Sardinia; but rather, if you find anything alienated to the detriment of the Roman Church from its domains, strive to reclaim it; ensure that the statutes which the same chaplain has reasonably issued for the honor of the Apostolic See and the tranquility of Sardinia, with the consent of the clergy and laity, are firmly observed. Suppress any disturbers or troublemakers of Sardinia, whoever they may be, lowly or high-born, when necessary, by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside any appeal. Given at Anagni, on the third day before the kalends of August, in the year of our pontificate.

For, as we have learned, the locust destroys the tender herb of spiritual things and the hail breaks the wood of temporal things in the field of the Grandmont order, leading it to such ruin that it can hardly, if ever, be restored to its former state unless it feels the aid of the Apostolic See's providence with divine grace assisting. We rejoice not only in the progress of your soul but also in the support generously offered to the Apostolic See, and we have joyfully offered the calves of our lips to Him from whom all good things proceed and whose is all that is best. Inspired by His spirit, having conceived the spirit of salvation, you have resolved to put forth your hand to strong deeds and to serve in the cause of Christ's spouse. Inspired by His grace, you have devoutly offered to pursue the vows inspired within you by His grace, with His help. You should also rejoice with spiritual exaltation and offer a sacrifice of praise to the giver of all good things, as it seems He has chosen you among so many kings, princes, and great men as a faithful son of the Church, to follow Deborah, sitting under the palm, or rather ascending into victory, against Sisera, who excluded true joy from himself, lest he be consigned to the pains of hell! For he has become so senseless that he does not feel the bitterness of the blow of the spiritual sword; nor is he ashamed to the point of returning to the one striking him to be healed, but persists with a mind hardened in wickedness, forgetting God's mercy, without whom he becomes inglorious, indeed nothing. This too brings joy to your devotion, from the joy of the internal and eternal, that you have turned the left hand of temporal substance, forewarned by the largesse of divine gifts, into the right hand by offering it to the aid of the Church, to free the people of God from the yoke of unjust servitude. Therefore, commending such a healthy purpose and fervor with worthy praises in the Lord, and wishing that the effect of such a healthy affection may increase from the fruits of your devotion, we have deemed it appropriate, with the advice of our brothers, to grant your wishes, that you may personally come with a powerful hand to serve Jesus Christ, intending firmly to embrace you as a special son in the arms of sincerity and to hold you in the bowels of charity, and to support your progress and honor, as far as we can with God, both spiritually and temporally. Wherefore, we earnestly ask and admonish your nobility, and in remission of sins, we enjoin upon you and those who will come with you, that as you have generously offered, you hasten as soon as possible with a multitude of knights to support the spouse of Christ, to serve the Lord under blessed Peter, leader of his army. Given at Perugia, on the first of the Nones of June, in the third year.

To the chapter of Reims and other chapters. The presented documents of the Senonensis and Parisiensis chapters have exhibited to us a bundle of bitter myrrh anew, sacrificed on the cross of the flesh and the gibbet of the spirit, which has inscribed on the page of our heart with the pen of unheard-of turmoil and the ink of new bitterness, such that neither the lament of a mournful mind nor a river of tears can erase the script which the style of engraved sorrow has impressed on our soul, as if with an adamantine nail, by a new form of coining. How a grieving person might console one in sorrow, or a sorrowing one soothe griefs, when opposites are treated by their contraries, is not easy to discern. Let no one seek from bitterness what may taste sweet, from exasperation what may soothe, for in bitter words the honey of sweetness is exterminated where the force of pain occupies the whole heart. The beginning of the illustrious prince, the once glorious king Louis of clear memory, who faithfully promoted the matter of peace and faith, brought laughter and joy to the Church, his mother; but being miserably snatched away by the fate of envious death, he turned laughter into mourning, joy into lamentation, and gravely wounded the whole cause which, with God as its author, was being advanced under auspicious beginnings by the sword of his death; yet, with the succession of his offspring, it somewhat revived, and did not entirely remove the hope of future fruit from past labors. However, we report with grief that there is fear lest new misfortune should so unfortunately succeed in the matter of peace and faith as to extinguish the spark of hope, which remained in the devotion of the clergy, by the breath of arising malignity. Yet let it not happen that this cause, for which the blood of so many martyrs cries out unceasingly beneath the altar of God, should perish through the fault of one, especially since you have thought it right to appeal for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty rather than to avoid the cause's assistance. We indeed recognize and confess that the Church of France, after the Apostolic See, is a certain mirror of all Christianity and an immovable firmament of faith, as it does not follow others in the fervor of Christian faith and devotion to the Apostolic See, but, as we might say with their peace, it leads; the devotion of which we deem superfluous to extol in words, since it is manifest by its illustrious deeds. Therefore, understanding the grievances imposed on you by our beloved son R., Cardinal Deacon of St. Angelus and Legate of the Apostolic See, through a certain ordinance issued at Sens, moved by inner sorrow of heart and grave admiration, we have rebuked the same legate with the severity of our letters, as was fitting, and have immediately commanded him, in the virtue of obedience, firmly with precepts to revoke the ordinance itself, or by whatever other name this act may be called, entirely without delay, so that this revocation should not be postponed beyond three days after the receipt of our letters, and expressly forbid anyone to presume to exercise violence against you, or other ecclesiastical persons, or their possessions, on the pretext aforementioned, and to cause all things to be restored if anything has been occupied from ecclesiastical goods on the said pretext. Finally, wishing to provide more fully for you and others whom this matter concerns, we have ordered, by our writings, our venerable brothers the Bishops of Le Mans and Orléans, and our beloved son the Abbot of Bourg-Moyen in Blois, that, if the cardinal himself, which we do not at all believe, neglects or delays to fulfill the precept, or perhaps returning to our presence, has exceeded the term of his legation, they, executing it by apostolic authority, should declare the ordinance issued against you at Sens and later intimated to you by the letters of the said legate, utterly void and invalid, and expressly prohibit anyone from presuming to invade or disturb ecclesiastical goods on that pretext, restraining all who may have presumed to attempt otherwise from such presumption. Finally, we firmly intend to do everything that we shall see should be done for the preservation of your honor and status, according to God and propriety.

To the Bishop of Bamberg. The matters resolved by judgment. Given at the Lateran, 10th day before the Kalends of January, in the first year of our pontificate. The tenor of this composition is as follows: In the name of the Lord. Amen. This is the form of composition and concord between Ekebert, the venerable Bishop of Bamberg, and Bernhard, the illustrious Duke of Carinthia, arranged by Eberhard, the venerable Archbishop of Salzburg, and Leopold, the illustrious Duke of Austria and Styria. Namely, the Duke of Carinthia gave to the Church of Bamberg the ownership of the castle of Werdenburch and other goods which he bought from the Abbot of St. Paul pertaining to the same castle, and the Duke received the same castle and goods in fief from the Bishop of Bamberg, in such a way that both the sons and daughters of the Duke have a feudal right in those goods. Moreover, the aforementioned Duke destroyed a bridge begun under the same castle, and from now on will neither rebuild it nor another to the detriment of the Church of Bamberg, nor will he have a public market there, nor will any goods be deposited there, nor will he have tolls or a levy there. Similarly, on the adjacent island, he will make no fortification nor market. Furthermore, the said Duke donated those men whom he accused in Villach to the Bishop and Church of Bamberg, and similarly handed over the area he bought from the Victorians to the Bishop and Church of Bamberg, so that the Bishop may not erect major buildings in the same area, but must maintain it in its current state unless there are ruins there which the Bishop can repair to their former state. Furthermore, the aforementioned Duke yielded the lawsuit he had concerning the exchange on the mountain of the Bishop of Bamberg, namely regarding the silver mine, and yielded the right he had in the castle of Richenevelsse, and Wichard of Charlsparch and others who were enfeoffed by him also yielded the right they had or seemed to have there, nor shall the Duke himself build or erect any new castle at Richenevelsse. For all these aforementioned matters, five thousand marks of silver of Cologne weight are to be handed over. And so that these remain perpetual and unbroken, this present document is signed with the seals of Lord Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, and Lord Ekebert, Bishop of Bamberg, and Leopold, Duke of Austria and Styria, and the aforesaid Bernhard, Duke of Carinthia, with the addition that this form of concord should be confirmed by the instruments of the Lord Pope and Emperor. These acts were done at Greze, on the 15th day before the Kalends of December, in the year of the Lord 1227, in the presence of Rudeger, Bishop of Chiemsee, and Karul, Bishop of Seckau, Henry, Margrave of Istria, Bernhard of Liebenau, Hermann of Ortenburg, and Wilhelm of Hinnenburg, Counts Ulrich and Liutold of Beka, Chimer of Senneche, Wilhelm of Hoheneche, Otho of Trabenfurth and Henry his son, Rembert of Mureche and Rembert his son, and Ulrich, marshal of Walchstein, Henry of Prunne, Irnfrid of Himpfurch, Choloni and Rudolf of Rase, Otho of Chungesfurth, Dietmar and Ulrich brothers of Lichtenstein, Henry of Starphenfurth, and many others.

To the Dean of Lincoln and the Archdeacons of Lincoln and Stowe in the Diocese of Lincoln. The beloved daughters in Christ, the prioress and convent of Campsey, have taken care to inform us that a dispute arose between them on one side, and the prior and convent of Butley in the Diocese of Norwich on the other, concerning certain tithes and other matters they were convened about before the Abbot of St. Benedict of Holme and his colleagues, who were appointed judges by apostolic authority. They appealed to us due to sufficient grievance and sent their envoy to pursue the appeal, yet the aforementioned judges subsequently imposed a sentence of excommunication upon them. Therefore, having obtained our letters concerning the aforementioned appeal through the same envoy to the prior of Anglesey and his co-judges, the opposing party claimed, falsely, that they had appealed because the judges denied accepting the exception of the aforementioned excommunication against them. They obtained our letters regarding this appeal to the prior of Gernemue and his co-judges; where it was proposed on behalf of the prioress and convent that, since the sentence was pronounced after a legitimate appeal, and it is known that any excommunicated person has the right to a defense, the aforementioned judges did not accept, as they should not have, the exception of the opposing party. But when the said prior of Gernemue and his co-judges did not accept such an exception from them, they appealed to our hearing. Therefore, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that if this is the case, restore to the proper state whatever you find to have been rashly attempted after such an appeal, and in the same matter, proceed with due reasoning according to the tenor of our previous mandate directed to the prior of Gernemue and his co-judges; otherwise, refer the parties back to their examination; condemning the appellants in legitimate expenses. Witnesses, etc. If not all, etc. Given at Perugia, 5th Kalends of June, in the third year.

To the Archbishop of Milan and his suffragans, and to other prelates and clerics of the churches of the province of Milan. Although it is a natural vice to neglect what is commonly possessed, it is the virtue of charity to meet imminent general danger with united strength as if it were a personal interest. Truly, Frederick, called the emperor, not content with trampling the Church of God wherever he had power with diligent malice, has now openly overthrown ecclesiastical freedom. With the business of the Holy Land irreparably confused, unable to conceal his unjust plan, he has rushed publicly against the Roman Church, engaging wholly in its persecution, believing that if he can oppress it in any way, the universal Church cannot stand, but rather is subjected to his harsh servitude, thinking that whatever freedom or honor the Bride of Christ holds is lost to him alone. Hence, since he and his followers neither fear God nor respect ecclesiastical censure, and do not cease to covet the damnable occupation of the patrimony of blessed Peter, where, with certain fortresses invaded and our faithful wickedly slain by the Saracens, they burn, with unfulfilled malice, to extend the boundaries of invasion, we, clearly seeing that unless their audacity is curbed, their continuous ferocity would not cease, have begun to exercise temporal power to recover the invaded lands and repel the injuries, and moreover to relieve the oppressed churches and uphold ecclesiastical freedom, having gathered many armies for this under ample stipends, because nothing should be spared when the universal Church is so fiercely attacked. However, since these armies cannot be maintained without a great expenditure, we affectionately ask your charity, earnestly exhort and strictly command through apostolic writings that each of you, as if one man, bearing unanimously the cause of the Church, provide us with pleasing support in persons or things, liberally granting a tenth of your revenues and incomes, by which the remaining will be healthily preserved, indeed the general state of the Church as well, so that, strengthened by your aid, with the Lord as our author, we may suppress such adverse pride, that others may fear to rise up against God and the Church hereafter, and the sons of the Church may enjoy due freedom, and we, recognizing your sincerity more perfectly by the affection and effect of the assistance provided, may embrace you more dearly in the bowels of Christ. But if anyone, out of his own greed, has refused to support this so urgent cause of the general Church, he may rightly fear that, since a part not corresponding to its whole is base, moreover it should not even be called a part which departs from integrity, such a grave fault may be proclaimed by the ensuing penalty. Whatever you decide to do about these matters, let each of you express to us through your letters. Given at Perugia, on the tenth day before the kalends of December, in the second year of our pontificate.

Dat. Perusii, X kalendas decembris, anno secundo pontificatus nostri.

To the abbot and convent of St. Peter in Cielo Aureo, Pavia. Since we have written to our venerable brother, the bishop of Piacenza, to diligently and carefully admonish and induce the prior and canons of Mortara to exhibit obedience to you, dear abbot, and to inquire about any objections they might have as to why they should not do so and faithfully report the truth to us, and after receiving the report of the bishop himself, we entrusted the examination of it to our beloved son, S., cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. Upon his faithful report of the matter to us, we found the statements of the canons to be diverse: some said it would be beneficial for your monastery to be the head of the Mortara order, while others proposed otherwise. Finally, out of reverence for St. Augustine, whose body rests in the same monastery, the authority of the place, and the devotion of the clergy and people of Pavia, who would not tolerate the head of the Mortara order to be transferred elsewhere, as well as due to the uninhabitability of the Mortara site, which is known to be exposed to wars and tumults and other unforeseen events, so that its members have sometimes been miserably compelled to wander from their head and disperse to various places, we, with the counsel of our brothers, have decided that the head of the entire said order should be the aforementioned monastery, and it should be governed by its abbot, while the house of Mortara should be governed by its provost, according to the providence given to them by God and the statutes of the same order. Moreover, all the churches which were subject to the said monastery before the Mortara order was introduced there should obey the abbot of the said monastery, and the members of the Mortara church, which were once subject to it, are to render obedience. Furthermore, the abbot of St. Peter should correct in the provost and chapter of Mortara what he sees fit to correct, but he should have no correction over the members unless the provost of the named church has been negligent after a third admonition. Let no one, therefore, infringe our constitution. If anyone does so, etc. Given at Perugia, on the 8th day before the ides of April, in the third year of our pontificate.

Augustini, auctoritatem loci, et devotionem Papiensium. Statuit ut abbas ipsorum monasterii domum Mortariensem gubernet, cum subditis ecclesiis obedientiam praestantibus, et correctionem solum post trinam ammonitionem exercere possit. Datum Perusii, VIII idus aprilis, pontificatus nostri anno tertio.

To the Bishop of Paris. Since charity, not seeking its own interests, considers nothing human as foreign to itself, anyone who loves charity can rightly regard anything threatening the general Church as his own concern. He should not spare his own resources when he can counter a common danger, lest he seem to prioritize private interests over universal benefit. Indeed, the Roman Church is now positioned at such a critical juncture that it seems driven to one of two outcomes: either, supported by the aid of the faithful and with the Lord's help, it will protect itself and the universal Church, or, God forbid, it will allow itself and all its members to be trampled and subjected to severe servitude. This is due to Emperor Frederick, who, opposing God and the Church, deceitfully disrupts the business of the Holy Land and impiously plans forces with Saracens and other infidels. Therefore, seeing and lamenting that the unjust pride and proud injustice of Frederick always increases unless it is restrained by the obstacle of justice, we have deemed it right to oppose his endeavors, lest he who provokes wrath be exalted. Thus, having full trust in your sincerity in the Lord, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your fraternity, through apostolic letters, by the virtue of obedience and under the obligation of your oath, strictly ordering and enjoining you for the remission of sins, both yours and those who will come in service to the Church, to take care, as you hold divine and our grace dear, mindful that necessity reveals kinship, to personally come to us with a suitable force of warriors, or send them without delay, to serve the Roman Church from the heart, so that you may gain the merit due to you, and we may be obliged to reward your devotion worthily.

Recently, when your church became vacant, and you gathered on the appointed day to elect a new bishop, a provision could not be reached by the arbitrators chosen for this purpose. Suddenly, one of your members exclaimed, "Let us choose the cantor," with more than two-thirds agreeing to this. The dean, alone and in public, without any written records and with the cantor present who refused to leave despite being asked to do so, inquired about the intentions and nominated the cantor as the bishop of Paris, although some did not consent. He also said that he did not agree with the cantor as bishop and that the election was against all forms of the council. To G., priest cardinal of the title of Saint Mark, legate of the Apostolic See. That dragon, who, as we believe, has instigated a grave discord between the Paduans and Trevisans, through which the Paduans, as we have learned, have been strongly armed against the Trevisans, putting their trust in flesh, invade the villages, possessions, and goods of the Trevisans with hostile devastation. Churches are desolated, orphans oppressed, the poor and widows are open to plunder, and, what is worse, the aforementioned dragon abducts captive souls, delighting primarily in their destruction. Unless this old leaven is quickly purged, the whole of Lombardy and the March could be leavened, because the world is set in evil and the nature of the human race, corrupted in the first man, is prone to evil. We command your discretion through apostolic writings that, without any delay or excuse, since danger is prolonged by delay, and medicine is prepared too late when evils have grown strong through long delays, you go to both cities, and effectively admonish and prudently induce the citizens to reform the bonds of peace between them. And if they will not accept the word of peace, since, as it is said, all those of the society of Lombardy and the March are bound by oath to abide by the arbitration and command of the rectors concerning all disputes that arise among them, and since the Trevisans, as they assert, when requested by the aforesaid rectors, have sworn to obey their mandates in these matters over which discord has arisen, if this is the case, compel the aforementioned Paduans to keep such an oath, as they are bound, especially since, according to the Apostle, an oath is the end of all controversy. You are to admonish our venerable brother, the patriarch of Aquileia, who is said to have entered into an alliance of hostility with his district's men on one side and the Paduans on the other against the Trevisans, not to improperly inflict trouble or grievance upon the same Trevisans through himself or his men, especially since, as they assert, they have neither offended him nor his men, after they reformed the bonds of peace among them, with us mediating in a lesser office, nor to, on the occasion of the alliance made, grant them further assistance or favor against the Trevisans, but rather to faithfully and diligently pursue what belongs to peace, restraining his men with the necessary jurisdiction if they presume to attempt otherwise, and if necessary, compelling him to this by the appropriate censure, with justice intervening, the appeal being removed. Given at Perugia, on the seventeenth day before the calends of June, in the third year of our pontificate.

To the Masters of Theology residing in Paris. The vessels of silver and gold should be taken from the Egyptians in such a manner that, once they have been deprived of them, the Hebrews become enriched, not so that the Hebrews are brought into servitude to them, as if sold to share in the price. For even if the doctrine of heavenly eloquence sometimes borrows from the wisdom and eloquence of philosophical doctrine to adorn itself, it should not serve it, nor should its intellect in any way incline towards it. When also a girl captured from the enemies, with her hair shorn and nails clipped, is joined to an Israelite man, she should not dominate him but rather serve as a subordinate. Indeed, the theological intellect, like a man, ought to preside over every faculty and, like a spirit over the flesh, exercise dominion, directing it in the path of righteousness lest it stray. Finally, he who endeavors to divert the words of the divine oracle by adulterous mingling with the doctrine of philosophers and his own sense, inflated and knowing nothing, and inclines them towards philosophical understanding, seems like the adulterous man adhering to a woman of Samaria, who when asking for living water, which leaps to eternal life, is instructed to call her husband, dismissing the adulterer, namely, a pure and simple understanding, corrupted by no earthly eloquence. Those who walk around, following the folly of their heart, and believe they know something, cannot reach the center of truth. The makers of silver, i.e., natural eloquence, and those who are diligent about it, as the prophetic word says, have been destroyed and have descended to the depths, because they have ignored the way of heavenly discipline and did not understand its paths. The sons of Agar, who seek wisdom that is of the earth, and the merchants of the earth, and Theman, fabricators and seekers of understanding, namely worldly understanding, did not know the way of wisdom. For although they recognized God from the greatness of creatures, they did not give Him glory nor did they give thanks, as to God, saying: "We will make great our tongue; our lips are with us, who is our Lord?" they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened, and considering themselves wise, they became foolish, given over to a reprobate sense, abominable and corrupt, acting deceitfully with their tongues, and carrying the venom of asps beneath their lips. Truly, touched with inner sorrow of heart, we are filled with the bitterness of wormwood because, as has been intimated to our ears, some among you, inflated like a bladder with the spirit of vanity, are striving to profanely move the boundaries set by the Fathers with new things, inclining the understanding of the heavenly page, limited by the certain bounds of expositions of the Holy Fathers, which it is not only rash but profane to transgress, towards the philosophical doctrine of natural things, for the display of knowledge rather than any advantage to their hearers; so that they are seen not as divinely taught theologians, but rather as showy talkers of God. For while they ought to expound theology according to the approved traditions of the Saints and, not with carnal arms but those powerful in God, destroy every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and lead captive every thought in obedience to Christ, they, distracted by diverse and strange doctrines, reduce the head to the tail, and make the queen, namely the celestial teaching, serve the handmaid, ascribing to nature what is of grace. Indeed, insisting more than is due on the knowledge of natural things, returning to the weak and needy elements of the world, to which, when they were children, they were in bondage, and serving them anew, as weak in Christ, they feed on milk rather than solid food, and appear to not have established a heart with grace: wherefore, stripped of free gifts and wounded in their natural abilities, they do not recall to memory that of the Apostle, which we believe they have frequently read: "Avoid profane novelties of words and oppositions of knowledge falsely so-called; which some professing have erred concerning the faith." O imprudent and slow of heart to believe all that the defenders of divine grace, namely the prophets, evangelists, and apostles, have spoken! Since nature by itself can do nothing for salvation unless aided by grace. Let such presumptuous ones say, who embrace natural doctrine and offer the leaves but not the fruits of words to their hearers, whose minds, as if fed on husks, remain empty and void, and their soul cannot delight in fatness, for it is thirsty and not watered by the silent waters of Siloam, but rather by those drawn from the torrents of philosophers, of which it is said: "The more they drink, the thirstier they become," because they do not bring satisfaction but rather anxiety and toil.

To the archbishops of Reims, Sens, Rouen, Tours, Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, Narbonne, Lyon, Embrun, Tarentaise, Besançon, Aix, Arles, and Vienne, and their suffragans, and to the abbots, priors, chapters, and other prelates of churches established in the dioceses of these archbishops. With ardent desire, aspiring to cleanse the land of the Albigensians from heretical filth, we renew the indulgences previously granted by the Apostolic See to the faithful signed with the cross or to be signed, who are laboring for this cause. We send our beloved son, R., deacon cardinal of St. Angelus and legate of the Apostolic See, knowing the nature and circumstances of this business, as he once worked effectively in it, a man notable for his counsel and discretion, diligent in honoring the realm of the Franks and fervent in this business, who, though he is very necessary to us at the Apostolic See and his presence opportune, because the matter itself, due to its arduousness, required the diligence of such a great man, we have decided to send him to your parts for the said business and other matters the Apostolic See has to deal with there. Therefore, trusting in the mercy of Almighty God and the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, relying on the power of binding and loosing which God has conferred upon us, though unworthy, we grant full remission of their sins to all who undertake this labor in their own persons and at their own expense, of those sins of which they have truly repented in heart and confessed with mouth, and promise an increase of eternal salvation in the reward of the righteous. To those who do not go there in person, but send suitable men at their own expense, according to their ability and status, and likewise to those who, though at another's expense, go there in person, we grant full forgiveness of their sins. We also wish and grant that all who contribute suitably from their goods to the assistance of this same business, or provide opportune counsel and aid concerning the aforesaid matters, share in this remission according to the extent of their support and the devotion of their affection. Indeed, since, by the just judgment of the heavenly emperor, those adhering to his service should rejoice in a special prerogative, we will and command that if any of those setting out there are bound by oath to pay usury, you are to compel their creditors, by ecclesiastical authority, to release them from their oath given and to desist from the exaction of usury. If any creditors force them to pay usury, compel them by the same judgment to make restitution. Moreover, compel the secular power to force the Jews to remit usury, and deny them the communion of the faithful until they have remitted it. Furthermore, if any of those signed with the cross cannot currently pay their debts to the Jews, take care to ensure that secular judges provide them with such useful delay that, after undertaking the pilgrimage, until it is certainly known of their death or return, they do not incur the burden of usury. Compel the Jews to count the proceeds from pledges, which they have received in the meantime, towards the principal, deducting necessary expenses. Also, compel the debtors of those signed with the cross to pay what they owe, with usury ceasing, urging their creditors to extend the time for payment of debts as necessary. Because some are said to have laid aside the cross assumed against these heretics by their own authority, compel them to take it up again. Therefore, we admonish your discretion and exhort you in the Lord Jesus Christ, by the authority of this letter, to diligently explain all the above to the people subject to you, and to encourage them with diligent exhortations to lend assistance in goods and persons to the aforementioned business, and to carry out each of the above articles which pertains to your concern, so that you may be found diligent and attentive, that the flame of your charity may kindle your neighbors, and that you may expect grace from us in this present life and a reward from God in the future.

To O., Cardinal Deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legate of the Apostolic See. Previously, it was understood that our venerable brother, the bishop of Metz, as soon as he was transferred by the Apostolic See to the bishopric of Metz, which was then gravely fallen, from Verdun, opposed himself as a wall for the justice of the church of Metz and bravely resisted the greater and more powerful figures of the whole empire around the Rhine. By divine grace favoring him, after many labors and grave dangers, he gave peace and tranquility to the aforementioned church and acquired the county of Metz and with it four noble castles, one of which is equivalent to a city, with their appurtenances, all of which he bestowed to his church to be possessed perpetually. Because of this, since he had to incur greater expenses on this account, he had undertaken not a small burden of debts by which he was gravely oppressed. We, considering the cause so praiseworthy for which the said bishop contracted the debts mentioned, and noting both his integrity and the fervor of his devotion and faith, also considering that the clergy of the bishopric of Metz should be concerned with the business that the same bishop had promoted, and that each should share both the benefit and the burden, have given our letters to the beloved sons, the prelates and clergy of the city and diocese of Metz, instructing them to provide the aforementioned bishop with suitable aid liberally and kindly, each contributing according to their own abilities so that, by sharing the burden among them, they might bear it more lightly, and the often-mentioned bishop might be able to be freed from those debts. We have granted our venerable brother, the archbishop of Trier, as executor over this matter, lest the church might be crushed under the burden of debts. After obtaining the counsel of many wise men, he providently assessed how much each should contribute, considering the abilities of each, for the solution of debts amounting to seven thousand and five hundred marks, and pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon those contradicting and rebelling. We, therefore, regarding the taxation made by the aforementioned archbishop on the premisses as agreeable and fixed, command by apostolic writings to your discretion that you ensure the excommunication pronounced by the aforementioned archbishop upon the contradictors and rebels is observed inviolate until due satisfaction, removing the obstacle of appeal. Given at Perugia, VII Kalendas November, in the third year of our pontificate.

Therefore, we command your discretion through apostolic letters that, if this is the case, you revoke to a proper state whatever you find has been rashly attempted after such an appeal. Hear the arguments from both sides and conclude with due end what is just, removing the appeal, and ensure it is observed, etc., unless the parties are sent back to the prior judges, etc. The appellant, etc. Witnesses, etc. If not all, etc. Given at Perugia, the 15th day before the Kalends of February, in the third year of our pontificate.

To the priors and canons of Mortara and all churches directly pertaining to the Mortara church, of the Order of Saint Augustine. Formerly, when we were in a lesser office, serving as legate in the regions of Lombardy, and some other trustworthy religious men informed our predecessor Pope Honorius of blessed memory through our letters that the monastery of Saint Peter in Ciel d'Oro of Pavia, immediately subject to the Apostolic See, had severely deteriorated both spiritually and temporally, to the extent that the abbot of that place was killed due to great neglect to which the monastery had fallen, and with usuries continually increasing, it was not hoped that the place could be reformed by the black monks. They suggested to him that he should transfer the head of your house to the aforementioned monastery, where the body of Blessed Augustine is known to rest. He, through his letters, gave us the mandate to proceed in this matter with all circumstances considered, with the authority of the same, as we saw fit before God. We, however, being occupied with various matters at that time, entrusted this task to James, the bishop of Turin, of blessed memory, instructing him to personally visit the mentioned monastery, diligently inquire the will of the bishop, clergy, and people of Pavia, and if he saw it could be done without scandal, to grant the often-mentioned monastery to the Mortara house; otherwise, he should inform us of what he found regarding this matter through his letters. The aforementioned Bishop of Turin, personally visiting the city of Pavia according to our mandate, diligently inquiring about the will of the bishop, clergy, and people regarding the aforementioned matter, found them all unanimous and concordant in this. And when, after deliberate counsel, they responded that they greatly accepted this kind of transfer, saving nevertheless the rights of the Apostolic See and the Empire, and the rights and honor of the advocates of the mentioned monastery, the same Bishop of Turin, proceeding to the aforementioned monastery with the bishop of Pavia and a large multitude of clergy and people, granted the monastery with all its churches, possessions, rights, and other pertinences freely and absolutely to the Mortara house with the authority with which he was endowed, declaring that the monastery should henceforth be regarded as the head of the Mortara order. He inducted the provost of Mortara, who was at that time there, in the name and place of the said house into the corporeal possession of the monastery, granting him the free faculty of acquiring the possession of all temporal and spiritual things pertaining to the monastery by his own authority. We later judged to confirm his process by the authority of the legation committed to us. Wherefore, our aforementioned predecessor, after thoroughly and diligently inspecting the instruments in which all the above were contained, corroborating the aforementioned concession, confirmed the monastery with all its rights, possessions, churches, and other temporal and spiritual pertinences to you and through you to your order by apostolic authority and fortified it with the protection of his writing, decreeing that the order of Mortara should be observed perpetually there. Since there are four things which seem especially to demand this, namely the reverence for Blessed Augustine, whose body rests there, the authority of the place, the devotion of the clergy and people of Pavia, who would not patiently endure that the head of your order be transferred elsewhere, and the unsuitability of the Mortara location, known to be exposed to wars and many other fortuitous occurrences, due to which the members are sometimes miserably compelled to wander from their head and roam through diverse places, we have deemed it right to ask and admonish your entire community through apostolic letters, ordering that you humbly and devotedly obey the abbot of the same monastery. Given at Perugia, on the second day before the Kalends of November, in the second year of our pontificate.

Proinde, auctoritate apostolica, Gregorius IX confirmationem concessionis ab antecessore suo factam ratam habet, et ordinem servandum in perpetuum decrevit, mandans eis obedientiam abbati monasterii praestare. To the abbot of Saint-Remi, Hugo of Burgundy, formerly an archdeacon, and Master Girard of Laon, canons of Reims. Our apostolate has been informed by the beloved masters Guibert, John, and Hugo of Mont-Saint-Éloi, along with certain other clerics, that there is a church founded in honor of the blessed Apostle Peter almost in the middle of Arras, in a location suitable for secular canons. Historically, there were thirteen or more secular canons, whose revenues the monks of Saint-Vaast of Arras have held for a long time by apostolic authority, as they say, with few of the canons less solemnly serving such a place. That church has also been improperly treated for numerous years, being used by various craftsmen practicing their crafts, with heaps of wood, grain, and similar materials gathered there as if in a barn. Additionally, in a city as significant as Arras, there are two congregations of clerics, one of canons and the other of monks. They humbly petitioned us to grant them the vacant walls of the desolate church, which they intend to repair honorably at their own expense, so that they might establish new prebends there from their own rents and revenues, to the praise and glory of Almighty God, the glorious Virgin Mother, Saint Peter the Apostle, and all the saints, saving the rights of the monastery. Especially since there are certain schools descending from that church, contiguous to them, whose students, often numbering two hundred, would largely serve there unitedly with the canons, as is the custom of the region, whose number, it is hoped, will greatly increase shortly, since even for the monks serving in that church, it is more of a burden than a convenience to travel to it day and night, having left the monastery. Therefore, intending to expand the worship of the divine name, as our duty requires, we command by apostolic letters that you, personally going to the place, diligently inquire, with the removal of any appeal, into the truth concerning this matter and its circumstances, and transmit to us under your seals what you find within four months of receiving these letters, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed more securely in this matter. If not all of you can go, then two of you at least should do so. Given at Perugia, on the ides of October, in the third year.

To the Archbishop of Bordeaux. Our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Bourges, has shown us through his report that, with the authority of the primacy he claims to have over you and your province, he has deemed it necessary to suspend you from both metropolitan and pontifical office because you refused to personally attend the council when summoned by him, and did not wish to revoke the prohibitions you imposed on your subjects, preventing them from receiving him during his visitation of the province of Bordeaux, nor to lift the sentences of excommunication and interdict pronounced against them if they dared to oppose. You not only ignore the sentence of suspension but also do not allow others to observe the sentences of suspension, interdict, and excommunication pronounced by the said Archbishop of Bourges against them because they refused to receive him. By causing further disruptions, you are greatly injurious and troublesome to the possession of the primacy of the same church, or are acting as if you were.
