Therefore, wishing to bring an end to these disputes so they do not become endless, to spare the parties labor and expenses, and to prevent malicious delays, we strictly command your fraternity to present yourself in our presence at the beginning of the next forthcoming Lent with either yourself or a suitable procurator sufficiently instructed to contest the case and to perform all other necessary acts for the decision of the matter. Moreover, we firmly command our beloved sons, the Archdeacon of Tours and Master Martin, canon of Tours, through apostolic letters, to ensure that they summon you peremptorily to the same term with our authority in accordance with the above-mentioned form, and, if you cannot be found, they are to make sure that the edict of citation is publicly posted at your church, reporting back to us on what has been done concerning these matters. To the bishop of Paris and the abbots of Cîteaux and Firmity, of the diocese of Chalon-sur-Saône. Upon understanding the damnable presumption with which certain sons of Belial have not feared to attack our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Lyons, with sacrilegious audacity, we are touched with deep grief and our soul is greatly troubled. Indeed, through the complaint of the same archbishop, it has come to our hearing that certain sons of iniquity, having cast aside the fear of God, wickedly presumed to seize him, having despoiled him and his companions of their goods, and detained him by force for several days, not without injury to the Apostolic See and the entire clerical order, according to their arbitrary will. Therefore, unwilling that such a great presumption should remain unpunished, we command your discretion, by apostolic writings, that you publicly announce and have announced, throughout the Kingdom of France on every Sunday and feast day, with bells ringing and candles lit, that those who were not afraid to seize the aforementioned archbishop with such temerity, and all those who gave them counsel or assistance in this matter, and also those to whom the sacrilegious ones resorted at the time of the crime, either simply or with the spoils of him and his men, should be publicly proclaimed excommunicated and avoided by all as excommunicated, until they have adequately satisfied the injured party, and, having restored all that was taken from him, come to the Apostolic See to be absolved with testimony of your letters. For those in whose district this crime was committed, or where the aforementioned sacrilegious ones reside, or where the goods of the aforementioned archbishop and his men are wickedly detained, you are to carefully admonish and induce them to compel the sacrilegious ones to adequately satisfy the aforementioned archbishop, and both them and all others under whose jurisdiction those who hold the goods taken from him and his men reside, to restore all to him, with authority handed to you, by ecclesiastical censure, removing any appeal, notwithstanding the constitution of the general council, which provides that no one can be brought to judgment by apostolic letters beyond two days' travel outside their diocese. If not all of you, then at least two of you. Given at Perugia, the third calends of December, in the third year of our pontificate. Also to the Archbishop of Vienne in the same manner.

To the Archbishop of Vienna and the Abbot of Ferté, of the Cistercian Order, of the Diocese of Chalon. Our venerable brother, the Bishop of Sabina, having been assumed from the Bisontine church into the fellowship of our brothers, we, desiring that someone who would be suitable for the burden and honor would succeed him in the same church, instructed the chapters of Saint John and Saint Stephen in Besançon, with the counsel of the abbots of Saint Benignus of Dijon and of Morimond, and brother G., prior of the Order of Preachers in Besançon, that within forty days after receiving our letters, they should, canonically and unanimously, elect a suitable person as pastor: otherwise, the same abbots and the prior should provide an archbishop for them. Therefore, on the appointed day for the election, said chapters, following the advice of the aforesaid, as the procurator of the abbot of Saint Benignus stated, delegated their power to six of them, lasting until the consumption of a certain candle which was lit for this purpose. When the electors unanimously agreed on the aforementioned Abbot of Saint Benignus and sought the advice of his associates on this matter, they said they wished to deliberate. However, as the candle waned and there was therefore no time for deliberation, the electors, without awaiting their response, elected the aforementioned Abbot of Saint Benignus as Archbishop of Besançon. However, the aforementioned Abbot of Morimond and the prior, asserting that the election was presumed against the form of our mandate, annulled it and appointed our venerable brother, the Bishop of Chalon, as Bishop of Besançon. It was therefore claimed against this election that, since the response of the aforementioned was not awaited in the election, the form of our mandate was not observed, and therefore it was to be considered null or voidable: but it was countered that the electors had previously dealt with the same abbots and prior about the election, and had sought their counsel; for which, if, after they converged on the Abbot of Saint Benignus, they proceeded to such an election without awaiting the response, what they did should not be subject to censure, but their election should be confirmed. We, having heard and understood what was proposed on both sides, after deliberating with the counsel of our brothers, mandate to your discretion by apostolic writing that if it is evident to you that the electors consulted about the election and sought the aforementioned counsel, so that the advice was sought in the discussion of the election, and the abbot of Saint Benignus is seen to be suitable for the church in terms of learning, life, and other requirements for an archbishop, and nothing canonical obstructs, you should confirm the election and ensure due obedience and reverence are shown to him. But if in the discussion of the election the aforementioned counsel was not sought, although it was sought later but not at an appropriate time, nor was their response awaited, since the blame for this rests with those who imposed a narrow time limit on themselves, or if the abbot is not suitable, you should declare what was done invalid in regard to him. For we indeed revoke the process of the aforementioned two as null. Given at the Lateran, the twelfth calendar day of April, in the year of our pontificate.

To the provost of St. Mary of Magdeburg, the dean of Meissen, and the schoolmaster of Zeitz, in the diocese of Naumburg. Since our predecessor, of blessed memory, Pope H., instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Naumburg, and his co-judges to return the matter sufficiently prepared to the Apostolic See, regarding those things that were conducted before the dean of Trento and his colleague concerning the status of the monastery of Pegau in the diocese of Merseburg, and certain articles between the church of Merseburg and the said monastery by the authority of Pope I., our predecessor, and after the proofs from both parties that were necessary for the instruction of the matter were received, and when certain acts had been transmitted to him, the matter was postponed due to the absence of our venerable brother, the bishop of Merseburg, who had set out to aid the Holy Land, and the same acts were reserved at the Apostolic See. We afterwards summoned the parties to our presence, and when their procurators appeared, the procurator of the monastery called the aforementioned acts into question. Since the originals are said to have remained with the aforementioned former judges, we command your discretion through apostolic writings that you diligently seek them out. If they can be found, and if there are matters that the parties deem lawfully to bring forward, reduce them to writing and send them back to our presence; otherwise, since there is no doubt about the litigation contestation regarding the status of the monastery and certain despoilments done against the abbot by the bishop of Merseburg, take the proofs of the parties anew, and if the parties wish to have a hearing concerning a composition, hear it. Procure to send back to us what you find concerning this matter, as well as the case sufficiently prepared, setting for the parties a term by which they may send their procurators to the Apostolic See sufficiently prepared to receive a composition, provision, or sentence. If not all of you, then two of you, etc. Given at Perugia, on the 6th of October, in the third year of our pontificate.

Quare eisdem discretioni per apostolica scripta praecipit ut originalia acta diligenter requirant et, si reperiantur, cum necessariis probationibus ad Sedem Apostolicam remittantur; sin autem, probationes de novo recipiant et compositionem audiant, causam instructam ad Sedem Apostolicam remittentes. To the bishop and chapter of Naumburg, both present and those canonically to be appointed in the future, in perpetuity. Our beloved sons, L., the provost, and A., a canon of your church, were sent to us on your behalf and presented a privilege on papyrus of our predecessor Pope John of blessed memory. Since it was partially consumed due to excessive age and written in a style different from the modern one, they humbly requested its renewal. We, having diligently examined the privilege, decided to transcribe it word for word into the present document, as far as it could be gathered, granting it the authority known to have been in the original. We supplemented certain syllables and letters in some words that were deemed appropriate and presumed to have been in the original, especially since a privilege of our predecessor Pope Innocent II of blessed memory, shown to us, served to corroborate such supplementing in certain words. Therefore, for clarity, we commanded the syllables and letters to be inscribed in this page with larger letters. John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ildewardus?, the bishop of the church of Zeitz, perpetual salvation in the Lord. If to strangers and private individuals we grant apostolic assistance more elegantly, how much more zealously should we strive to extend it to the needy Holy Church, believing that we will gain the greatest reward in the heavenly realms from the Creator of all, God, when places are undoubtedly brought to a better state through us. Therefore, since our most Christian son, Emperor Conrad, fervently requested with his letters and messengers, asking license which he would not undertake without counsel, that it be permitted to you and to him, whose foresight and moderation had discovered it, to transfer the bishopric of Zeitz, consecrated to the honor of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, to the fortified place of Naumburg, and removed from the usual enemy ravaging it. The heir of a certain Duke Wichard, unable to bear the daily desolation of that place, at the request of said emperor, granted it perpetually to the holy church of Zeitz by right. Inclined by the requests of our brother H., the archbishop of Magdeburg, and the heirs of the said Wichard, namely Hermann the margrave and his brother Eikard, with the counsel of all our bishops and clerics, we grant license and judge by apostolic authority that it be transferred and established in Naumburg and remain there perpetually. We confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity the same place with all its appurtenances to the holy church of Zeitz, consecrated to the honor of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and all the resources and possessions it now seems to have and those it shall acquire in the future. For the holy canons, compelled by necessity, do not oppose, and what we have often read was done, we do not prohibit in our times. If anyone, which we do not believe, with rash daring should attempt to contravene or presume to infringe upon this our apostolic privilege in any way, or should become a violator, let them know that by the authority of Almighty God and the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and ours, they are bound by the chain of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God, and let them be a companion with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in hell, and be subject to excommunication until, repenting, they return to satisfaction and appropriate amendment. But whoever in pious intent becomes a protector and observer of this our apostolic privilege, may they deserve to receive the grace of blessing, eternal life, and the joys of the heavenly kingdom from the Lord for ages of ages. Amen. Written by the hand of George, regional notary and scriniary of the Holy Apostolic See, in the month of December, in the twelfth indiction. Farewell in Christ. Let no one, therefore, etc. But if anyone, etc. Given at Perugia on the sixth day before the ides of November, in the second year of our pontificate.

To the Patriarch of Antioch. You submitted in our presence and that of our brothers that some time ago, the citizens of Brescia, greatly burdened by the reparations of damages inflicted upon each other, which they incurred due to many civil discordances, approved and affirmed by oath a statute issued by you, then elected bishop of Brescia, namely that they would not in the future seek or receive such reparations. Recently, however, with much effort and diligence, you procured that regarding the discord which heavily vexed the citizens, the consuls and council swore precisely and absolutely to comply with all your mandates. However, unless provision is made by the community of Brescia for those who suffered damages at least regarding the expenses they incurred due to this occasion, you cannot fully quell the discord without the risk of recurrence. Therefore, you requested that an apostolic remedy be applied. Since the restoration of damages is different from the satisfaction of expenses, and therefore in the oath given concerning damages it should not be understood that the matter of expenses is included, we mandate through apostolic letters that notwithstanding the aforesaid oath, you provide by our authority that the said community, for the sake of concord, contributes towards the satisfaction of expenses, to be moderated by you as you deem expedient, according to your discretion. Given as above.

Dat. ut supra.

To the Abbot and Cistercian Convent. The Holy Roman Church. Given at Perugia, on the 20th of February, in the second year of our pontificate.

1. Privilege of King Richard:
Richard, by the grace of God, King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, greets archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justiciars, sheriffs, and all his servants and faithful in France and England. Know that we have given and by the present charter confirmed to God and the Church of Saint Mary of Cîteaux in pure and perpetual alms, for the soul of King Henry, our father, and for the salvation of our soul and that of our mother, and of all our ancestors and successors, our church of Scarborough, with all its chapels and all other appurtenances. We desire that the Cistercian Abbots be provided for at Cîteaux for three days during the general chapter. Moreover, whatever may remain beyond the three-day provision from all the revenues of our aforesaid alms, we decree shall be used for the needs of the house of Cîteaux, as may seem best to the abbot and brothers of that house, for we desire that this alms shall in no way be alienated from the house of Cîteaux in the future. Therefore, we desire and firmly command that the aforementioned Abbey of Cîteaux receive, hold, and have in perpetuity freely and honorably, whole and entire, quietly, and without any disturbance or contradiction or diminution, the aforementioned church of Scarborough with all its chapels, both those that are anciently in the castle and others, both inside the walls of the town and outside, and with all its other appurtenances, and with all its liberties and free customs, and with all its lands, houses, and tithes of land and sea. And lest any contention or contradiction might arise against the church of Cîteaux, by reason of the vicarage of the church of Scarborough, we fully grant to the house of Cîteaux the right to appoint the vicar, and whatever right we had in the vicarage, retaining nothing for ourselves, and we amputate completely the opportunity of disturbing our deed or altering the alms for all our successors and others of whatever persons. The Abbot of Cîteaux may choose and present a vicar to the Archbishop at his discretion and will; the vicar, when presented, shall swear upon the Holy Gospel to be faithful in all things to the church of Cîteaux and its procurator; nor shall he knowingly sustain damage or loss to its revenues. If he should fail in this and, having been warned thrice, not amend, the vicarage shall be taken from him. We have also decreed that the chaplains who shall serve in that church or in the adjacent chapels for the time being, shall be bound by the same oath of fidelity, and may be admitted or removed at the will of the Abbot of Cîteaux or his procurator. We furthermore desire and command that while the church is without a vicar, the procurator of Cîteaux shall see that it is served, and shall receive all the revenues for the use of the house of Cîteaux and for the provision of the Cistercian chapter until the Abbot of Cîteaux shall elect another vicar to be presented to the Archbishop of York, as aforesaid. And so that all these things may be possessed peacefully, quietly, and without any claim or exaction in perpetuity by the aforementioned house of Cîteaux, we firmly prohibit any person, secular or ecclesiastical, other than the house of Cîteaux, from erecting a chapel or altar in the whole parish of Scarborough, or doing anything else that might at any time turn to the detriment or harm of the house of Cîteaux, upon the forfeiture of ten pounds. 

Witnessed by: Geoffrey, Archbishop of York; Philip, Bishop of Durham; Hugh, Bishop of Salisbury; Master Malger; Nigel, Treasurer; Master Roger of St. Edmund; William, Marshal; Joel of Mayenne; Geoffrey of Cella; Robert of Harcourt; Matthew of Gammage; Brito, our chamberlain. Given by the hand of E., Bishop of Ely, at Lyons, on the 14th day of May, in the ninth year of our reign.

To the Bishop of Tournai. It has come to our attention, as it has been reported to us, that several people from Cahors and some other foreigners living in the town of Ypres presume to lend money at interest publicly, in contempt of divine law and at the peril of their souls, as well as to the scandal of many, since the natives, as it is said, are not permitted to do so. Therefore, in order to prevent others who keep their hands clean from being infected by their contagion with this sort of depravity, we firmly command you by apostolic writing that you restrain the usurers of the aforementioned place, both foreigners and natives, from the often-mentioned depravity of usury, in the manner prescribed by the penalty issued against usurers at the Lateran Council, removing any appeal, and enjoin all and each of the sheriffs and the community of the said town under the same penalty not to have any commerce or interaction with them, nor to presume to receive them unless they cease from the aforementioned depravity. Given at Perugia, on the third day before the calends of February, in the third year [of our pontificate].

Dat. Perusii, III kalendas februarii, anno tertio.

To the illustrious King of Aragon. We give thanks to the giver of all graces, because, as we have heard and indeed accept, He, by mercifully inspiring your mind with the fear of His name and love, you recognize the glory of the royal dignity from Him who alone has power in the kingdom of men. You venerate His bride, the Church, and ecclesiastical persons with due honor, offering and exposing yourself to the Apostolic See and our good pleasure with prompt faith and ready devotion, desiring to please us with will and action. Therefore, we, delighted in the glory of your gentleness, embracing your person with the prerogative of love and grace, aspire to your advancement in both aspects of man. Moreover, we have benignly and gratefully received the pleasing and honest petitions, which your highness sent to us through our beloved son John of Buccados, your messenger, a truly faithful, well-mannered, and provident man, concerning receiving the royal diadem from our hands, and we have cheerfully admitted them to the grace of hearing, commendably praising your magnificence in the Lord. However, because all good things come in their time, and so that the gifts sought may be more graciously granted, they are sometimes deferred, to be conferred more opportunely. We, considering the various current disturbances, as is fitting, from which many inconveniences could arise for such a matter, have decided to wait for a more suitable time, in which the matter, with the Lord as a guide, may be directed without hindrance and may attain the desired effect with everything cooperating for good. Therefore, we ask and urge your royal serenity in the Lord not to be moved by such a delay, since we are ready to exhibit grace to you both in this and in other matters. But, confidently expecting in a short time, as we trust, when you see fit, you may confidently request us, since in the meantime we diligently arrange what is necessary. Strive, therefore, son of blessing and grace, to do your works in gentleness, according to the advice of the wise, so that you may be directed above the glory of men, and that the Lord may add days to the days of the king, strive to be exercised in His commandments. Because when the ways of a man please the Lord, He will even make his enemies to be at peace with him, and so that, with you as ruler, with you as leader, His people will dwell in the beauty of peace and abundant rest, and eventually, you will happily exchange the transitory kingdom for the eternal one. Given at Perugia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the third year of our pontificate.

To the bishop of Senlis, the abbot of Compiègne in the diocese of Soissons, and Master J., the archdeacon of Paris. It was presented before us on behalf of our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Laon, that, having the authority of an apostolic indulgence allowing them to exercise ecclesiastical censure against their wrongdoers who seize their common goods, they had pronounced sentences of excommunication on the noble man J., lord of Coucy, and interdict on his land. When the procurators of the parties came to the Apostolic See because of this, and the case was contested there on various articles, we entrusted the matter to you for resolution, with the addition in our letters that letters obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties should not stand in the way. Before you, the cited nobleman argued that proceedings should not occur based on those letters because W., who had obtained the letters, had been a false procurator since he had revoked the mandate given to him before obtaining those letters due to suspicion against him. The opposing party claimed that this revocation had not reached us or them. After hearing both sides, you issued an interlocutory decision that you should proceed based on those letters. At the request of their procurator, among other things, to inspect the aforementioned indulgence as was mandated to you, the nobleman's procurator countered that they should not proceed based on the aforementioned letters, presenting other letters obtained later, which included a clause that if proceedings were to occur with the consent of the parties, you should conclude the same case; otherwise, you should send it adequately instructed to the Apostolic See for examination with the mentioned indulgence. These latter letters were claimed to be invalid by them because they had been obtained by the same W. after the revocation of the mandate. Since you had not yet declared through which of the letters you should proceed, they were compelled to seek remedy at the Apostolic See. Since, according to the general statutes of the council, letters of the Apostolic See obtained without a special mandate from the lord should not be valid unless from those persons from whom a mandate is not required by law, we command you by apostolic writs, if it is so, since letters obtained from someone whose mandate has been revoked by the lord should be less valid, to proceed in the matter according to the content of the prior letters, notwithstanding the later ones, removing the obstacle of appeal as reason dictates. Witnesses etc. If not all can, then you, brother bishop, with one of them etc. Given at Perugia, 21st of January, in the third year of our pontificate.

Dat. Perusii, XII kalendas februarii, pontificatus anno tertio.

To the bishops of Le Mans and Senlis, and Master John, archdeacon of Châlons. In order to guard and cultivate that paradise of delights entrusted to our care, we must be very careful not to allow the river of delights, which waters the land of that place, to be diverted from its course, and, divided into streams, to dry up; lest, the irrigation being withdrawn, the paradise become desolate and, turning into barrenness, produce thorns and thistles, and the vines of Sorek planted therein, having prohibited clouds from pouring rain upon them, degenerate into wild grapes. It is also greatly to be feared that, with such dryness ensuing, the wells dug by Isaac's servants, namely, the wells of disputation descending from the noise of causes and enmity arising from the battle of words, descending from the discussion of the liberal arts and extending the ways of the Lord's commandments with an enlarged heart, may be blocked by the Philistines, opponents of Isaac, and his flocks may perish from thirst. Indeed, the river is the study of letters, by which, after the grace of the Holy Spirit, the paradise of the universal Church is watered and made fruitful, the channel of which is known to have been the city of Paris, because this study has flourished in Paris up to now. Hence, we should not calmly tolerate it being transferred elsewhere in our time, lest perhaps, being divided into many places by such a transfer, it may be reduced to nothing, and the heaven of Scripture be closed, and the clouds withhold their rain, and the land of the universal Church remain unwatered, and the sun and moon be turned into darkness, and the stars be enveloped in their mist. Truly, it has come to our notice that a dispute has arisen between our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, and the queen, his mother, on the one hand, and our beloved sons, the masters and scholars of Paris, on the other. These masters, along with the scholars, having suffered damages and injuries, have left Paris, intending to transfer the study elsewhere; by which they seem to have taken away the key of knowledge, and to want to close the kingdom of heaven before men, not entering themselves and not allowing those who wish to enter to do so. Therefore, aspiring to the benefits to come from the return of the aforementioned river to its channel, and wishing to prevent the inconveniences that may arise from the departure, we command you, through apostolic writings, to intervene diligently between the king and queen and the aforementioned masters and scholars. Provide diligent care and effective effort to satisfactorily compensate the aforementioned masters and scholars for the inflicted damages and injuries, such as justice and judgment, from which they seem not to have proceeded, offer such an oath. If, perhaps, some of them see fit to excuse themselves with such an obstacle, the circumspection of the Apostolic See will take care, by the Lord's authority, to provide for this in such a way that no stain of infamy will be spread from this. And since delay seems to bring danger upon itself, carry out what we command without any delay, and quickly inform us of what you find concerning these matters with your letters, so that, instructed by your report, we may proceed, by the Lord's authority, as we see fit to be provided. Given at Perugia, on the eighth calends of December, in the third year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Honorius III, episcopis Cenomanensi et Silvanectensi et magistro Johanni, archidiacono Cathalaunensi mandat ut inter regem Francorum et reginam eius ac magistros et scolares Parisienses dissensiones componant, utque magistris et scolaribus de iniuriis satisfiat, ne studium alibi transferatur. Datum Perusii, VIII kalendas Decembris, anno tertio.

To the Archbishop of Milan. The church of Milan, as far as the memory of men reaches, has always been obedient and devoted to the Apostolic See; but due to the fault of the citizens of Milan, Pope Innocent, of happy memory, our predecessor, placed their city under interdict and ordered the suffragans of that church not to obey it. The venerable brother, the Bishop of Cremona, consecrated at the Apostolic See, as it is said, received a special mandate in this regard. However, as time passed and the citizens returned to obedience to the Church, Pope Honorius, of good memory, our predecessor, instructed you, then elected Archbishop of Milan, on the advice of his brothers, to come to his presence to receive the gift of consecration along with the restitution of the suffragans of the Milanese church. Finally, bestowing the gift of consecration upon you, and restoring your church to its usual state, he ordered the suffragans of the Milanese church, absolutely and without distinction, to obey it as their metropolis, and to serve and obey devoutly and humbly. He also renewed the privilege of the Milanese church, which noted among other suffragans the Church of Cremona. Since the bishop, after such restitution and order, repeatedly summoned for reasonable causes and finally to a synod, completely refused to come, you pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him, which our venerable brothers, the Patriarch of Antioch, then of Brescia, and the bishops of Vercelli, and the beloved son, a canon of Milan, messengers from the Milanese church to the Apostolic See, asked to be confirmed by apostolic authority and ordered the said bishop not to show himself contumacious or rebellious to you or the Milanese church. To the illustrious King of the Franks and to B., his mother, the queen. The Kingdom of France, following the model of the Holy Trinity, in the appropriation of the name to the three persons - power, wisdom, and kindness - has clearly excelled over other kingdoms for a long time past, powerful with the strength of its soldiers, wise with the clergy endowed with the knowledge of letters, and kind with the benevolence of its merciful princes. If two of these elements are missing, the extremes turn into vices: for power, unless tempered by wisdom, leads to presumption, raising itself in arrogance; likewise, kindness, if not supported by the same, degenerates into dissolution and becomes akin to folly. Therefore, wisdom is necessary for both, without which neither can obtain the name or effect of virtue. Wisdom, indeed, is nurtured by the study of letters, which, like a river flowing from a place of delight, irrigates and fructifies not only the aforesaid kingdom, after the grace of the Holy Spirit, but also the paradise of the universal Church, whose channel is known to have been the city of Paris, because this study has flourished there until now. Hence, we believe it to be in your interest to diligently strive and exert careful effort, so that during your days, the study which has been transferred from Paris may be brought back there like a river to its channel, lest it perhaps becomes nullified by being divided among many places, like a river diverted from its channel and split into streams, it dries up. Consequently, the heavens of Scripture might be closed, the clouds may restrain their rain, and the land of the universal Church might remain unwatered, and the sun and moon might be turned into darkness, and the stars might be enveloped in the gloom of such darkness, and thus the preeminent vestige of the Trinity might be erased from the aforementioned kingdom; for it would reflect poorly on you if the same kingdom were deprived of such glory during your days; nor would it befit you that the loss of such honor, which illustrious kings have strived to preserve with their innate clemency in their times, be attributed to those reigning in it; benignly supporting and kindly nurturing the multitude gathered from various nations of the world in the aforesaid city to draw from the waters of wisdom, and providing support if ever it exceeded. Indeed, it has come to our attention that, due to a dispute arising between you on one side and the dear sons, the masters and scholars of Paris, on the other, these masters, along with the scholars, having been provoked by losses and injuries, have left Paris, transferring the study elsewhere. Therefore, aspiring to the benefits to arise from the return of the aforesaid river to its channel, and wishing to prevent the inconveniences that may emerge from their departure, we instruct by our letters our venerable brothers, the bishops of Le Mans and Senlis, and Master John, archdeacon of Châlons, to diligently intercede between you and the aforementioned masters and scholars, and to exert careful diligence and effective effort to ensure that the masters and scholars are adequately compensated for the incurred losses and injuries, and, having restored the accustomed liberty granted to them by the late illustrious King Philip of France, the study is brought back to Paris. Therefore, we earnestly ask and admonish your excellency, and exhort you in the Lord, that, adhering to the footsteps of your predecessors' kindness, for the reverence of the Apostolic See and ours, you may fully admit them into your royal grace and favor, complying with the admonitions and exhortations of the aforementioned, executing these with prompt implementation, as is fitting, with your usual clemency: lest, if you act otherwise, which we do not anticipate, you seem to have rejected wisdom and kindness, without which the unity of power can scarcely persist, and we, who cannot calmly endure that the same kingdom, hitherto blessed from heaven, be disgraced by such a lack of decorum, be compelled to provide otherwise in this matter. Given at Perugia, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, in the third year of our pontificate.

Since the age of minority is so favorable that it is considered not only impious but also disgraceful to unduly burden minors, and those who show them kindly affection seem to merit what they are known to owe, because virtue shines more clearly when exercised freely and willingly rather than out of necessity: just as it is fitting and commendable to hold our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of the French, who is in his minority, in honor by his faithful subjects, so it is known to be indecent and disgraceful for his adolescence to be scorned by them, as they seek to subvert the debt of fidelity by refusing to obey their lord. Therefore, since we embrace the aforementioned king with a special prerogative of love and grace, and zealously care for the state of the kingdom, we cannot bear his distress without our own distress. On behalf of the bishop, they were ordered under pain of excommunication to accept a certain Cluniac monk, whom they appointed as a pastor to the monastery, without specifying any reason why they should be deprived of the right to elect. Therefore, they again appealed to our hearing. The bishop, disregarding the appeal, promulgated a sentence of excommunication against them and those communicating with them, and solemnly has this sentence published throughout the city and diocese of Beauvais every Sunday and feast day with bells ringing and candles lit; and having seized all their goods, some he converted to his own use and others he entrusted to be kept by others, leaving them nothing at all, broadly prohibiting under pain of excommunication that rents and other revenues be paid to them, further threatening that unless they renounce the appeal made, he would imprison the most prominent among them. Therefore, they, since no one dared to communicate with them due to the excommunication, and being deprived of all goods, having nothing to live on, were forced to leave the monastery, and thus they are begging, and the lands and vineyards of the said monastery lie uncultivated. Additionally, the Cluniac monk, coming to the monastery, having broken their doors and locks of the cloister and all the offices, forcibly entered by the violence of the bishop. To the same. We have received with grateful affection and due honor, our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Capua, who was sent to us by imperial majesty, and we have diligently understood what he proposed to us on your behalf. However, after having suitable deliberation with our brothers about these matters, although it might seem somewhat difficult to some, especially those who do not consider the circumstances, what we now decide to respond will surely please those who understand the purity of our mind and the quality of the times, as it is supported by very clear reason. Indeed, since it was decreed in the general council that lands infected with heretical depravity should be exposed to crusaders unless cleansed by their lords, saving the rights of the principal lords, provided they do not present any obstacle or opposition, although the Roman Church may have begun to retain lands situated in Provence and others, acquired after infinite hardships and countless expenses in blood against heretics, so that the wicked may not creep back in or attack, He who forms the hearts of men individually and understands the thoughts of each, knows that we never intended to derogate from the rights of the empire, which we rather propose to preserve inviolate. However, since the conversion of that land is still so recent and fragile that it could easily relapse into error from a slight change, which would be worse than the previous error, there is no doubt that it is to the health and honor of you to defer your petition to an opportune time, at which we may be able to address it with the honor of the Church and yours, because, since a new disturbance has now arisen in that land and the old has not been entirely quelled, if any misfortune, God forbid, should happen, many would principally blame us and you. But it should not be unknown to you that the castle of Felicitas, now called Civitas de Castello, belongs to the Apostolic See by full right, as appears from many public charters, and the privileges of your predecessors attest, and the statements of emperors acknowledge. Hence, listen to what the said archbishop will say to you on our behalf, and if you see it befitting your honor to pursue the right you intend, you will find us ready for the fulfillment of justice. To the Archbishop of Pisa. We fear that the citizens of Lucca, who ought to act according to their name by shining through the purity of devotion and faith, are truly deprived of light, in whom we must bind what was broken with pastoral diligence and bring back what was cast away. Indeed, the said citizens, incited by a spirit of fury and the goads of pride, have dared to invade the patrimony of the Apostolic See, namely the land of Garfagnana, against our warnings, pleas, and multiple prohibitions, wishing to enslave it and subject it to their servitude. Therefore, caring to restrain them from our injury and their future disgrace, we excommunicated them and subjected their land to ecclesiastical interdict. However, having despised the sentences of excommunication and interdict, they have become more obstinate, always falling into worse, committing worse things day by day. Therefore, aggravating the hands of the Apostolic See against them, we have decided to withdraw the aforementioned land of Garfagnana from the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Lucca; but they, disregarding it, as well as the censure of ecclesiastical discipline, refused to turn away from their evil way. Recently, having hostilely destroyed the aforementioned land and exercised excessive cruelty, among other wicked things they committed there, they impiously profaned the sanctuaries of God, demolished and reduced the churches to ashes and cinders, and even dug up the altars. Considering also that nothing is more just than that one should be punished in that which he is known to have offended, with the counsel of our brothers, we have decreed that unless the aforementioned citizens return to our command by the next coming feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, willing to give full satisfaction regarding those things for which they were excommunicated and interdicted, they shall be deprived of the episcopal honor, which they have rendered themselves unworthy of, and the dignity of canons of the cathedral church, if they have any, by the Apostolic See. Therefore, we strictly command your fraternity by apostolic writings that you do not delay to publish such a decree. And if the mentioned citizens do not return by the prescribed term, as they are rejected by divine judgment due to the magnitude of their fault, you are to renew the promulgated sentences both against the aforesaid citizens and their supporters and subject their entire land to a very strict interdict; so that except for the penances of the dying and the baptisms of infants, no ecclesiastical sacraments are to be conferred there. Furthermore, you are to strictly forbid the surrounding peoples under the penalty of excommunication, which the contemptuous incur by law, from exercising any commerce with them or from appointing anyone from the city of Lucca to any magistracy or other office, nor may any of them receive any office in the same. Also, you shall decree by our authority that the statutes which the Lucchese government and its officials may issue, and the sentences which judges may pass, and the documents which notaries may draw up after the noted term, are to be of no validity; ready nevertheless to receive, when required by us, the portion of the aforementioned diocese which we have granted to you and the Church of Pisa to be divided among neighboring bishops, and to defend that received as other rights of the Pisan diocese. Given at the Lateran, 5th day before the Nones of July, in the year of our pontificate.

We, therefore, after a considered decision of the Supreme Pontiff and the brothers, through inspection of prior letters which Jocelin had obtained from Lord Honorius, in which the prior of Saint Martin of the Fields and his colleagues only received the power of compulsion upon the bishop, realized that the second letters of Lord Honorius and others of our Lord Gregory had been obtained by false suggestion, in which it was contained that the aforesaid judges had conferred the prebend by apostolic authority to the aforementioned subdeacon, when in fact they received the power not of conferring, but of compelling by the priors. To Master Nicholas, our subdeacon, archdeacon of Reggio. Since the kindness of the Apostolic See, which frequently exceeds the merits and desires of supplicants, ought to pursue with grace those who are well-deserving and devoted, our predecessor, of blessed memory, Pope Honorius, recognizing the purity of your devotion and faith, and the pleasing services you have long rendered to the Roman Church, once instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Lodi, that if any position or other benefice in the regions of Lombardy were to become vacant, which would seem suitable for your provision, he should confer and assign it to you, notwithstanding any statutes or indulgences, restraining opposers, etc.; he, upon the vacancy of the archdeaconry of Reggio, conferred it upon you with all its rights, pronouncing a sentence of excommunication on any opponents; and enjoined the chapter of Reggio to receive you as their archdeacon. Upon coming to the church of Reggio, having assigned you a stall in the choir, he instituted you in the aforesaid archdeaconry and inducted you into its possession; and while some of the chapter humbly complied, the archpriest and some others attempted to oppose you recklessly; because of this, they incurred the aforementioned sentence of excommunication. And since certain letters on behalf of the chapter of Reggio were presented under the name of our same predecessor to our venerable brother, the bishop of Parma, and his fellow judges, which could justly be considered suspect as obtained through fraudulent means; and so that you might not proceed by their authority without consulting the same predecessor, you appealed to our hearing: meanwhile, a certain prebend in the aforementioned church became vacant, and both those who complied and others, disregarding you, elected three as canons to your prejudice after the legitimate appeal by your procurator to us was made. When you brought this complaint to our ears, since full faith could not be established in these matters in the absence of the other party, we summoned all those from the aforesaid chapter who would oppose you to our presence, setting a fixed term for them. Therefore, the parties having appeared first before our venerable brother, the bishop of Albano, and afterwards before our beloved son, R., cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, appointed by us as your auditors, after much was requested, you asked us to allow you to peacefully possess the aforesaid archdeaconry with the prebend, chamber, and other appurtenances, and to restore to you the fruits received from the time of the collation, and to satisfy you for the expenses which the adverse party had compelled you to incur, especially since the appeal they had frivolously lodged was not pursued, as they had obtained letters not on appeal but on the principal matter. You also requested the annulment of the election of the aforesaid three canons, and other matters attempted to your prejudice in the meantime. These and other matters having been faithfully reported to us by the same cardinal, since the aforementioned bishop of Lodi was found to have observed the form given to him in these matters, holding what was done by him as ratified, with the advice of our brothers, we decree and wish you to be assigned the said archdeaconry along with the chamber and fruits received from the time of collation. Concerning the others, and also the sentence of excommunication incurred by the opposers, and concerning the fact that it is said that the excommunicated celebrated divine services, we have not deemed it necessary to proceed at present. Chapters of Anibaldus, the senator, and the people of Rome issued against the Patarenes. All heretics in the city, namely the Cathars, Patarenes, Pauperes of Lyon, Passagines, Joseppins, Arnalists, Speronists, and others who are named by any heresy, as well as their believers, receivers, supporters, and defenders in the city, shall be perpetually outlawed by the senator each year when he takes the oath of his office. Also, in the city, the aforementioned actions shall be enforced against the believers in heretical errors after they have been denounced by the Church. However, the aforementioned citizen sought to discredit the instrument's authenticity, arguing that the notary B. was not believed to be a public notary at the time of the instrument's creation, and that he was under excommunication at that time, imposed by our venerable brother, the bishop of Arezzo, on all who did not pursue their crusader vows. Furthermore, B. had been accused of falsifying certain instruments, and the sureties he provided were condemned to a sum of money. The case was further complicated when the original instrument was lost, and a new one was fabricated in the first person by B., differing in several respects from the original. Witnesses who had signed it also contradicted themselves in many points. To these claims, it was countered that B. was indeed recognized as a public notary in those parts, and that his authenticity could be fully verified if necessary, and that the aforementioned sentence of the bishop of Arezzo did not bind him specifically, as it was general, and for six years prior, he considered himself absolved from it; additionally, the bishop had dispensed B. regarding his vow, as contained in his letters, although it was argued that such letters should not prejudice others. Furthermore, the accusation of falsity against the notary B. had not been substantiated, as one is not guilty until proven so; and whether a notary uses the third or first person in drafting an instrument is of no consequence, provided the truth is not altered. To the archdeacons of Sens and of Étampes, in the diocese of Sens, and to the dean of Sens. P., a widow, presented a petition to us showing that once upon a time our predecessor, Pope of happy memory, I. [Innocent], had committed the case that was unfolding between her and the late Count of Vendôme regarding her dowry and marriage portion to G., Bishop of Palestrina, then Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, following various and diverse commissions obtained from the Apostolic See by appeals made to him on her behalf. With a proper legal contestation taking place, and the case being subsequently assigned by our predecessor, with the assent of the parties' procurators, to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Meaux and his co-judges, the count's party made a frivolous appeal against it. The said judges considered this appeal frivolous and issued a definitive sentence, pronouncing sentences of excommunication against the count and interdict upon his lands. Then, after the representatives of the widow and the count had appeared at the Apostolic See, an auditor of blessed memory, J., Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata, was appointed. Our predecessor, having understood the matters presented before the cardinal, ordered the archdeacon of Paris and his co-judges to uphold the sentences of excommunication and interdict against the count until he complied with the definitive sentence, without any hindrance of appeal. However, with the count passing away in the meantime, the widow procured letters from our venerable brother, the Bishop of Paris and his co-judges, ordering that unless the new Count of Vendôme, the deceased count’s successor, properly compensated her for what the deceased had been condemned, they should issue sentences of excommunication against his person and interdict upon his land, setting aside any appeals, and cause the body of the deceased to be exhumed from the cemetery, restraining any objectors by ecclesiastical censure, disregarding appeals. Despite the mandate faithfully executed by the judges, the new count appealed to the Apostolic See and obtained letters from Pope H., our predecessor, to the Abbot of Saint-Germain of Auxerre and his co-judges against her. The widow, feeling sufficiently aggrieved, made an appeal to the Apostolic See and obtained letters to the dean of Paris and his co-judges. As they proceeded to receive testimony, the abbot of Saint-Germain and his co-judges improperly relaxed the sentences of excommunication and interdict without any satisfaction made to her, neglecting due legal process. Meanwhile, the abbot of Saint-Germain and his co-judges having died, our predecessor, upon the widow's petition, ordered their successors to restore the process to its rightful state and refer the case to those to whom it seemed legally proper to remit it. As they proceeded in the matter according to the given form, the new count, alleging a manifest grievance, appealed against them and obtained our letters to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Beauvais and his co-judges. The widow, feeling unjustly aggrieved by their acceptance of the count’s improper appeal, appealed to us. She humbly petitioned us to mercifully provide for her, since more than twenty-five years have passed without a resolution due to the malice of the other party. Therefore, not wishing for the conclusion of the case to be further delayed by malice, we command your discretion by apostolic writings to have all letters obtained from the Apostolic See regarding this matter presented to you, disregard any frivolous exceptions intended to delay it, and restore to its rightful state anything found to be improperly attempted against her interest since the widow's procurator began the journey to the Apostolic See. Hear the case, sufficiently instruct it, and remit it to our examination, setting a competent term for the parties to present themselves or competent procurators before our sight, to receive a just sentence, God willing. If not all of you can act together, two of you can proceed. Dated at the Lateran, 2nd nones of June, the fourth year.

We rejoice in the Lord, and boast in the praises of the beloved sons, the provincial prior and the brethren of the Order of Preachers in Germany, who diligently fulfill their ministry and show themselves to be unshakable workers. Furthermore, whatever is bequeathed to them by those deceased in the final will shall be applied to their uses, saving the canonical rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Given at the Lateran, the 15th day before the kalends of April, in the fourth year of our pontificate.
