For although efforts have been made for ten years or more, not without great pains and expenses, and though the monastery was first inducted into possession of the said hamlet for the sake of custody due to the contumacy of the other party, and later, with the growing obstinacy of the defiant, was deprived of the true possession of the same hamlet after a year elapsed, yet due to the procrastinations of the knight, the principal case could never be brought to contestation. Afterwards, when the parties approached the Apostolic See concerning this, and it was litigated for a while before the aforementioned bishop who was granted as a listener to them, we decided to entrust this matter to certain judges in those parts under a specific form by common consent of the parties; however, as two of them, who were then at the Apostolic See, did not cross over to those parts, and the third died, no progress could be made in the same matter. Indeed, with the aforementioned knight and nearly his entire offspring removed from human affairs, the said abbot and convent, due to the turmoil of the kingdom of Cyprus, claim not to have full certainty as to into whose hands that hamlet has passed. Wishing therefore to put an end to the disputes, we command that, after summoning those who ought to be summoned for this matter, you have all the letters obtained on both sides and the processes held through them presented to you, and that you approve what you see should be approved by law, nullifying the rest entirely with the removal of any appeal, but if you see none of them fit for approval, to completely annul the mentioned processes and whatever has followed or been caused by them, and to hear the case, etc., rendering justice. Witnesses, etc. Notwithstanding the constitution regarding two journeys, etc. If not all, etc. Given at Anagni, the 5th day before the Kalends of February.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX episcopus Tripolitano et Anteradensi episcopis et cantori Anteradensi mandat ut, super controversia recuperationis casalis Perego a dicto abbate et conventu monasterii Belli Montis, perituris litteris et processibus iniustis contra abbatem et conventum obtentis, sublato appellationis diffugio, causam audiant et justitiam faciant, propter contumaciam W. militis de Riveto et perturbationem regni Cypri, difficilem rem esse determinantes. Datum Anagnie, V kalendas februarii.

**Translation to English:**

To Masters J. de Monte Mirabili and H., archdeacons of Paris, and Vertnaciol, canon of Treviso, residing in Paris. We inform you that we have received a message from the greater prior, the provost, the cellarer, and some other obedientiaries and monks, both external and internal, of the monastery of Coulombs, of the Benedictine order, in the diocese of Chartres. They informed us that when the monastery lacked a pastor, the convent was unable to reach a unanimous agreement among themselves. They delegated their votes to the sub-prior of the same monastery to nominate twelve monks of that place, who, with a thirteenth associate, would provide a pastor for the monastery. However, when the sub-prior nominated certain monks, it caused dissension within the convent. Due to this disagreement, the sub-prior and the convent deviated from the established procedure, and the convent later entrusted the decision to three of their monks. Eventually, as the monks could not agree on an election, the convent, despite opposition and appeal by the provost, granted the power to appoint an abbot for the monastery to our venerable brother, the bishop of Chartres. Ignoring the appeal, the bishop appointed H., a monk, who was the illegitimate son of a monk and priest of that place, as abbot according to his will. Consequently, an appeal was made to our audience on their behalf. The said bishop, disregarding their legitimate appeal, presumptuously removed them from their administrations and pronounced a sentence of excommunication unjustly against them. Regarding these actions, H. obtained apostolic letters to the abbot of the Major Monastery to ensure that the sentence would be observed inviolably until proper satisfaction was made. Therefore, they humbly requested us to provide assistance concerning these matters for them and the aforesaid monastery. Hence, we command you to summon those whom you deem necessary, absolve the prior, provost, and others mentioned according to the Church's form, as a precaution, notwithstanding the said letters of confirmation and the process undertaken through them. Restore them to their proper places as justice demands, and diligently inquire into all the aforementioned matters and others that may be presented before you from both sides, removing any appeal, and bring the case to a proper conclusion if it proceeds with the consent of the parties. Otherwise, sufficiently instruct the case to the point of receiving the sentence. Witnesses, etc. If not all, etc. Dated at Anagni, the nones of February, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Honorius III magistris J. de Monte Mirabili et H., archidiaconis Parisiensibus, et Vertnaciol, canonico Tervisino, Parisius commorantibus mandat ut, vocatis evocandis, prior, praepositus et alii absolvantur juxta formam Ecclesiae et restituantur ad loca propria, inquirant super dissensionibus et irregularitatibus in monasterio Columbensi, ordinis Sancti Benedicti, Carnotensis dioecesis; si procedat ex partium voluntate, causam terminent, alioquin sufficienter instructam usque ad sententiam recipiant. Dat. Anagnie, nonis februarii, anno sexto.

**Translation to English:**

To the archdeacon of Lisieux, the cantor of Saint-Omer in the diocese of Thérouanne, and Master R., canon of Le Mans, residing in Paris. We sympathize with parental compassion for our beloved son W., a poor cleric, who is worn out by the difficulties, labors, and expenses he has incurred in seeking a prebend in the church of Saint-Marcel, in the diocese of Paris, where the collation of prebends is said to belong to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Paris. As he presented before us with much bitterness of heart, many letters from the Apostolic See have been obtained by various judges over this matter, and not only have diverse but adverse proceedings been conducted through them, making the affair so entangled due to various exceptions and crafty subterfuges of the opposing party, that it seems almost completely confused rather than resolved; hence, what was meant as provision and grace has turned into punishment and sorrow for him, leading him to such poverty that he is now forced to beg miserably. Therefore, since he asserts that he is compelled to desist from pursuing his case due to the burdens of extreme poverty, and since we intend to put an end to his labors, especially because we have ordered that the next vacant prebend in the same church be reserved for our donation, to be conferred on a suitable person, decreeing null and void anything attempted against our mandate, we command that, notwithstanding any letters obtained from us on this matter, unless the dean and chapter of the said church of Saint-Marcel receive him or his procurator as a canon and brother within a month after receiving these presents, and the same bishop freely confer the prebend, if any is vacant there, or otherwise at the first opportunity, to the aforementioned cleric, you shall peremptorily cite them on our behalf to appear before us within two months after your summons, with all their documents and reasons, personally or through a suitable procurator, setting aside all excuses and delays, to do and receive what the order of law dictates. If not all of you, etc. Given at Anagni, the 7th ides of February, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Honorius III archidiacono Lexoviensi, cantori Sancti Audomari Morinensis diocesis, et magistro R., canonico Cenomanensi, Parisius commoranti mandat ut, nisi decanus et capitulum ecclesiae Sancti Marcelli clericum W. in canonicum et in fratrem infra mensem receperint, et episcopus Parisiensem prebendam vacaturam clerico liberaliter contulerit, eos citent ut coram papa compareant pro negotii prosecutione. Datum Anagnie, VII idus februarii, anno sexto.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble man, the Count of Montfort, Constable of France. From the gift of grace divinely inspired within you, as reported by the bearer of the present letter, we have previously learned that, considering you are created and redeemed by the King of Kings, Lord Jesus Christ, you have resolved to express the purity of faith with which you shine and to offer grateful service to Him by setting out with a fitting company of certain nobles, accompanied by an angel from heaven, to the Land consecrated by His glorious blood. From this, indeed, because much utility could come to the aforementioned Land, we have conceived great joy and we rejoice with you, because you strive to attain the delights of eternal life, not without reason. For what, O prudent man, if you wish to reconsider the plans of your youth, can you esteem more holy or more healthful than this? Do you not prove yourself a lover of your God through the exhibition of this work? Do you not in this endeavor to make yourself a co-heir of the heavenly kingdom, since it has been decreed by the providence of the Redeemer that His ministers should be received into the heavenly court, which He, the rewarder of the faithful, inhabits and illuminates? Do you not, by the example of this devotion, excite many to salvation, and from this gain the special favor of the Apostolic See for yourself? Moreover, these and other things, through such preeminence of probity, blessed son, you will achieve, as you can know better through the revelation of your conscience than can be taught by these presents. Therefore, arise to works of virtue with vigor! Arise in the name of Christ, teaching the military service of the true homeland to those who serve the deceitful world, so that, having a numerous multitude of warriors, you who have conceived the affair of holiness and glory may bear the fruit of life and salvation for both yourself and your neighbors. But because what is conceived often turns into an abortion if not firmly held, we earnestly ask, advise, and exhort your nobility, imposing upon you for the remission of your sins, that under the happy desire which the Lord of graces has inspired in your sincerity, until we communicate our pleasure regarding this to you, you maintain a firm spirit and indefatigable mind, striving nonetheless to render your companions, whom you made participants of your vow, firm in purpose, especially since with God as author, we intend to provide in such a way that it will redound to the praise of the divine name, the advancement of the Holy Land, and the salvation of your soul. Furthermore, that our spirit may more fully rejoice in God, we wish to be informed of the names of the barons whom you have laudably bound to this work of salvation, by your letters and theirs. Given at Anagni, on the calends of February, in the sixth year.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX nobili viro, comiti Montis Fortis, constabulario Franciae, gratias agit quod, divinitus inspiratus, decreverit cum nobilium comitiva in Terram Sanctam proficisci, hortatur ut propositum firmiter teneat ad salutem animae, et nomina baronum sibi adhaerentium per litteras aperiri petit. Datum Anagnie, kalendis februarii, anno sexto.

Translation to English:

To the same. Beloved sons, F. the archdeacon, Master John the canon, and Julian the portionary of the church of León, on behalf of the beloved son M. Alfonsi the archdeacon, who is acting on behalf of the elected of that church, have taken care to present themselves and their side in our and our brothers’ presence, stating that, upon the death of the bishop of León of good memory, the chapter of the said church, having called those who could conveniently and ought by law to be called, when their votes seemed to be divided into two parts, unanimously granted the power to provide them with a pastor from within the church to the dean, M. the prior, F. Garsie, and Lupo, the archdeacons of León, and Master P., the archdeacon of Oviedo, because no one could be found within the church who did not favor one of the parties; and that what would be done by all or the majority of them would be held firm and ratified by the chapter, as contained in the letters made about this; and that, after discussion about the election and multiple nominations and comparisons of persons, the said dean and prior conferred their votes for the beloved son, the dean of Compostela, while L. and F., the archdeacons, cast their votes for the said M. the archdeacon; the said Ovetensis archdeacon agreed with them and, in his and their name, with the invocation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, elected the same M. Alfonsi as the bishop and pastor of the church of León, whose election the archdeacon, canon, and portionary aforementioned requested to be confirmed by the apostolic authority, notwithstanding the malicious contradiction of the opposing party. The aforesaid dean of León, on his own behalf, and Johannes Sebastiani and G. Roderici, the procurators of the opposing party, claimed against it that in the election or nomination of the said M. Alfonsi, the form of the compromise was not observed, because, although it was committed to five, only one, namely P., the archdeacon of Oviedo, without the assent of the others, broke out with these words: because I find the number and authority for M. Alfonsi, I name, elect, and give him as the pastor of the aforesaid church. They also added that after a legitimate appeal had been made to us, and before the said M. consented to the election, the election thus attempted was solemnized, and he who spoke the prayer over the elected was bound by the bond of excommunication, knowing it, and both the elected and the Oviedo archdeacon were, at the time of the election, suspended from the execution of their office, and the same archdeacon, who had pronounced the election, was outside the election. They also assert that the elected is a transgressor of the general council because of the embroidered cope, saddle, bridle, golden breastplate, and spurs, which he presumed to use against the constitution of the said council, which our venerable brother, the bishop of Sabina, expressly ordered to be observed under the penalty of suspension, while he was fulfilling the office of legation in those parts. And when he swore to keep the constitutions made by P., the bishop of Albano of good memory, in the church of León, and confirmed by the Apostolic See, which the said Sabina bishop later renewed, because he neither kept nor keeps them, and accepted the bishopric in contradiction, which he swore he would not do, they propose that he incurred perjury. Moreover, as they assert, having been an archdeacon for sixteen years, he never proposed, nor does he know how to propose the word of God in the church, being devoid of theological knowledge, and having little knowledge of law. He is also said to be remiss in dispensing justice to his subjects, and hardly or never hears divine offices even in his own house, nor does he attend matins on the feast of the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord, and when he rises from the bed of illness, he does not occupy himself with reading the canons or divine page, but rather with hunting vanities. Due to an incurable disease with which he suffers and significant loss of sight, they assert him to be less fit for the burden of pontifical governance. Wherefore, since a proceeding of this kind ought not to be tolerated due to both the fault of the election and of the person, they earnestly request that what has been presumed in this regard be annulled by our authority or declared utterly null and void. But since we are not informed about the foregoing, with the assent of the procurators of both sides, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, having called those who should be called and having heard what the parties have proposed, you remit the matter to us

Translation to English:

To L., the illustrious King of the Franks. Would that, dearest son, as we wish, from the prime of your youth you accustom yourself to the fear of the divine name and love, and persist continually therein, so that by serving Him whom to serve is to reign, you may truly reign, and after the inevitable end of this present life, you may exchange the temporal kingdom for an eternal one with a happy exchange. It is said of you, as of your ancestors of clear memory, that you are the most Christian among Christian princes, you may never be moved by any impulse from the devotion of the Church, your mother, but that you, with a pious purpose of devotion, may venerate her who loves and honors you with sincere affection of heart, so that beyond the praise of men you may obtain eternal reward! Indeed, we have received the grave complaint of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Rouen, that, although in spiritual and temporal matters he has no judge after God except us, concerning the ancient liberty of the Church of Rouen and the custom observed until now, you, led and, would that you were not seduced by certain counsels, contrary to the custom of your forebears, who always revered the churches and ecclesiastical men with a pious and prompt affection, summoned him to your presence and wished to induce him to answer under your examination for having pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon certain persons and on certain other articles; because he, fearing not only danger to his right but also subversion of ecclesiastical liberty, refused to do this, submitting himself and the goods of his church to the protection of the Apostolic See, you, moved gravely against him, have despoiled him of houses, villages, lands, revenues, and possessions pertaining to his church, causing them to be detained by your ministers: in which we grieve and fear for you so much, as our special son of the Church, as we embrace your person with the arms of sincerity more specially among the other Christian princes, since the kingdom of the Franks, blessed by God, has always remained in devotion to the Apostolic See, and, as we believe, shall never depart from it at any time. We therefore admonish your royal highness, we beseech and implore you in the Lord Jesus Christ, that you may raise the eyes of your mind to Him who is King of kings and Lord of lords, and considering that devotion which your forebears had towards God and the Church, you may so correct and amend all the aforementioned matters that it may be meritorious for you before God, glorious before men, and from this, He who has exalted you above other kings may confer upon you fuller grace in the present and more abundant glory in the future. However, if your royal excellence claims to have any right in the aforesaid matters against the same archbishop, we will ensure that the fullness of justice is shown to him. And although we wish, as much as we can with God, to defer to your royal sublimity, yet because it is not to be deferred to man against God, nor is it expedient for your salvation that it be deferred to you in such matters, we give a mandate with our letters to our venerable brothers, the Bishops of Paris and Senlis, and to our beloved son John of Montmirail, Archdeacon of Paris, to compel your ministers, who are the detainers of these things, to make full restitution to the same archbishop by ecclesiastical censure, with an admonition given beforehand, removing the appeal, and subjecting the castles, towns, and villages pertaining to your special domain, which you hold in the province of Rouen, to ecclesiastical interdict. Given at Anagni, 3rd day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth year. Written on this matter in the same manner to the Bishops of Paris and Senlis, and to John of Montmirail, Archdeacon of Paris, that they may admonish and induce the same king effectively to this end.

REGESTO:

Gregorius IX illustri regi Francorum L. mandat ut, correctis et emendatis omnibus, quae adversus libertatem ecclesiae Rothomagensis fecerit, plenam restitutionem faciat, subjiciens castra, burgos, et villas ad speciale demanium spectantia interdicto ecclesiastico, si in premissis adversus archiepiscopum jura se habere proponit. Dat. Anagnie, III kalendas decembris, anno sexto.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Mainz. The letters presented to us by your fraternity conveyed that, when previously, through the suggestion of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Halberstadt, to whom we had entrusted the inquiry of the Monastery of Lorsch, it was understood that the same monastery, which used to flourish in contemplation and thrive in the abundance of resources, had so deteriorated in both aspects due to the malice of its inhabitants, that there was no hope it could be reformed to its former order. We had given you a mandate through our letters, that you, personally visiting the aforementioned monastery, should plant the Cistercian order there, provided that if you found any monks of this community ignited by the love of the Cistercian religion, you might retain them there, as long as no unfavorable opinion about them easily arose among the good and virtuous. Others were to be so carefully assigned across various places of their order in your diocese, to prevent a diseased sheep from contaminating the flock, but rather to bring back the lost to the fold. You, diligently attending to the ordination of said monastery, in order to effectively complete this according to the contents of our letters, took care to summon our beloved sons, the abbots of Eberbach, of Maulbronn, of Bronnbach, and of Schönau, of the Cistercian order, and certain brothers of the Dominicans and Franciscans, as well as other discreet and God-fearing men from the dioceses of Mainz and Worms, before whom and also in the presence of the convent of the aforementioned place, you had the series of our mandate read. However, when the brothers of the same monastery were asked if any of them were inspired by the love of the Cistercian order to serve the Lord there under its habit, they neither wished to do so, nor allowed themselves to be placed by you, according to our mandate, in the more prominent monasteries of their order established in your diocese. Instead, heedless of the sentence of excommunication which, by apostolic authority, you had pronounced against the rebellious, except for a few, they dispersed to various places, forgetful of their salvation and profession. You, by the counsel of the said abbots and other wise men, took care to place there many monks and converts of the Cistercian order, who would celebrate the divine office and reserve books and other things, though few, for the succeeding convent. You also directed your letters through the same abbots to the general chapter of the Cistercians, that they might send a convent to the aforementioned monastery. But the said chapter, since no authentic copy of our mandate was provided by them, although the same abbots were ready to testify that they had seen the authentic, did not proceed in this matter. However, they sent three abbots to inspect our authentic document and to consider the place and all its circumstances. Upon inspecting the lands, possessions, and other goods of the aforementioned monastery, they found them, in their judgment, sufficiently ample for a convent. Therefore, you requested from us that, since if the completion of this business should be postponed until the next general Cistercian chapter, according to their constitution, the aforementioned monastery might incur irreparable damage, we would deign to provide for these matters through the benevolence of the Apostolic See. Therefore, not wishing that the reformation of the aforementioned monastery might in any way be hindered by such occasion, we command, with full confidence in your fraternity, that if it is so, you proceed to the ordination of the said monastery according to the form given to you, with some religious God-fearing and discreet men joined to you, removing any impediment of delay. Those who oppose, etc. Given at Anagni, on the 16th day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa auctor est archiepiscopo Maguntino; committit ei ordinationem monasterii Laurissensis, quod per malitiam collapsum erat, cum ordine Cisterciensi reformandum, auctoritate litterarum datarum. Data Anagnie, XVI kalendas martii, anno sexto.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Arras. Our beloved son, Henry, a poor cleric, presented himself before us and reported that, having previously obtained various admonitory, preceptive, and executive letters addressed to different individuals from the Apostolic See at different times, he had canonically acquired a prebend in the Church of Saint Servatius of Maastricht, within the diocese of Liège, by apostolic mandate. He possessed it peacefully for some time, read and sang as a canon in said church, and made his personal residence therein. However, our beloved son, the nobleman H., the son of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, ever august, King of Jerusalem and Sicily, conferred the said prebend on G., a boy, wrongfully, and to the prejudice and detriment of Henry. Although T., a canon of Maastricht, the guardian of this boy, and his supporters, were bound by excommunication by our beloved son, the Archdeacon of Cambrai and his colleagues, by apostolic authority, for molesting Henry regarding this prebend, they nevertheless obtained letters addressed to the Provost of Werden and his co-judges, associates of the Provost of Maastricht, who, as it is said, procured all this on behalf of the boy, from Pope Honorius, our predecessor of blessed memory. And although these judges summoned Henry when the matter was still unresolved, after the death of the mandator, without specifying the place, since Henry could not attend their presence, they, considering Henry contumacious at their own discretion, although they had no jurisdiction over him, since the mandate expired with the death of the mandator, unjustly deprived him of the possession of the said prebend. After diverse commissions on this matter to various judges were obtained from us, and various processes were held through them, we first committed the case to the now deceased Bishop of Arras, your predecessor, and then to you, with a specific form established. Your predecessor and you, proceeding in the same matter, induced Henry, first for the sake of preserving the matter, and then into true possession of the said prebend, and decreed a sentence of excommunication against G. and the chapter of Maastricht, who refused to admit Henry to the said prebend, as contained in your letters shown to us. The said chapter, alleging that your predecessor had rendered an unjust definitive sentence against them regarding a certain prebend, which Henry claimed to have obtained in their church, and the fruits of the said prebend, from which they appealed to our audience, obtained from us letters addressed to the Dean and P., a canon of Nivelles, concerning their appeal. And since they did not wish to relax the sentence of excommunication pronounced by you and your predecessor by our authority against the said chapter by the authority of these letters, appealing to our audience and alleging the royal mandate as the reason for their noncompliance, they not only opposed admitting him but, without obtaining the benefit of absolution, did not fear, with damnable audacity, to celebrate divine services, or rather to profane them, in their peril of souls, to the contempt of the Apostolic See, grave scandal to others, and significant prejudice to the aforementioned cleric, who is said to have labored eight times before the Apostolic See for this prebend. Therefore, compassionating his labors and expenses and not wishing to leave such proud malice and malicious pride of the said chapter unpunished, lest, if not repressed, it should pass into abuse to others, and if they are not answered according to their foolishness, they may regard it as wisdom, we command you by apostolic writs to, if this is so, make Henry enjoy the peaceful possession of the said prebend, compel the chapter to compensate him for damages and expenses incurred due to their rebellion and for the fruits received from the said prebend from the time he was deprived of it by their fault, through the withholding of their revenues, setting aside any impediment of appeal, and proceed against G. concerning what he has received from the said prebend and for damages and expenses incurred by Henry due to his vexation, as shall be just, invoking the aid of the secular arm if necessary. As for the fact that the excommunicated celebrated divine services, inflict canonical penalties upon them. Suppressing contradictors, etc., as far as necessary. Fulfill our command in such a way that the aforementioned cleric is not compelled to labor to us further due to your failure. No letters standing in the way, etc. Given at Anagni, on the nones of October, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Gregorius IX episcopo Atrebatensi mandat quatenus Henricum clericum pacifica possessione prebendae in ecclesia Sancti Servatii Trajectensis gaudere faciat, capitulo Trajectensi ad restitutionem dam

**Translation to English:**

To the prior of Camaldoli. As we have learned, the monastery of Monte Cristo, in the diocese of Massa Marittima, which is said to belong directly to the Roman Church in both spiritual and temporal matters, has so collapsed due to the wickedness of its inhabitants that there is no hope for it to rise again in its order. Such a clamor has reached the clergy and people about their nefarious acts that all desire to remove them from there, as if they were lepers and unclean. Recently, they compelled our beloved son C., the abbot of the same monastery, who was trying to lead them to regular observance, to yield through defamation, starvation, and other bodily tortures. And although we decided to entrust the visitation and reformation of this monastery to our beloved sons, the abbot of San Paolo a Ripa d'Arno in Pisa and the prior of San Donato in Lucca, no process, as we have heard, has been undertaken by them. Therefore, we were humbly petitioned that, since it is believed that the monastery could be reformed by the brothers of the Camaldolese order, we might cause this order to be introduced into the said monastery once the current inhabitants are removed. Therefore, we have strictly commanded our beloved son, the elected bishop of Massa Marittima, that, after first restoring the aforementioned abbot to the said monastery, notwithstanding this resistance, and placing the monks and lay brothers of the same monastery who are unwilling to adopt the Camaldolese order into other monasteries of their order by our authority, he is to introduce the Camaldolese order into the aforementioned monastery, safeguarding the rights of anyone in things that do not contravene the statutes of this order, calling upon the aid of secular power if necessary. As for those who oppose, etc. But when the convent of the same monastery, through its own procurator, later offered to adopt whichever order we preferred, we decreed that the Camaldolese order be firmly and perpetually observed in the same monastery. To you and your successors, we fully grant perpetual power to correct and reform, institute and remove, both in the head and in the members, in the same monastery. Therefore, we strictly command you by apostolic writings that, upon receiving these presents, you personally go to the monastery, receive it with its obediences and appurtenances, and strive to incorporate it into the aforesaid order, correcting and reforming there, both in the head and in the members, what you know to need the office of correction and reformation, according to the statutes of the same order. If any of the monks or lay brothers of the aforementioned monastery might wish to adopt the said order, do not delay to place them in other monasteries of your order. Those who oppose, etc. Given at Rieti, 5 days before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Papa Honorius III priori Camaldulensi mandat ut, monachos et conversos monasterii Montis Christi, Massanfel dioecesis, qui ordinem Camaldulensem assumere nolunt, in aliis sui ordinis monasteriis collocet atque ordinem Camaldulensem in monasterio introducat. Eidem priori plenam concedit potestatem corrigendi et reformandi, instituendi et destituendi, tam in capite quam in membris. Dat. Reate, V kalendas maii, anno sexto pontificatus.

Translation:
To the masters Hemericus, archdeacon of Paris, Wernachus of Terouanne, and Bartholomew of Mouci, canons of Chartres, residing in Paris. A beloved son, Master Johannes de Templo, official of Laon and procurator of our venerable brother, the bishop of Laon, has presented before us that the chapter of Laon claims to have an indult from the Apostolic See, allowing them to promulgate ecclesiastical sentences against their malefactors, who seize their common goods, according to ancient custom, whether the bishop is present or absent, and that, when the perpetrators make satisfaction, they can receive and settle the redress of excesses, without the bishop and his ministers. However, they misuse this indult not only against laymen who are notorious invaders of their common goods but also extend it to others, including the choir of the church of Laon, other clerics, abbots, priors, chapters, and convents, as well as communities, without seizure of common goods, inflicting various grievances on them under this pretext. They further contend, through such abuse, to usurp the jurisdiction of the bishop himself; and to cover their malice with a veneer, they endeavor to defend this excessive presumption by custom, which should rather be called corruption, asserting that the bishop is bound to observe the said privileges and customs by an oath, although he did not intend to swear to uphold abuses. They presume to draw all causes that either concern all universally, or any one of them specifically, or a servant, man, or guest of a canon for whatever reason, or which they claim to concern them, to their chapter's judgment by the pretext of the aforementioned privilege and custom, proceeding as judges and plaintiffs when they should not, issuing citations, setting the day for the parties, admitting witnesses unreasonably without the contest of suit, proceeding to definitive sentences, and interdicting towns and castles, as well as suspending and excommunicating persons summoned to their judgment, as said, nor do they wish to revoke such processes unless given money for amendment or punishing opponents in person. They are not afraid to pass judgment on the bishop's ministers and men; for they have excommunicated some of the bishop's bailiffs, because they set boundaries on certain land, albeit by the bishop's command; and on the viscount of Clacy, because he arrested certain men, again by the bishop's command; and on another bailiff of the bishop, who forbade the bishop's men residing in their village from going to the market at Laon; and on the said Master Johannes, because he did not release the sentences of excommunication and suspension, issued against the brothers of the House of God of Laon, as justice demanded, at their admonition, and because he did not revoke the mandate made for excommunicating and suspending the dean and chapter due to their faults, as they claimed he had excommunicated the said dean, the archdeacon of Silvanectensis, and Master W., a canon of Laon. Therefore, they promulgated various sentences of excommunication by authority of the said indult and custom, abusing the indult in many ways. Thus, since one deserves to lose a privilege if they abuse the power granted to them, the aforementioned procurator humbly requested that the Apostolic See provide for the abuse of the privilege and all documents by which they claim to have jurisdiction, and that the bishop be competently compensated for the injuries inflicted upon him in this matter, and that the chapters by which they presume to usurp such rights and the words of the privileges be declared by the Church. Therefore, we command that, after summoning the parties and hearing what both sides have to propose regarding the abuse of the said privilege and documents and the aforementioned custom, you are to procure for us, sufficiently instructed, the cause at our presence by the feast of All Saints next, along with the tenor of the entire mentioned privilege approved by the parties, sealed with your seals, and order the parties to present themselves before us at the same time, by themselves or by suitable procurators, to receive just judgment from the Lord. Witnesses, etc. If not all, etc. Given at Anagni, on the 12th day before the calends of January, in the first year of our pontificate.

Regesto:
Gregorius IX magistris Hemerico archidiacono Parisiensi, Wernacio Tervisino, et Bartholomeo de Mouci, Carnotensi canonicis, mandat ut causam inter episcopum Laudunensem et capitulum super abusu privilegii et jurisdictionis ad Sedem Apostolicam mittant, instructam. Dat. Anagnie, XII kalendas januarii, anno primo pontificatus.

**Translation to English:**

To the prior of Valle Scolarum, in the diocese of Langres, master W., archdeacon, and H., canon of Langres. G. and N., monks of the monastery of Saint Symphorian of Metz, have indicated to us that, having understood that the abbot of their monastery, not having professed regular observances, had recklessly sought to intrude himself into the abbacy, and that he was squandering its goods, we had previously written, from our office, to our beloved sons, master J., archdeacon, the dean, and the cantor of Châlons, to diligently inquire into these and other matters, both concerning the head and members, which needed inquiry, and to establish what was canonical. However, the same abbot, maliciously proposing that the place to which the inquisitors were bringing him was not safe, to escape canonical discipline, as if guilty, appealed to us in a deceitful manner. And when his petition, read before us, contained that he had been compelled to appeal for the aforementioned reason, we wrote again to the said inquisitors to assign a safe place to the said abbot and to proceed in the matter according to the contents of the previous letters; nevertheless, we enjoin you, with the consent of the procurators of the same abbot and the monks who are pursuing this matter, that, if the inquisitors presume otherwise, you restore to due order whatever you find to have been wrongfully attempted after the appeal was made to us, proceeding in the same matter according to the form given to them. But the said abbot, maliciously suppressing the letters obtained on this matter, procured other letters concerning his appeal, in common form, to the abbot and prior of the monastery of Boson’s Ville, in the diocese of Metz, so that after such evasions of cavils, he might prevail in his malice. Therefore, we command that if this is so, strictly forbid the said abbot and prior from proceeding under the pretext of those letters, and restore to due order if anything has been recklessly attempted by them, and send the parties back to the examination of the aforementioned inquisitors so that either by them or by you the matter may proceed, according to the content of the letters directed to you and them. If not all of you can etc. Given at Anagni, 9th Kalends of March, in the [13th] year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Honorius III priori Vallis Scolarum, magistro W., archidiacono, et H., canonico Lingonensibus mandat ut, abbate Sancti Simphoriani Metensis mala fide appellationem ad . abbatem et .. priorem monasterii Bosonis Ville obtinente, si secus inquisitores Cathalaunenses caverint, in statum debitum revocent quidquid temere fuerit attentatum et partes ad examen inquisitorum remittant; inhibendo abbati et priori Metensis diocesis ne procedant. Dat. Anagnie, VIIII kalendas martii, anno XIII.
